REPORT
INTRODUCTION
Ever since the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) came into existence on August 3, 1954, it has
been engaged in advancing peaceful uses of nuclear technology across India. Successfully completing
the six decades of its existence, the department has been applying radiation technologies in the domains
that matter most to the common man: agriculture, health care, industry and basic research. The current
mandate of the Department, on which its programmes are based, extends to:-
• Increasing share of nuclear power through deployment of indigenous and other proven
technologies, along with development of fast breeder reactors and thorium reactors with
associated fuel cycle facilities;
• Building and operation of research reactors for production of radioisotopes and carrying out
radiation technology applications in the field of medicine, agriculture and industry;
• Developing advanced technologies such as accelerators, lasers, supercomputers, advanced
materials and instrumentation, and encouraging transfer of technology to industry.
• Support to basic research in nuclear energy and related frontier areas of science; interaction
with universities and academic institutions; Support to research and development projects
having a bearing in DAE's programmes, and international cooperation in related advanced areas
of research; and
• Contribution to national security.
2. MAJOR PROGRAMMES
2.1. The vision of the DAE is to empower India through technology, creation of more wealth and
improving standard of living of its citizens. To realise its vision, the Department has been engaged in the
design, construction and operation of nuclear power/research reactors and the associated nuclear fuel
cycle technologies across the country. Over the years, the Department has been able to establish a
network of institutions engaged in R&D as well as industrial activities and acquired expertise in all
aspects of the nuclear fuel cycle.
2.2 At present, Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL) is spearheading India's Nuclear
Power Programme with 21 Nuclear Power Reactors in operation, with total installed capacity of 5780
MW at seven locations. Of these reactors, the Kudankulam Nuclear Power Project-1 (KKNPP-1) of 1000
MWe commenced commercial operation from December 31, 2014. The second unit KKNPP-2 is also
in advanced stage of commissioning. First pair of indigenously designed 700 MWe Pressurised Heavy
Water Reactors (PHWRs) at Kakrapar in Gujarat followed by second pair at Rawatbhata in Rajasthan are
under construction. Work on the reactors to be launched in the third stage is being pursued in right
earnest.
2.3 DAE is also developing advanced technologies such as accelerators, lasers, super computers,
advanced materials and instrumentation and encouraging transfer of technology to the industry, which

2
could contribute to the national prosperity. A wide range of technologies have been developed to come
to the present stage of harnessing nuclear energy and efforts are continuing to develop such technologies
further with future requirements in mind. Technologies to be developed for future applications include
those necessary for building accelerator driven sub-critical reactor system (ADS), high temperature
reactor systems and fusion technologies. Several applications of radiation and isotope technologies for
improving the quality of life have been developed and efforts on this front are to be continued.
2.4 The Department is also engaged in the development of radiation technologies and their applications
for better crop varieties, techniques for crop protection, radiation-based post harvest technologies,
techniques for radio diagnosis and radio therapy of diseases particularly cancer, technologies for safe
potable water, better environment and industrial growth.
2.5 DAE contributes to the enrichment of knowledge domain by pursuing basic research in nuclear
energy and related frontier areas of science; interaction with universities and academic institutions;
support to research and development project having a bearing in DAE's programmes, and international
cooperation in related advanced areas of research.
2.6 The Department of Atomic Energy has mastered a host of highly complex technologies particularly
in the field of medical radiology, nuclear agriculture, desalination, food irradiation, radio astronomy,
supercomputing, particle accelerators, plasma and cryogenics. True to the visions of Dr. Homi J. Bhabha
and Jawaharlal Nehru of envisaging the usage of atomic energy to make a difference to the social life
of Indians, the DAE should now strive to scale it up and take it to the next level. The Committee feels
that the share of nuclear power which accounts for only 3.45 per cent of India's total electricity
generation, needs to be increased to the higher proportions.
3. ORGANISATIONS/INSTITUTIONS/CENTRES/PSUS
The DAE, over the years, has established a vast network of institutions and evolved into a broad-
based organisation comprising research centres, industrial units, public sector undertakings and fully
aided autonomous institutions along with service organisations. These organisations are engaged in
research, technology development and commercial operations in the areas of nuclear power and associated
technologies, radiation technologies and their applications, basic research and academic programmes to
support, sustain and carry forward its avowed objectives and activities. So far, it has established 107
installations spread across several States of the country. The organisations/institutions under the ambit
of DAE, category-wise, are as follows:
• Research Centres: Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC)- Mumbai; Indira Gandhi Centre
for Atomic Research (IGCAR)- Kalpakkam; Raja Ramanna Centre for Advanced Technology
(RRCAT)- Indore; Variable Energy Cyclotron Centre (VECC)- Kolkata; and Atomic Minerals
Directorate for Exploration and Research (AMD) - Hyderabad; Global Centre for Nuclear
Energy Partnership (GCNEP), Gurgaon.
• Industrial Organisations: Heavy Water Board (HWB) - Mumbai; Nuclear Fuel Complex (NFC)-
Hyderabad; and Board of Radiation and Isotope Technology (BRIT)-Mumbai.
• Service Organisations: Directorate of Purchase & Stores (DPS)- Mumbai, Directorate of
Construction, Services and Estate Management (DCSEM)- Mumbai; and General Services
Organisation (GSO)- Kalpakkam.

• Public Sector Undertakings: Nuclear Power Corporation of India Ltd. (NPCIL)-Mumbai; Bharatiya
Nabhikiya Vidyut Nigam Ltd. (BHAVINI); Kalpakkam, Tamil Nadu; Uranium Corporation of
India Ltd. (UCIL)- Jaduguda; Indian Rare Earths Ltd. (IREL)-Mumbai; and Electronics

5 comprises of budgetary allocations mainly for NPCIL and the Bharatiya Nabhikiya Vidyut Nigam

Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research for Prototype Fast Breeder Test Reactor.

7.5 Like-wise in the Power Sector under Demand No. 5, the Committee finds that the actual utilisation
of allocated resources was far less than the approved allocation. While in the year 2012-13 and
2013-14, the Budgetary Support allocation under Plan Head was ` 998.27 crore and ` 716.14 crore
respectively, the actual utilisation in the corresponding years stood at ` 571.88 crore and 581.62 crore
respectively.
7.6 It is surprising to note that BHAVINI which is entrusted with the task to plan, execute and operate
an integrated programme of Fast Breeder Reactors - the second stage of the Nuclear Power Programme,
could utilise ` 571.88 crore only as against the approved outlay of ` 998.27 crore under Plan Head in
2012-13, thus leaving ` 426.39 crore underutilised in the year 2012-13. The situation slightly improved
in the year 2013-14 where the Department could utilise ` 581.62 crore as against the approved Plan
outlay of ` 716.14 crores. A comparison of the BE, RE and Actuals of Plan Head the last two years,
i.e., 2012-13, 2013-14 reveals that the Actuals always remain far less than the BE suggesting that BE
allocation does not present a realistic picture of the likely utilisation of allocated resources; although the
Department claims that the approved outlay is likely to be fully utilised by the end of the financial year.
Based on the above inferences, it can be safely concluded that the actual utilisation of budgetary support
under the Plan Head is really low.
7.7 The Committee feels that the budgetary restriction imposed by the Ministry of Finance, as
pointed by the DAE, was not the only reason for reduction in allocation at RE stage in 2012-13,
2013-14 and 2014-15, under-utilisation of outlay by the Department might have also played a role
in reduction at R.E. level.
7.8 The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department needs to improve its capability
to utilise the allocated resources particularly in the Plan Head through strict monitoring at
regular intervals of the physical and financial performance of the projects and obviate the
possibility of any reduction at Revised Estimate Stage. It is felt that considering the strategic
importance of the institutions of the Department of Atomic Energy, financial cuts should be
minimized and should not be insisted upon if strategic programmes were to be delayed as a result
thereof.

10. BHABHA  ATOMIC RESEARCH CENTRE
10.1 Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) is a premier multi-disciplinary and multi-scale activity
R&D organisation which is engaged in pursuing comprehensive research and development programmes
for the ultimate objective of harnessing nuclear energy and its utility for the benefit of the society. With
the mandate that includes almost the entire spectrum of fuel-cycle activities, BARC's activities are
focussed but not confined to the development of futuristic nuclear reactors, fabricating nuclear fuels,
reprocessing of spent fuel, waste management, robotics, super-computers, lasers, accelerators, human
genomes, nano-technology, and super-conductivity. Other activities pursued by BARC include R&D for
application of radiation technologies (non-power application) in the areas of food preservation, radiation

13
mutation breeding of varieties of pulses, groundnuts and other seeds, radio-isotopes for healthcare, and
troubleshooting industries. The Centre continues to render support to national security and self-reliance.
Financial Performance

10.4 Explaining the reasons for increased allocation and additional activities undertaken/proposed by

10.6 So far as BARC's contribution to agriculture is concerned, it may be noted that BARC has developed
42 different varieties of crops including 19 pulses (eight of mung dal, five each of pigeon pea and Urd
dal, and one each of cowpea), 15 of groundnut, three of mustard, two of soybean, rice, jute and

of these varieties are suitable for rice fallow and have contributed significantly to farmers' income.
10.7 Highlighting the major contribution made by the Department to Agriculture in 2014-15, the Department
has informed that with 14.2 per cent breeder seed demand for Trombay Groundnut (TG) varieties, which
satisfy 10 per cent of national seed requirement, this works out to be around 80,000 ha. of the area
brought under TG varieties annually. For the last decade, this area under TG varieties can be translated
to approximately 800,000 ha. With an average productivity of 1,175 kg/ha., annual TG production will
be around 94,000 metric tonnes which is worth ` 360 crore with a current market price of
`38,000/ tonne.

14

of high yielding, short duration and large seed size, resistance against important diseases like powdery

12. VARIABLE ENERGY CYCLOTRON CENTRE (VECC)
12.1 The Variable Energy Cyclotron Centre (VECC) Kolkata is a premier research institute in the country
in nuclear sciences with excellent infrastructure for advanced R&D in the field of accelerator technology.
This Centre indigenously developed the first large accelerator in the country, the room temperature
cyclotron with K= 230 during seventies. It was stated that the Centre is installing a medical Cyclotron
both for research and medical purposes, which will serve as a major research facility for nuclear physics
and related fields.
12.2 VECC has been running a Regional Radiation Medicine Centre at Thakurpukur, which is the only
governmental nuclear medicine centre in the North Eastern region, providing state-of-the art facilities in
nuclear imaging at an affordable cost. The Committee has been given to understand that VECC has
continuously increased its support and involvement at the Regional Radiation Medicine Centre at the Saroj
Gupta Cancer and Research Institute at Thakurpukur which started with providing facilities for
Radioimmunoassay (RIA) tests. There is a shortage of nuclear medicine centres in eastern India. The
few that are there are private commercial organisations where the charges for nuclear imaging are
exorbitant. Thus, the patients from low income groups who need to undergo nuclear imaging come to
the Regional Radiation Medicine Centre which is the only governmental nuclear medicine centre in the
region.
12.3 The Department informed that around 200 patients undergo in-vitro RIA studies every month at the
Saroj Gupta Cancer Centre and Research Institute (SGCCRI). In collaboration with the SGCCRI, a
facility for High Dose Radio-Iodine-131 Therapy of Cancer of Thyroid patients is being operated regularly.

16
This is the only facility of its kind in the State of West Bengal. Around 65 patients of Cancer Thyroid

12.4 The Department has informed that India hosts two Tier-2 centres of the Large Hadron Collider Grid
(LCG) namely Variable Energy Cyclotron Centre (VECC) and Tata Institute of Fundamental Research
(TIFR). VECC is one of the two Tier-2 Centres of the Large Hadron Collider Grid other being the TIFR.
The two Tier-2 centres are performing large part of LHC computing. Additionally, VECC is the nodal
laboratory of the ALICE-India Collaboration, which consists of 13 Institutes and Universities in the
country.
12.5 The Committee notes the help the Centre is providing to people of North Eastern States in
the field of nuclear medicine facilities especially facilities for Radioimmunoassay (RIA) tests,

Hadron Collider and ALICE. The Committee recommends that facilities for treatment of Thyroid

covering the entire requirement in unskilled category is made on the basis of availability of

(ii) Filling of up to 30 per cent of vacancy in semi-skilled and skilled category from the awardees
provided they have the required skill.
(iii) One time grant-in-aid of `50,000/- for the construction of the houses of displaced people is
acquired, in addition to the actual cost of the house.
According to the Department, there are further provisions for project-affected people in R&R
Policy.

14. INDIAN RARE EARTHS LIMITED
14.1 Indian Rare Earths Limited (IREL) is engaged in mining and production of beach sand minerals and
rare earth compounds. Some of the minerals produced by IREL find use in the Nuclear Power Programme
while the others have wide ranging industrial applications. The main minerals separated by IREL from
the beach sands at its three Units at Chavara, Kerala, Manavalakurichi, Tamil Nadu and Chatrapur, Odisha
are ilmenite, rutile, zircon and monazite. IREL also produces uranium, thorium, and rare earth salts.
14.2 IREL was involved in the production of Rare Earth compounds from monazite processing plant at
its unit in Rare Earths Division (RED), Aluva, Kerala from 1952 to 2004. About 1.47 lakh tons of
monazite had been processed by IREL during this period. While deposing before the Committee, the
Secretary, DAE informed that market conditions for RE products are extremely volatile and the domestic
demand for Rare Earth products could never exceed more than 10 per cent of the annual production.
As a result, about 90 percent of the production of IREL has usually been exported.
14.3 Explaining the efforts made by the Department to increase domestic production of rare earth
including monazite and whether there was any proposal to encourage the private Indian companies to
enter the field, the Department informed that in order to take advantage of the current demands of Rare
Earth in the International market, IREL has set up a 10,000 tons per annum monazite processing plant
at its unit in OSCOM, Odisha which will be producing about 11200 tpa of Mixed Rare Earth Chloride
(MRCL). Commissioning of the plant is in progress and IREL was awaiting clearance from AERB for
commercial plant operation. About 50 per cent of MRCL produced will be transported to IREL's plant
at RED, Aluva for production of separated Rare Earth of various purities including very high pure Rare
Earth oxides.
14.4 The Secretary further added that Monazite is an associated mineral found along with other beach
sand minerals. IREL has set up plant facilities for producing about 10,900 tpa of +96 per cent monazite
at its three units located in Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Odisha.
14.5 When asked about the reason behind the Department of Atomic Energy not permitting Indian
domestic companies that have resources and technical knowhow to assist in the exploration of Uranium

19
and other rare earth metals to enter the field, the Secretary informed that as regards Monazite, because
of its association with Thorium and Uranium, the DAE has not permitted to pass the contract to any
other private company. The Indian Rare Earths Limited was able to separate Monazite for the purpose
of separation of thorium. However, he added, there was no proposal to encourage private sector
companies to enter the field of commercial exploitation of Uranium, Thorium, Monazite and other rare
earth metals. Uranium, thorium and monazite are prescribed substances as per the Notification No. SO
61 (E) dated 18.01.2006 issued under the Atomic Energy Act, 1962. Monazite is also an atomic mineral
as per the First Schedule (part- B) of the Mines & Minerals (Development & Regulation) Act 1957.
14.6 The Committee understands that India has second largest Rare Earths reserves after China
and the prices of Rare Earths have increased significantly in the recent past. The Committee
feels that the Department needs to seriously explore the possibilities of increasing the production
of Rare Earths and if possible by involving private sector domestic companies forming joint
ventures with State-run companies for extraction and processing of non-radioactive Rare Earth
minerals and selling the same in international market.
15. INDIA BASED NEUTRINO OBSERV ATORY PROJECT (INO)
15.1 The India-based Neutrino Observatory (INO) Project is a multi-institutional effort aimed at building
a world-class underground laboratory with a rock cover of approx.1200 metres for non-accelerator
based high energy and nuclear physics research in India.
Physical Performance
15.2 As regards budgetary allocation for pre-project activities, it was informed that ` 85.00 Crores have
been allocated as part of the project budget for pre-project activities and according to the Department,
the amount is sufficient to complete the pre-project activities. Informing about the timeframe for the
project, it was stated that the pre-project activities could be completed after getting necessary approvals
in about one-and-a-half-year's time.
15.3 Regarding pre-project activities started for the observatory, it was informed by the Department that
construction of the boundary wall at Madurai as well as the chain link fencing at the INO site have been
completed. Water pipeline has been laid to bring water to the project from the nearby river. Various
detector components to construct the Engineering Module at Madurai have been ordered. The construction
of the road to the INO project site has been taken up by the Tamil Nadu Highways Department. There
is temporary disruption in these activities due to the Orders of the Hon'ble High Court and lack of some
clearances by the Tamil Nadu Government. The pre-project activities can be completed by 31 March,
2016 subject to clearances by the Hon'ble High Court and the Tamil Nadu Government.
15.4 The Committee hopes that all the pre-project activities, construction of the underground
and surface facilities will be completed as per the schedule by 2016 and the Iron Calorimeter
(ICAL) detector will be completely ready in four years.
15.5 The project includes construction of an underground laboratory and associated surface facilities at
Pottipuram in Bodi West hills of Theni District of Tamil Nadu; construction of a Iron Calorimeter (ICAL)
detector for studying neutrinos and setting up of National Centre for High Energy Physics at Madurai,
for the operation and maintenance of the underground laboratory, human resource development and

20
detector R&D along with its applications. The underground laboratory, consisting of a large cavern of
size 132m X 26m X 20m and several smaller caverns, will be accessed by a 2100 m long and 7.5 m
wide tunnel.
15.6 The initial goal of INO is to study neutrinos. The ICAL detector is designed to address some of
the key open problems in a unique way. Over the years, this underground facility is expected to develop
into a full-fledged underground science laboratory for other studies in physics, biology, geology, hydrology
etc. Development of detector technology and its varied applications are an important aspect of the
project.
15.7 In response to the query relating to the likely benefits of INO, it was informed by the Department
that the primary goal of the INO is to study the properties of the fundamental particle called" neutrino"
which is the most exciting area of research in particle physics after the discovery of Higgs Boson. In
the light of Neutrino research having attracted serious attention of the scientific community world over,
the project will have an international standing and will have a good potential in bringing out scientific
findings of very high impact. The project will also lead to Human Resource Development in basic science
research and strong industrial base in detector technology. Science students across the country will have
the opportunity to develop sophisticated detectors and electronics using their own hands.
15.8 Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR), Mumbai is the host institute for INO project. All
INO related activities will be coordinated through the INO centre, which is to be located at Madurai.
This centre will be responsible for the operation and maintenance of the underground laboratory, human
resource development and detector R& D. The construction of the underground and surface facilities
is expected to be completed in four years and the entire ICAL detector will be completed in the next
three years. Preliminary data taking is expected to start in 2020. The budgetary outlay earmarked for this
purpose is ` 1583.05 Crores.
15.9 The Committee takes note of the joint initiative taken by the Department of Atomic Energy
and the Department of Science & Technology, in setting up the India-based Neutrino observatory
for cutting-edge research in Neutrino studies. The Committee recommends that necessary
budgetary provisions should be made for the research facility in particle physics.
15.10 The Committee hopes that observatory in years to come will turn into an observatory of
excellence providing high quality research facility in Neutrino studies.
15.11 Disposal of construction debris of INO has been one of the controversial issues amongst the local
people around Madurai that has drawn attention of the media. When Committee asked about the manner
in which the Department was going to dispose the construction debris without affecting the natural
resources in neighbourhood areas, the Department informed that the tunnel excavation debris are hard
charnockite granite rock pieces which is used in construction. The excavated rock will be the property
of Tamil Nadu Forest Department. The rock debris will be temporarily stored in a storage yard within
the project site. This storage yard will be protected by dry stone masonry wall, all around except for
entry and exit points, to prevent contamination of any nearby water sources. Therefore, it is not likely
to affect the natural resources in neighbourhood areas. The Department also informed that the project
site is at least 2 km away from the nearest village and it has been proposed by the State of Tamil Nadu

21
that the disposal of this material may be entrusted to TAMIN Ltd, Salem and the sale proceed may be
remitted to Tamil Nadu Forest Department.
15.12 Dispelling the doubts about the length of the tunnel that is required for the INO project, the
Department informed that the tunnel is only 1.9 km long. This tunnel will be a horizontal tunnel just like
road tunnels and there is no question of harming the mountain due to the construction of a 2 km long
tunnel. Geo-technical studies were carried out by Geological Survey of India before finalising the details
of the tunnel.
15.13 The Committee, while taking note of the explanation given by the Department on disposal
of construction debris and utility of the ICAL detector, would like to emphasise that grievances
and apprehensions of the local people need to be dispelled. For that purpose, a proper public
outreach programme to educate the local people about potential benefits of Indian-Neutrino
Observatory should be started in local language and through the social media tools.
16. TATA MEMORIAL CENTRE (TMC)
16.1 Tata Memorial Centre is an autonomous body under the Department of Atomic Energy. It comprises
Tata Memorial Hospital and the Advanced Centre for Treatment, Research & Education in Cancer. The
main purpose of the Centre is to render services and carry out research on cancer under its mandate
"Service, Research and Education in Cancer". Diagnosis, treatment and research in Cancer as well as
training and education to provide the highest standard of patient care form the core mandate of TMC.
Tata Memorial Centre has the responsibility to set standards of therapy for treatment modalities for
cancer and a centre to train doctors, scientists and para-medical staff in the field. It has established itself
as an internationally well recognised cancer treatment institution and has a number of national and
international accolades to its credit.
Financial Performance
16.2 As regards budgetary allocation to Tata Memorial Centre, B.E. Plan allocation of ` 315.00 crore to
Tata Memorial Centre was reduced to ` 174.00 crore at R.E. 2014-15 due to pruning of Plan allocation
by Ministry of Finance.
16.3 The Committee, however, finds that this year budgetary allocation for TMC has not been reduced
in comparison to that of the last year. The total allocation, i.e., both Plan and Non-Plan has gone up from
` 525.00 crore in the BE 2014-15 to ` 540.00 crore this year, which is an addition of ` 15.00 crore.
There has been an increase in the Non-Plan allocation which has gone up from ` 210.00 crore in
2014-15 to ` 225.00 crore in 2015-16. The Department has informed that TMC will be utilising Plan
Allocation of ` 315.00 crore mainly for National Facility for Hadron Beam Therapy, establishment of
cancer hospitals at Vizag and in Punjab.
16.4 Reduction of allocation from ````` 525.00 crore at BE stage in 2014-15 to ````` 391.00 crore at RE
for a Centre like TMC is hard to fathom. Therefore, considering the gravity of challenge of
Cancer looming large over the country, the Committee strongly recommends that the Centre
should be allocated adequate grants.

22
16.5 The Committee also recommends to the TMC to ensure that the enhanced allocation is
utilised fully and efficiently in expanding facilities and services, particularly in border districts
and in the far flung area of the country especially in the north-east.
Physical Performance
16.6 The Committee is given to understand that approximately 50,000 new patients register annually;
most of whom are from India and as also from neighbouring countries. There are eleven Disease
Management Groups and approximately 200 patients visit each DMG every day for first consultation/
follow-up. On an average, TMC handles in a year fifty thousand new patients and three lakh fifty
thousand follow-up cases. It has succeeded in developing the capability of saving thousands of lives in
India, and even abroad, at a negligible cost of ` One hundred only. Cancer Research Institute (CRI), the
basic research wing of the Advanced Centre for Treatment, Research and Education in Cancer (ACTREC),
was established in 1952 and is located at Navi Mumbai. It is one of the units of TMC and conducts basic,
community-based and clinically oriented research on multiple facets of cancer. These include research
on cancer of oral cavity, cervix, leukaemia and lymphomas and tobacco related cancers.
16.7 This Cen tre is running several programmes like, mobile cancer screening, TMC - Rural Outreach
Programme, TMC - Urban Outreach Programme, Cancer and public health research, basic and translational
cancer research, National Cancer Grid upgradation for development of apex cancer institute in each zone
of the country for facilitating uniformity in criteria, for prevention, early diagnosis, treatment and follow-
up of patients suffering from Cancer.
16.8 Indigenously manufactured Tele-Cobalt Machine 'Bhabhatron-II' built in cooperation with BARC has
so far treated sixteen thousand patients. TMC contributes to more than sixty per cent of national
oncology human resources in the country. It is also running several programmes to cater to the requirements
of Cancer treatment through outreach programmes, running Mobile Cancer Screening & Urban static
screening Centres, Cancer registries at identified sites, undertaking population based Cancer screening
and epidemiology as preventive oncology, etc. The Committee was informed that to further strengthen
the required infrastructure for Cancer treatment, the Department proposes to establish two new Hospitals/
Centres - one at Vizag, Andhra Pradesh and the other at Chandigarh in Punjab and support Dr. B. Borooah
Cancer Institute, Guwahati, Assam and Tata Medical Centre, Kolkata. Besides, the Department is also
running a National Cancer grid for integration of service, research and education in Cancer.
16.9 The Committee commends the work done by the TMC in the area of Cancer treatment and
Cancer research. However, in view of the prohibitive cost of treatment of cancer for poor and
middle class people, the real challenge for the Centre is to provide/develop affordable treatment
and develop tool/instrument for its early detection and preventive medicine particularly in the
far-flung areas of the North East, bordering and backward districts of the Country. The Centre
should try its level best to live up to the expectations.
16.10 During the discussion, the Committee raised the issue of setting up of Regional Cancer Research
Centres/hospitals in Mizoram, the Gangetic belt and in remote areas including border districts to cater
to the people affected by the disease.
16.11 Apprising the Committee about the progress made in setting up of Cancer research centre for the
whole of North Eastern region, it was informed by the Department that TMC has trained people to run

23
five cancer registries including one at Mizoram and 2 centres in North Eastern region having support
for infrastructure at Guwahati and Silchar. TMC was in the process of finalising Radiotherapy units for
Mizoram. For West Bengal, the House of Tatas had started the state-of-art Cancer Centres at Kolkata.
TMC is instrumental in supplying Human Resources and development of infrastructure.
16.12 The Committee was also informed that gall-bladder cancer is unique to Ganga and Brahmaputra
river basin apart from Mekong River and Chile. As per the preliminary findings those who eat "Liver
fluke" parasite affected roasted fresh water fish, are more prone to getting affected by cancer. Apprising

was informed that TMC was the chief advisor to Hon'ble Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh to plan the
establishment of the Cancer Centres within the State, focussing mainly on oral cancer (Tobacco-related)
and gall-bladder Cancer. TMC is about to complete a study to decipher the positive factor for the cancer
for its prevention.
16.13 The Committee notes the functioning of Tata Memorial Centre National Facility for Hadron
Beam Therapy in Punjab and at Visakhapatnam but establishment of cancer hospital at
Visakhapatnam and in Punjab has not yet taken off the ground. The Committee recommends
for upgradation of facilities of Cancer Research Centres in the Gangetic belt States and North-
Eastern region to be completed as per the target and efforts should be made to develop tertiary-
level cancer care facilities in each State/Region.
16.14 The Department and its institutes/organisations should proactively engage with the State
Governments, stake holders and the farming community with a view to identifying the causes
of cancer in different regions and ways to combat the menace.

December 2014. Target for Kudankulam unit-2 was rescheduled from September 2014 to January

that considering the enormous energy challenge and the grim energy situation of the country,
the Department has to work harder and needs to be fully supported by all concerned in this
regard.

of nuclear reactors and reduce the average construction time taken from seven-eight years to
five years. Currently, India has an installed capacity of 5,780 MWe of nuclear power, including
the 1,000 MW of electricity being generated by recently inducted Unit-I at Kudankulam. The
1,000 mw Unit-II at Kudankulam is also slated to begin power production soon. Five nuclear
reactors with a total capacity of 3,300 mw are under various stages of construction. In addition,
work on 19 new reactors, with a cumulative generation capacity of 17,400 MW, is scheduled to
begin in the next few years. If all these start producing electricity between 2025 and 2027, the

total installed capacity would still come to only 27,840 MW. However, the Integrated Energy
Policy in 2006 had projected a target of 63,000 MW of nuclear energy by 2032. This still leaves

and intensify its efforts to ensure that the proposed nuclear project are completed and commissioned
within the scheduled deadline in order to achieve the target of producing 63.000 MW of electricity
through nuclear energy by 2032.

REPORT
Department of Scientific and Industrial Research is one of the three Departments of the Ministry
of Science & Technology. The mandate of Department of Scientific and Industrial Research includes
promotion of industrial research for indigenous technology promotion, development, utilization and transfer.
1.1 The primary endeavour of DSIR is to promote R&D by the industries; support industrial units to
develop state-of-the-art globally competitive technologies of high commercial potential; catalyze faster
commercialization of laboratory-scale R&D; augment technology transfer capabilities; enhance the share
of technology intensive exports in overall exports; strengthen industrial consultancy and establish a user-
friendly information network to facilitate scientific and industrial research in the country.
1.2 The DSIR has two public sector undertakings viz. National Research Development Corporation
(NRDC) and Central Electronics Ltd. (CEL) and two autonomous organizations viz. Council for Scientific
and Industrial Research (CSIR) and Consultancy Development Centre (CDC). The Department also
provides host facilities and assistance to Asian and Pacific Centre for Transfer of Technology (APCTT)
as the focal point in the country.
1.3 The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technology, Environment
and Forests considered the Demands for Grants (2015-16) of the Department of Scientific and Industrial
Research at its meeting held on 9th April, 2015.

5. AUTONOMOUS INSTITUTIONS
Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR)
5.1 The Council of Scientific & Industrial Research, constituted in 1942 is an autonomous body. The
detailed functions assigned to the Council are as follows:
(i) Promotion, guidance and coordination of scientific and industrial research in India, including
the institution and financing of specific researches;
(ii) Establishment or development and assistance to special institutions or departments of existing
institutions for scientific study of problems affecting particular industries and trade;
(iii) Establishment and award of research studentships and fellowships;
(iv) Utilization of the results of the researches conducted under the auspices of the Council
towards the development of industries in the country and the payment of a share of royalties
arising out of the development of the results of researches to those who are considered as
having contributed towards the pursuits of such researches;
(v) Establishment, maintenance and management of laboratories, workshops, institutes and
organizations to further scientific and industrial research and to utilize and exploit for purposes
of experiment or otherwise any discovery or invention likely to be of use to Indian industries;

8
(vi) Collection and dissemination of information in regard not only to research but also to industrial
matters generally;
(vii) Publication of scientific papers and journals;
(viii) To enter into arrangements with foreign scientific agencies and institutions for exchange of
scientists, study tours, training in specialized areas of science and technology, conducting joint
projects, providing technical assistance in the establishment of scientific institutions and for
other matters consistent with the aims and objectives of the Society;
(ix) To do all other such things as the Society may consider necessary incidental or conducive to
the attainment of the above subjects; etc.
CSIR has been striving to perform these functions in accordance with the priorities laid down in
Five Year Plans and perceived needs of the nation from time to time.
5.2 The Council of Scientific & Industrial Research is known for its cutting edge R&D knowledge base
in diverse S&T areas. Having pan-India presence, CSIR has a dynamic network of 38 national laboratories,
39 outreach centres, 3 Innovation Complexes and 5 units. CSIR's R&D expertise and experience is
embodied in about 4000 active scientists supported by about 7000 scientific and technical personnel.
5.3 CSIR covers a wide spectrum of science and technology from radio and space physics, oceanography,
earth sciences, geophysics, chemicals, drugs, genomics, biotechnology and nanotechnology to mining,
aeronautics, instrumentation, environmental engineering and information technology. It provides significant
technological intervention in many areas with regard to societal efforts which include environment,
health, drinking water, food, housing, energy, leather, farm and non-farm sectors. CSIR is the Nation's
custodian for Measurement standards of Mass, Distance, Time, Temperature, Current etc. CSIR has
created and is the custodian of Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) which is a powerful
weapon against unethical commercial exploitation of Indian traditional knowledge. CSIR maintains Microbial
Type Culture collection (MTCC) and Gene Bank.
5.4 CSIR published 5086 research papers during 2013 with an average impact factor per paper as 2.86
in SCI journals of national and international repute contributing to 8.72 % of Indian R&D literature.
Several research papers were in high impact factor journals like Chemical Reviews (IF 41.298), Lancet
(IF 38.278), Nature (IF 38.597), Science (IF 31.20), Chemical Society Reviews (IF 28.76) etc.
5.5 Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) is implementing following Ten Plan Schemes
to achieve its objectives of 12th Five Year Plan:
(i) National Laboratories;
(ii) National S&T Human Resource Development;
(iii) Intellectual Prope rty & Technology Management;
(iv) R&D Management Support;
(v) New Millennium Indian Technology Leadership Initiative;
(vi) Innovation Complexes;

(vii) CSIR Scheme for Open Innovation;
(viii) CSIR-800;
(ix) CSIR Initiative for Inclusive, Participative, and Collaborative Research & Development; and
(x) National Programme: National Civil Aircraft Development Programme.
Last three Schemes at Serial Numbers (viii), (ix) and (x) have since been merged with National
Laboratories Scheme.

8. Bus mounted Reverse Osmosis (RO) Water Filter
8.1 During the meeting of the Committee held on the 9th April 2015, the representatives of DSIR
informed the Committee about a bus mounted Reverse Osmosis (RO) water filter which houses RO
plant. The Committee desired to know the details of the said RO plant. The Committee was informed
by CSIR that CSIR- Central Salt and Marine Chemicals Research Institute (CSIR-CSMCRI), Bhavnagar
has designed and developed a bus-mounted Reverse Osmosis (RO) water filter which houses RO plant.
The plant runs on auto engine of the bus. It has also facility to install solar cells on the top of the bus.
This RO plant can process the water with salinity ranging from brackish upto sea water. The capacity
of the plant is 3000 Litre Per Hour in case of brackish and 1000 Litre Per Hour for sea water. The bus
also houses training and video facility to create awareness about quality of water. Mobile RO bus was
deployed in areas affected by natural calamities like floods in Bihar, West Bengal, Uttarakhand and Jammu
& Kashmir. Three persons including bus driver are needed to operate the system. The bus, costing
` 65.00 lakh (in 2008) has been modified to install the RO plant, costing ` 30.00 lakh. Along with some
other accessories, the total cost of the bus-mounted RO plant is approximately ` 105.00 lakh. The
Committee desired to know as to how many such units were available with CSIR. In response, the
Committee was informed that there was only one such mobile RO unit.
8.2 The Committee appreciates the bus mounted Reverse Osmosis water filter developed by
CSIR. However, the Committee is appalled to know that instead of commercialising such a path
breaking innovation at least to States/State agencies, at present there is only one such RO unit
with the Department. The Committee is at a loss to understand as to why, in the current climatic
scenario, when natural disasters are on the rise in the country, no thought has been given to
increasing the number of such mobile RO units or the commercialisation of this technology. At
a time when the country is making preparations for meeting the challenges of disasters, the
availability of such RO units has great relevance during disaster times.
8.3 The Committee is of the view that during natural calamities, the mobile RO Unit can be
of immense help in providing clean water to the affected people. These mobile RO units can also
contribute to the quality of life of the people by providing clean drinking water. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the Department, in consultation with National Disaster Management
Authority, Ministry of Home Affairs, should take necessary steps for the commercialisation of
its mobile RO unit so that at least one such unit is available to each and every State/Union
Territory in the country which can be made use of in times of need.

programme are as under:-
(i) To have an integrated approach to the national Human Resource Development for science,
engineering and technology (S&T) in close collaboration with academic institutions;

technology of tomorrow; and

seminars and conferences.

Group of CSIR has programmes to develop and nurture S&T manpower at the national level by awarding
the Junior Research Fellowship (JRF) through National Eligibility Test (NET); JRF-GATE scheme for

10. NATIONAL CIVIL AIRCRAFT DEVELOPMENT PROGRAMME (NCAD)
10.1 National Civil Aircraft Development Programme had been included as a new scheme in Twelfth Five
Year Plan of CSIR with an initial allocation of `10 crores in BE 2012-13. It had been initiated to reduce

15
India's dependence on imports for procurement of civil aircraft and associated services. The project
aimed at building a 90 seater civil aircraft with state-of-the-art techniques developed with CSIR-NAL
collaboration. The Committee was earlier informed by the Department that CSIR-NAL had made an
assessment of the programme by carrying out a Feasibility Study for the development of a 70-90 seater
National Civil Aircraft. The Feasibility Study Report included Market Assessment, Configuration Definition,
Development Strategy, Cost Estimates and the Business Model.
10.2 In 2013, the Committee was informed by the Department that they were unable to initiate the
programme as the nodal agency for the implementation of the programme was yet to be identified.
Similar reply was furnished to the Committee in February, 2015.
10.3 The Committee sought to know from the Department the reasons for not indentifying the nodal
agency for implementation of the programme even after a lapse of more than two years. Further, the
Committee noted that no allocation has been made for the programme in 2015-16. In response, the
Committee was informed by the Department that financial constraints during 2012-13 to 2014-15 led to
reduced allocations to CSIR, due to which the programme could not be approved. Now the programme
was proposed to be initiated in the format of a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) to be set up by Hindustan
Aeronautics Ltd. (HAL), Bengaluru in partnership with CSIR's National Aerospace Laboratories (CSIR-
NAL) and that had been agreed to in-principle by both Hindustan Aeronautics Ltd. and CSIR. However,
that has still not been implemented because all the required administrative approvals are yet to be obtained
and Hindustan Aeronautics Ltd. was doing the needful in this regard.
10.4 The Committee is extremely disappointed to note that a programme of great national
importance such as National Civil Aircraft Development Programme (NCAD) Programme has
made very little, rather no progress, at all during the last three years. The Committee is
constrained to state that although our country has mastered space technology, we are yet to
develop technology for developing a commercial aircraft. The Department has inter alia  indicated
financial constraints for non-approval of the programme during the last three years. The Committee
recommends that the administrative approvals for the fresh initiatives taken in collaboration
with Hindustan Aeronautics Ltd. may be obtained at the earliest so that the actual work on the
programme could be initiated in right earnest. The Committee also recommends that adequate
financial allocations be made for the above programme so that its execution is not delayed any
further. A comprehensive review of the causes of delay of the project needs to be undertaken
and responsibility fixed for the delay alongwith an action plan for successfully implementing the
project within a stated time-frame considering the strategic importance of the project.
11. CSIR-800 SCHEME
11.1 CSIR-800 was initiated as a new scheme during 12th Five Year Plan. The scheme aimed at bringing
in the desired S&T interventions for augmenting the income, removing drudgery and improving the
quality of life of people at the base of the economic pyramid, geographically spread across the country.
The Committee noted that the amount of ` 5.00 crore allocated for the above scheme in BE 2014-15
got reduced to ` 1.00 crore at RE stage and no allocation has been made under this scheme in
2015-16. The Committee desired to know the reasons therefor from the Department. The Committee was
informed that as per the direction of Government of India to rationalize the implementation of schemes,

16
CSIR reviewed the scheme and merged it with 'National Laboratories' scheme. Accordingly, no separate
allocation was made for CSIR-800 scheme in budget allocation of 2015-16.
11.2 Keeping in view the importance of the objectives of CSIR-800 scheme, especially its benefits to the
poor people of the country, the Committee desired to know the achievements of the CSIR-800 scheme
in 2014-15 and details of the programme/activities proposed to be undertaken by CSIR during 2015-16
to fulfill the objective of erstwhile CSIR-800 scheme in the new programme. In response, the Department
intimated that during 2014-15, CSIR continued to provide S&T knowledge base to villages to promote
employment generation and income augmentation. Some of there activities are as under:
(i) CSIR developed KrishiShakti, a small range (11.2 hp) diesel engine tractor for farmers with
small land holdings for effective tilling. The technology has been transferred and manufacturing
has been initiated in West Bengal. The tractor was launched in Delhi on 20th November 2014.
(ii) A food processing unit has been set up at CSIR-Centre for High Altitude Biology (CSIR-
CeHAB) in the remote tribal region of Lahaul and Spiti. A brining unit has been designed and
prototype developed for the preservation of locally and abundantly produced peas and
cauliflowers. The knowhow was showcased at the Tribal Fair at Keylong and training organized
for the benefit of farmers in the area of food and food processing: making novel products
from Buckwheat; and also brining of the peas which is a major crop.
(iii) CSIR introduced aesthetic appeal, standardisation and new ranges of leather products in North
East for higher profits to leather artisans. The handbags and other leather products crafted and
designed with the ethnic designs and materials of the North-East based on Ornaments, Dresses
& Artifacts adorned by tribal folks of the North East India.
(iv) CSIR introduced and commercialized Lilium cultivation in Lahaul and Spiti region of Himachal
Pradesh. CSIR played a catalytic role in the promotion of commercial floriculture in Himachal
Pradesh enabling enhanced income to flower growers of Himachal Pradesh.
(v) CSIR has been contributing in the area of healthcare. Some recently developed technologies/
interventions benefitting the common people include: nonClonableID technology for medical
product authentication; Diagnostic system for affordable, point of need testing to manage HIV
and TB; and eHealth Center (eHC), a platform for the fourth paradigm of science, data-
intensive discovery, while bringing affordable healthcare services to the doorstep of people).
11.3 The Committee was further informed that during 2015-16, CSIR technologies, useful for the
identified communities, will be implemented in a planned manner in partnership with government machineries.
CSIR will be providing its S&T knowledgebase for utilization in rural areas in form of relevant technological
interventions, skill development and up-gradation for targeted people at the base of economic pyramids
so as to promote creation of new micro enterprises through S&T interventions.
11.4 The Committee is at a loss to understand as to why a scheme launched to augment the
incomes and improve the quality of lives of one million rural citizens geographically spread
across the country, was merged with another scheme, the objectives of the new merged scheme
have no direct relation whatsoever with CSIR-800 scheme. The Committee hopes that with the
merger of the CSIR-800 scheme with the National Laboratories scheme, the objectives of the

17
original CSIR-800 scheme will not be lost. The Committee recommends that there should be no
let up in the activities of the Department on this front and adequate financial support should be
provided to the Department for achieving the objectives of the scheme in the new merged
scheme.
12. TREATMENT OF MUNICIPAL, URBAN WASTE etc.
12.1 During the meeting of the Committee held on 9th April 2015, the Committee was informed by the
Department about the CSIR's involvement and contribution in clean Ganga Mission. One of the points
highlighted by the Department was demonstration project on Phytorid Technology for treatment of
sewage to avoid pollution load to River Ganga. It was informed that the project was a single solution
to treat municipal, urban, agricultural and industrial effluents. Further, it was a low cost project with
facility for reuse of treated water.
12.2 The Committee desired to know whether the above project was successful in practical terms and
whether the technology had actually been applied to treat municipal and city waste. In response, the
Committee was informed that extensive research work on the project had been done at National Environment
Engineering Research Institute, Nagpur. In response to a further query as to whether the application of
the technology could be actually seen at the ground level, the DG, CSIR failed to provide a categorical
reply to the Committee.
12.3 The Committee is of the view that treatment of municipal, urban, industrial effluent etc.
is one of the major problems not only of municipal authorities but of Town Planners also, which
is also responsible for the increasing pollution load of our riveres. The Committee recommends
that the Department should take immediate necessary steps to test the Phytorid technology at
the ground level and, if required, further researches on the above technology should be carried
out on urgent basis to make it a successful model in a time bound manner.
13. ROBOTICS TECHNOLOGY
13.1 During its meeting, the Committee desired to know from the Department as to where do we stand
in the field of robotics. The Committee was informed by DG, CSIR that they had two laboratories in
the country, one was Central Mechanical Engineering Research Institute (CMERI), West Bengal which
was working on subsea or ground level robots and other was National Aerospace Laboratory, in Bengaluru
which was working on micro air vehicles.
13.2 The Committee feels that Robotics is the technology of the future as the future management
of human civilisation was going to depend heavily on robotics. Already, in countries like USA and
Japan, robots were being used for treating and taking medical care of the aged people. Compared
to these countries, India was way far behind in this critical field. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Department should make an action plan to make rapid progress in the field
of robotics so as to be able to compete with advanced countries in this field in a given time frame.
The Committee also recommends that required budgetary support should be provided to the
Department to make rapid strides in this field.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS — AT A  GLANCE
FINANCIAL ACHIEVEMENTS OF THE DEPARTMENT
The Committee notes that inspite of utilizing more than 99% of the allocation during
2012-13 and 2013-14, the budgetary allocation of the Department was reduced at RE stage during
the last three financial years. The Committee is of the view that investments in scientific
research are extremely important for the development of the nation and that reduction in
budgetary allocation at RE stage results in delay in implementation of schemes/programmes of
the Department. The Committee, therefore, recommends that since the Department has the
potential of fully utilising its budgetary allocation, reduction in allocation at the RE should not
be resorted to. (Para 2.2)
SCHEMES OF THE DEPARTMENT OF SCIENTIFIC AND INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH
In all the above cited four schemes viz Promoting Innovations in Individuals, Start-ups and
MSMEs, Patent Acquisition and Collaborative Research and Technology Development, Building
Industrial R&D and Common Research Facilities and Access to Knowledge for Technology
Development and Dissemination of the Department, there has been gross underutilisation of
allocated resources. The reasons cited for the same are administrative and in a way were
avoidable. Because of underutilisations, allocation at BE stage for 2015-16 for all the said schemes
was reduced quite drastically. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Department
should strengthen its administrative and monitoring mechanism for utilising the allocated resources
in each quarter. Not utilising the allocated fund during first three quarters of the year and then
using one third allocation during last quarter as an explanation for underutilisation, is untenable.
(Para 3.13)
RESULT FRAMEWORK DOCUMENT (RFD)
The Committee notes the performance of DSIR evaluated by third party under Result
Framework Document (RFD) and finds that performance is declining continuously. From a score
of 96% in 2010-11, it has nosedived to 80% in 2014-15. The Committee strongly disapproves such
a trend. What is more appalling is the excuse of enforcement of model code of conduct in March,
2014 as reasons for under-performance. The Committee understands that model code of conduct
prohibits only new schemes/programmes but it is applicable to ongoing schemes/projects, is a
news to it. (Para 4.6)
In view of the above, the Committee recommends that the Department should find out the
reasons for its continuous decline under RFD and prepare a time bound action plan to improve
its RFD score. (Para 4.7)
INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY AND TECHNOLOGY MANAGEMENT
The Committee observes that the number of patents granted to CSIR during 2014-15 both
in India and abroad has been way behind the target set for grant of patents. CSIR has been
granted only 60 patents as against the target of 150. CSIR has itself admitted that the activities
in the area could not be pursued at the desired level due to paucity of funds. The Committee

BE stage which was reduced to ````` 35 crores at RE. In BE 2015-16, again an amount of ````` 40 crore

Management has remained constant, with little margin to offset even the inflationary cost over
the years. (Para 6.5)
The Committee recommends that increased funds should be provided to CSIR for Intellectual
Property and Technology Management scheme so that fund constraint does not come in the way
of achieving progress in this sector. Since patent filing is one of the major indicators of the
scientific and technological advancements of a country, the Committee also recommends that
CSIR should further intensify and galvanise its efforts and try to improve upon its performance
in terms of fding and grant of patents. (Para 6.6.)
WORLD RANKING OF CSIR
The Committee is extremely disappointed to note that the world ranking of CSIR has dipped
from 73 in 2011 to 84 in 2014. The Asia ranking of CSIR has also gone down from 15 in 2011
to 17 in 2014. Budgetary constraints and inadequate manpower are not potent reasons to justify
the decline of CSIR in world ranking during the last three years. CSIR may be holding No. 1
position in the country but its 17th rank in Asia again is indeed a matter of concern. The
Committee is of the view that CSIR's contribution in the fields of research, innovation and
technology development to improve its world ranking can bring laurels to the country and
therefore, reiterates the recommendation made on this issue in its 244th Report that in order
to fulfil the aspirations of modern India, CSIR should aim to become amongst at least first
10 global organisations in its field and it should strive hard to achieve that ranking within next
5 years. (Para 7.6)

implement the programmes of the Department. He also asked the Secretary to inform the Committee of
the steps taken to acquire a global leadership role in genomes, increasing publications by Indian scholars
in international scientific journals and increasing share of patented technologies. The Chairman also
desired to know whether any projects have been formulated to provide new seismic hazard map which
could be useful for coastal cities and nuclear power plants of the country.
3. The Director-General, CSIR made a power-point presentation on the various aspects of the Demands
for Grants of the Department during 2015-16 and the achievements during 2014-15. It was also informed
that the DSIR had done a lot of work in Swachh Bharat Abhiyan and Make in India programmes of
the Government. The Chairman observed as to how the Department could have achieved a lot in the two
programmes which had started only ten months back. The Director General, CSIR explained that they
had tried to categorise their contributions in these areas and that CSIR had been active in Make in India
since its inception.
4. The Committee was also informed about the Phytorid Technology for treatment of sewage to avoid
pollution load to River Ganga. It was informed that the project was a single solution to treat municipal,
urban, agricultural and industrial effluents. Further, it was a low cost project with facility for reuse of
treated water. The Committee desired to know whether the above project was successful in practical
terms and whether the technology had actually been applied to treat municipal and city waste. In

27
response, the Committee was informed that extensive research work on the project had been done at
National Environment Engineering Research Institute, Nagpur.
5. During the presentation, the representative of DSIR informed the Committee about a bus mounted
Reverse Osmosis (RO) water filter. The Committee desired to know as to how many such units were
available with CSIR. In response, the Committee was informed that there was only one such mobile RO
unit. The Chairman stated that in view of the enormity of the challenges of natural disasters in the
country, the country needed to have more such RO units. He advised the Department to take necessary
steps for the commercialisation of its mobile RO unit so that at least one such unit is available to each
and every State/Union Territory in the country.
6. The Chairman then desired to know about the support the Department was giving for developing
the future of the science and technology in the country. The Committee was informed that the Department
was in the forefront in terms of providing the highly competitive CSIR and UGC-Net Fellowships to pure
sciences, Chemistry, Physics, Mathematics, Biology, Geo-sciences, etc. They also had nearly 2,000 plus
Fellowships from CSIR and an equal number from the UGC. They also had more than 8,500 research
scholars availing CSIR fellowships. Further, they also provided awards for recognizing excellence like
CSIR Young Scientist Award, Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Award and G .N. Ramachandran Gold Medal.
7. The Committee then desired to know as to where the country stood in the field of robotics. The
Committee was informed by DG , CSIR that they had two laboratories in the country, one was Central
Mechanical Engineering Research Institute (CMERI), West Bengal which was working on subsea or
ground level robots and other was National Aerospace Laboratory, Bengaluru which was working on
micro air vehicles. Stating that the future management of human civilization was going to depend a lot
on robotics, the Chairman asked the Department to make an action plan to make rapid progress in the
field of robotics to be able to compete with the advanced countries in this field.
8. The Committee then raised various issues such as process for fabricating photonic crystal fibre;
technologies developed under Joint Technology Agreements; incremental innovations in material sciences,
publications of CSIR etc. The representatives of the Department also replied to some of the queries raised
by the Members. The Chairman then asked the Department to send written replies to all the queries raised
during the meeting to the Secretariat at the earliest.

REPORT
INTRODUCTION
Department of Science and Technology (DST) strives to establish and foster India's leadership and
excellence in the field of science and technology. The DST serves as a robust facilitator and aligns its
initiatives with India's developmental aspirations mainly to help optimise human, infrastructure and
financial resources through appropriate inter and intra institutional mechanisms.
2. DST plays several roles which have evolved over time. DST develops S&T policies, strengthens
human resources and institutional capacities, enables development and deployment of technologies, create
opportunities for societal interventions through S&T establishes and engages in mechanisms of cooperation,
partnerships and alliances. These approaches that reflect its mission ensure a holistic systemic influence,
immediate, medium and long term relevance/gains.
3. The following constitute the mandate of DST:-
• Formulation of policy statements and guidelines on Science and Technology (S&T);
• Promotion of new areas of scientific research;
• Co-ordination of inter-Departmental S&T efforts;
• Support basic and applied research in universities and other institutions;
• International S&T Co-operation;
• Support high quality research in autonomous bodies where specialization ranges from advanced
medical research materials to astronomy;
• Catalysing S&T interaction in societal programmes, and entrepreneurship development;
• Science popularisation, communication and S&T Management Information System;
• Promotion of Commercialisation of indigenous technology;
• Support to technology development programmes, technology information and assessment; and
• Providing services in the areas of:
(i) Surveying and Mapping;
(ii) T echnology Development and Application
4. OBJECTIVES
Main objectives of the Department of Science and Technology are:
(a) Formulation of Policies relating to Science and Technology;
(b) Strengthening basic research and Expanding R&D base-Human capacity;

2
(c) Strengthening Basic research and Expanding R&D base-Institutional Capacity;
(d) Implementing Technology Development Programmes;
(e) Societal interventions of Science and Technology; and
(f) International Science and Technology Cooperation
5. ORGANISATIONAL SETUP
5.1 The Department of Science and Technology is the nodal Department of the Ministry of Science and
Technology. Broadly, the organisational set up of the Department has been divided into Autonomous
Institutes, Scientific Groups, Technology Development Board and Scientific Services besides the
Administration and Integrated Finance divisions. There are 19 Autonomous Institutes and 5 Science/
Engineering Professional bodies which are working in diverse areas for the promotion of Science and
Technology. In addition, one new autonomous body viz. National Centre for Molecular Material Research,
Thiruvanathapuram has been recently set up and National Innovation Foundation, Ahmedabad which was
earlier a 'Corpus Funded' Financial Institute has been taken over by the Department as fully funded
autonomous Research Institute. The Scientific Groups inter-alia consists of the Science and Engineering
Research Council (SERC), National Council for Science and Technology Communication (NSCTC),
National Resources Data Management System (NRDMS), International Division, National Entrepreneurship
Board (NEB), National Science and Technology Management Information System (NSTMIS). The Scientific
Services have two subordinate offices, namely, National Atlas and Thematic Mapping Organisation
(NATMO) and Survey of India (SoI) under their administrative control.
5.2 The detailed budget allocation of the DST for the year 2015-2016 was considered by the Department-
related Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and Forests on the 9th April 2015.

7.2 After examination of B.E. and R.E. allocations vis-a-vis Actuals for the financial year 2013-14 and
2014-15 (up to 28th February 2015) of the Department of Science and Technology, it is found that the
Department had almost fully utilised (> 99%) the allocated funds in the year 2013-14 and 2014-15.
7.3 In the financial year 2012-13, the total B.E. allocation including Plan and Non-Plan was ` 2,882.86
crore and R.E. was ` 2,559.83 crore. In comparison to this, for the year 2014-15, the total BE outlay
of ` 3,544.00 crore for the Department was reduced to ` 2898.00 crore at RE stage.
7.4 In response to the query about the schemes for which budgetary allocation remained underutilized
it was informed that budgetary allocations for the plan schemes like Fund for Inclusive Innovations for
Common Man, National Geographical Information System, Supercomputing Facility and Technical Research
Centres could not be utilised during 2014-15 as necessary approvals for spending the allocations for these
schemes could not be obtained during 2014-15.
7.5 Reduction in these schemes amounted to `212.00 crore during 2014-15. Another `434.00 crore was
reduced at RE stage from other plan schemes of the Department due to financial resource crunch. The
reduction at RE stage was not due to underutilisation of allocations. The Department has informed that
it had utilised more than 50 percent of the allocated amount by September 2014. However, there was
no major impact on the ongoing schemes of the Department due to reduction of the plan allocation at
RE Stage except that some of the projects approved during the current financial year would be provided
with the funds during the financial year 2015-16.
7.6 The Committee finds that though utilisation of allocated resources by the Department
improved considerably in the last three years, the allocation to some of the schemes was reduced
due to delay in seeking administrative approval. The Committee is of the view that grounds cited
by the Department are of routine administrative nature which could have been avoided by the
Department as delay in completion of infrastructure projects leads to time and cost overrun and
affects research and development work. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the loopholes
which led to underutilisation of funds should be plugged and delay in seeking administrative
approval should be avoided, and also responsibility for delay should be fixed.
8. MECHANISM TO MONITOR AND REVIEW THE ONGOING SCHEMES
8.1 The Department informed the Committee that the physical and financial performance of various
schemes is being monitored by various expert groups and committees constituted by the Department.
Feedback mechanisms including stakeholder consultations, wherever necessary, have been put in place
during the implementation of some of the schemes to fine tune the programs. Separate reviews have also
been done during the year for several schemes of the Department. Some of the key activities of the
Department have been included for performance monitoring through Results Framework Document
mechanism. Monitoring of targets and financial progress is also undertaken in the Department at Secretary
level. In the opinion of the Department, these mechanisms have served their purpose well.
8.2 However, the Committee finds that the score of the Department on Result Framework Document
Index for the year 2012-13 is 85.27 out of 100. The Department has submitted Performance Statement
against the targets given in the Result Framework Document for 2013-14 to the Performance Management
Division of the Cabinet Secretariat for final approval. The Department has further informed the High
Power Committee is yet to examine and approve the Performance Statement for 2013-14.

5
8.3 The Committee is of the opinion that a robust monitoring mechanism is essential for
ensuring timely completion of various projects to avoid time and cost overrun and to ensure full
utilisation of the allocated funds. The Committee notes the performance of the Department of
Science & Technology evaluated by third party under Result Framework Document and finds
that there is a considerable scope for improvement in the performance and the Department
needs to further strengthen its monitoring mechanism to make it more robust for timely
completion of projects and optimum utilisation of funds in the year 2015-16.
9. BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2015-16
9.1 The Department has been allocated `3,835.70 crore in the fiscal year 2015-16, an increase of
`291.70 crore compared to the BE allocation in 2014-15. The BE Plan allocation of ` 3,125.00 crore
in 2014-15 has been enhanced to `3,401.50 crore in 2015-16.
9.2 The Department has been allocated B.E. Plan outlay of ` 3,401.50 crore against the projected
demand of ` 4,065.00 crore for the year 2015-16.There is reduction of about 15 percent of the projected
demand. There has been a reduction against the proposed demands in allocation under some of the
programmes/schemes, viz. Research and Development Support, State Science and Technology Programme,
support to Autonomous Institutions and Professional Bodies, Science and Engineering Research Board,
and Alliance and R&D Mission.
9.3 On being asked whether the Department has made demands for additional funds from the Planning
Commission/Ministry of Finance in 2013-14 and 2014-15 and if so, with what results, it was informed
that the Department had raised its concern for additional funds with the Planning Commission in
2013-14 and 2014-15. However, no enhancement in allocations was made.
9.4 When BE Plan Allocation for the Department of Science and Technology which is `3,401.50 crore
is compared with BE Plan allocation for 2014-15 which was ` 3,125 crore, it is observed that it is
11.30 percent higher than the previous year.
9.5 The Non-Plan allocation has been increased from `4,19.00 crore in RE 2014-15 to `434.20 crore
in B.E. 2015-16; thus, showing an increase of `15.20 crore. Explaining the reasons for the increased
allocation for 2015-16 the Department submitted that enhancement was for Salaries which accounts for
80.52 percent of the total Non-Plan allocation.
9.6 The Committee takes strong exception to the fact that despite Department's request for
allocation of more funds, the Ministry of Finance has not paid any heed to the matter in the past
two years. Such constraints only circumscribe the functioning of important projects undertaken
by the Department. The Committee, therefore, recommends that in future the Ministry of
Finance should give a favourable response to the request of the Department.
10. PERFORMANCE OF THE DEPARTMENT
Several New Initiatives have been taken by the Department during last two years, some of the
important ones are as follows:
(i) Innovation in Science Pursuit for Inspired Research (INSPIRE) is national programme to
attract students to the study of science and pursue a career in research. INSPIRE has reached
out to more than 1.5 million students so far.

6
(ii) A new scheme namely Knowledge Involvement in Research Advancement through Nurturing
(KIRAN) has been launched that consolidates all women-centric programmes into a holistic
scheme that (i) promotes gender equality, (ii) empowers women with S&T inputs to develop
and adapt appropriate technology, (iii) enables transfer of proven technologies and demonstration
of live technology models, and (v) supports /encourages women scientists constrained with
a break in their career to return to main stream science.
(iii) India's participation in Thirty Metre Telescope (TMT) Project at Mauna Kea, Hawaii, has been
approved. TMT will be one of the largest optical telescopes in the world based on segmented
mirror technology. The project is jointly funded by DST and DAE and DST is the Lead Agency
for this project. This will be a major international scientific collaboration for Indian institutions.
(iv) A prototype application service has been developed and implemented using the Web Map
Services and Web Feature Services from Surveykshan Geo-portal of Survey of India, Bhuvan
Geo-portal of National Remote Sensing Centre, and the Indian Railways data services from the
India Geo-portal. The application -'Spot your train' - for the running trains of the Northern
Railway has been hosted on the web (from Karnataka Geo-portal) and is useful in providing
the passengers with actual departure and arrival information of the running trains of the
Northern Railway.
(v) A road map has been prepared for setting up of five Technical Research Centres (TRCs) in
the existing autonomous research institutions of DST.
(vi) Under Clean Energy Research Initiative (CERI) Development and Demonstration of Modular
Light Weight Solar Aluminum Tubular Air Heater (SATAH ), Solar Cooling and production of
potable water with two stage silica gel-water adsorption system, and Energy Efficient Community
scale PV powered Reverse Osmosis (RO) Desalination Unit at CSMCRI, Bhavnagar has taken
place.
(vii) Convergent solution for augmentation of water resources in Koraput region of Odisha; Chirawa
block in Rajasthan; and Sabarkantha district in Gujarat were successfully provided. Convergent
solutions in three clusters namely Mamsapuram, Thirupattur and Buja Buja for drinking water
purification and waste water treatment were successfully demonstrated incorporating a unique
self sustainability model and were handed over to the local authorities in Tamil Nadu and
Andhra Pradesh.
(viii) International S&T Cooperation Programme has launched new program on Industrial R&D
with selected partner countries which are high on the innovation index like Canada, Finland,
Germany, Israel, South Korea, Spain, UK and USA. The joint R&D projects implemented
through industry-academia partnerships are applied in nature with the potential towards
commercialisation. In order to engage with neighbouring countries, the India Science Research
Fellowship has been launched for scientists from these countries to undertake R&D work in
India. Similarly, the C.V . Raman Fellowship provides an opportunity to researchers from
African countries to undertake scientific research in Indian institutions. So far, more than 200
Africans from 42 countries have been awarded this Fellowship. While new programs of S&T

7
cooperation have been initiated with Poland, Peru, New Zealand and Sri Lanka, partnerships
have been strengthened with Australia, Canada, Finland, France, Russia, Sweden, UK and
USA.
(ix) Concerted efforts were made by the Department to take forward the activities related to S&T
interventions for societal benefits. In this endeavour, several initiatives having people centered
approach to provide technological solutions at the grassroots level with special schemes for
Rural Areas, Women, Scheduled Caste and Tribals Science Express-Biodiversity Special (SEBS)
was flagged-off from Delhi on 28th July 2014. In the current phase, 28th July 2014 to 06
February 2015, the Science Express has travelled to 57 locations across India. More than 1.30
crore people have visited science express so far including 23 lakh during the ongoing run.
(x) The Nano Mission continued to forge linkages with other Government agencies and industry
organisations in promoting Nano science and technology in the country and also orchestrate
national dialogues on issues which are manifestly multi-agency issues. Efforts for Development
of Standards for Nanotechnology continued in association with National Physical Laboratory,
New Delhi.
11. MEGA FACILITIES FOR BASIC RESEARCH
11.1 The basic research in the country is dependent on mega and capital intensive facilities created by
other countries and this practice has led to asymmetries in credit sharing. Further, Indian expertise to
build advanced scientific instruments and devices does not get fostered outside the strategic areas of
research where technology denial forces prevent the building of capacities. The Department along with
Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) has identified several areas where an effective partnership of the
two departments can bring about an effective capacity building in the academic sector for building mega
facilities for basic research. For the same purpose, a Memorandum of Understanding has been signed
between the Department and the DAE.
11.2 The Mega Facilities for the Basic Research Programme has twin objectives:
(i) to enable Indian scientists to participate in building very large international facilities which are
manifestly multinational efforts and gain access to the same for scientific studies, and
(ii) to create some facilities of international standards in the country. India's participation in the
