12. INDIA-BASED NEUTRINO OBSERV ATORY PROJECT (INO)
12.1 The India-based Neutrino Observatory (INO) Project is a multi-institutional effort aimed at building
a world-class underground laboratory with a rock cover of approximately1200 metres for non-accelerator
based high energy and nuclear physics research in India.
12.2 The project includes construction of an underground laboratory and associated surface facilities at
Pottipuram in Bodi West hills of Theni District of Tamil Nadu; construction of an Iron Calorimeter
(ICAL) detector for studying neutrinos and setting up of National Centre for High Energy Physics at
Madurai for the operation and maintenance of the underground laboratory, human resource development
and detector R&D along with its applications. The underground laboratory, consisting of a large cavern
of size 132m X 26m X 20m and several smaller caverns, will be accessed by a 2100 m long and 7.5
m wide tunnel.
12.3 The initial goal of INO is to study neutrinos. The ICAL detector is designed to address some of
these key open problems in a unique way. Over the years, this underground facility is expected to develop
into a full-fledged underground science laboratory for other studies in physics, biology, geology and
hydrology. Development of detector technology and its varied applications are two of the most important
aspects of the project.
12.4 In response to the query relating to the likely benefits of INO, it was informed by the Department
that the primary goal of the INO is to study the properties of the fundamental particle called" neutrino"
which is the most exciting area of research in particle physics after the discovery of Higgs Boson. In
the light of Neutrino research having attracted serious attention of the scientific community world over,
the project will have an international standing and will have a good potential in bringing out scientific
findings of very high impact. The project will also lead to Human Resource Development in basic science
research and strong industrial base in detector technology. Science students across the country will have
the opportunity to develop sophisticated detectors and electronics using their own hands.
12.5 The Committee takes note of the joint initiative taken by the Departments of Science and
Technology and Atomic Energy in setting up the India-based Neutrino observatory for cutting-
edge research in Neutrino studies. The Committee wishes all the success to "Asia's first state-
of-the-art facility" to provide research facility in particle physics. Furthermore, the Committee
recommends that necessary budgetary provisions should be made available for the observatory.
12.6 The Committee hopes that in the years to come, the observatory will transform into an
Observatory Par Excellence setting international standards and provide high quality research
facility to science students across the country, and help them develop sophisticated detectors and
electronics using their own hands and producing new insights in Neutrino studies.

10
13. THIRTY METER TELESCOPE
13.1 The Thirty Meter Telescope (TMT) is world's largest night time Astronomy Telescope to be set up
in USA by several international partners. TMT will be the world's most advanced and capable ground-
based optical, near-infrared, and mid-infrared observatory. It will integrate the latest innovations in
precisions control, segmented mirror design and adaptive optics.
13.2 Thirty Meter T elescope Project is located at Mauna Kea, Hawaii, the USA. India has become a full
'Member' of the project on 2nd December, 2014.
13.3 The TMT will be constructed at a cost of US$ 1.47 billion (in 2012 Base Year Dollars) by an
international consortium consisting of institutions from the USA, Canada, Japan, India and China. From
the Indian side, this will be a joint project of the Department of Science and Technology (DST) and the
Department of Atomic Energy (DAE). With its contributions, India will be a 10 percent partner in the
project and 70 percent of its contributions will be "in kind". This will translate into 25 to 30 observing
nights on the telescope for Indian scientists per year. Total budgetary allocation to the project will be
` 1299.80 crores from 2014-2023.
13.4 This will enable Indian scientists to access a state-of-the-art telescope to answer some of the most
fundamental questions in modern science. Indian institutions and industry will acquire gaining access to
sophisticated technologies of relevance to the country. India will also become a founding member of an
important international scientific project. This partnership will also enhance India's technological capabilities
in high-technology areas such as primary mirror segment figuring and polishing, mirror support system
and edge sensor assembly and testing, software for observatory controls, data analysis pipelines, and
adaptive optics techniques.
13.5 As regards Indian contribution, the Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA) is leading the Indian effort
in the TMT project. Crucial part of the mirror segment contribution of TMT will be made by the IIA.
13.6 This will be a national project anchored in Bangalore and led by IIA, Aryabhatta Research Institute
of Observational Sciences (ARIES), Nainital and Inter-University Centre for Astronomy and Astrophysics
(IUCAA), Pune. It will leverage the best of science and technology from wherever available in the
country from R&D institutions, higher educational institutions and industry. All interested scientists from
the country will get time on the TMT for their scientific studies on competitive basis.
13.7 The Committee believes that the proposed Thirty Meter Telescope has tremendous potential
to unravel the myriad mysteries of the universe. It is likely to become a tool for the Indian
astronomy in keeping up the level of excellence in research in astronomy and astrophysics of
the country. The Committee hopes that the TMT project would help the country to embark on
world class, international science collaborations and also help develop the required human resources
in the field.
14. NATIONAL SUPERCOMPUTING MISSION
14.1 National Supercomputing Mission is driven by the aim to consolidate and build synergy in various
ongoing efforts in supercomputing across the country.

11
14.2 Some of the mission oriented departments such as Defense and Research Development Organisation
(DRDO), DAE and other few leading academic institutions were involved in the use of supercomputers.
However, in the recent times, many more departments and research laboratories in government, financial
sector, telecom industry, e-governance, UIDAI, education, and intelligence agencies have also come into
the fold of users of supercomputers. Private sectors such as pharmaceutical industry, automotive industry,
online gaming industry, entertainment industry, online services with Indian language contents.
14.3 Supercomputing has potential applications in the fields of climate modeling, weather prediction,
engineering including CFD, CSM, CEM, Agriculture Research and Education, Computational Biology,
Materials & Chemicals., Molecular Dynamics, Atomic energy simulations, Security and defence applications,
financial and Big Data Analytics. Additionally it can also be used in the disaster simulations and management,
discoveries beyond Earth (Astrophysics) and Information Repositories & Government Information Systems.
14.4 The major objectives of the Mission are:-
(i) Make India a world leader in HPC and to enhance the national capability in solving grand
challenge problems of national and global relevance
(ii) Empower scientists & researchers with state-of-the-art compute facilities for their cutting-
edge research in respective Domains
(iii) Reduce redundancies and avoiding duplication of efforts and investments and
(iv) Attain global competitiveness and self-reliance in HPC
14.5 The Mission is partnered by the DST, the Department of Electronics and Information Technology
in consultation with the Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru and Centre for Development of Advance
Computing (C-DAC), Pune. These organisations are preparing the strategies for implementing the
Programme. In view of the inter-ministerial nature of the proposed mission, National Supercomputing
Mission follows six principles namely ONE Mission, ONE Goal, Mission First, Centralised Planning,
Decentralised Implementation, Clear Division of Roles, Responsibilities and Costs, Harmonisation,
Coordination and Sharing; and Federated Governance Structure.
Financial aspects
14.6 Total budget allocated for the Supercomputing Mission is ` 4, 500 crore out of which DST will
be contributing ` 2,740 crore; whereas ` 1,760 Crore will be contributed by DeitY. The project is to
be completed within seven years. Some of the key deliverables of the project are 70+ HPC installations,
HPC Grid, Million-core cloud, development of HPC applications, 20000 HPC-aware manpower, R&D for
next-generation Exa-Scale HPC. The total cost of this seven years mission is ` 4500 crore with following
breakup: In the present situation, the requirement of DST is ` 599.25 crore during the remaining two
years of the XII Plan and the balance of ` 2,140.75 crore to be allocated in the XIII Plan. Similar
requirements for DeitY are ` 387.25 crore during the remaining two years of the XII Plan and the balance
of ` 1,372.75 crore to be allocated in the XIII Plan.
Physical Performance
14.7 The Department submitted that the capability building during the XII and XIII Plan would be
towards solving computational problems that would move the nation up the value chain with higher levels

12
of intellectual and scientific talents. The changing ecosystem in the country as well as in the world
renders this initiative, to build indigenous supercomputers, as an essential area for the country. In spite
of the exponential growth in the computing power, both in terms of available technology and the need
of the nation, the cost of the computing and the network has not grown exponentially. In fact, they have
come down significantly to make supercomputing more affordable today than ever before. During the
X Plan, the peak computing powers were in Teraflop/s range and they have grown to Petaflop/s now
and are likely to reach Exascale by the end of XIII Five Year Plan. Further the advent of accelerators
has enabled large computing power enhancements, for specific applications at very low cost and power.
With advancements in cluster computing and the birth of cloud computing, it has become possible to
build home brew supercomputers by interconnecting off-the-shelf components to yield multi-
Teraflop/s, multi-Terabyte storage and easy to maintain computers. The storage revolution is witnessing
rapid growth than the computing revolution, providing the paradigm shift from computer-centric to data-
centric supercomputing. It is now called as the Fourth Paradigm. With these technological changes,
newer areas of applications of supercomputing such as biology, materials science, finance and data
repositories are coming up in large scale.
14.8 The Department submitted that Government S&T Departments/Agencies such as Council of Scientific
and Industrial Research (CSIR), Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES), and many other institutions under
the Ministries of Science & Technology (MST/DST), Communications & Information Technology
(MCIT) and Human Resource Development (MHRD) have recognised greater need for Supercomputing
facilities.
14.9 The Department further added that the national challenges and global issues such as energy, climate
change, water and terrorism/Homeland Security call for global solutions and facilities that are comparable
to that available elsewhere in the world. Thus, all problems from the research in fundamental sciences
to solutions for an inclusive society need supercomputing.
14.10 The Committee finds that India was a leader in Supercomputing till 2005 but it has now
slipped down in the global ranking to 14th place. The Committee is of the view that boosting
indigenous efforts in Supercomputing capability is in strategic interests of India, more so when
Information Technology capabilities of the country are recognised worldwide. The Committee
hopes that the mission will help India attain leadership and self-reliance in the field of
Supercomputing. The Committee recommends that considering the significance of Supercomputing,
the Department should make every possible effort including establishment of requisite ecosystem
for the success of the Mission to successfully implement the project in a time-bound manner. The
Committee further recommends that the Department must ensure that the allocated outlays for
the scheme are fully utilised.

15

research grants through the extramural funding schemes of various S&T agencies of the
Government of India. Since its inception, 184 Indian origin scientists working abroad have
been offered this "Fellowship". In the last 5 years, total number of 781 scientists applied for
Ramanujan Fellowship 275 selected, 161 accepted and finally 116 scientists were absorbed.
(ii) Ramalingaswami re-entry Fellowship of Department of Biotechnology (DBT) is a targeted
schemes aimed to attract highly skilled researchers (Indian nationals) working overseas by
providing them attractive avenue to pursue their R&D interests in Indian institutions. In the
last 5 years, total numbers of 791 scientists applied for the fellowship, 222 were selected, 119
accepted and finally 61 scientists were absorbed.

19
(iii) Under the Innovation in Science Pursuit for Inspired Research (INSPIRE) Faculty Scheme of
DST, young Indian citizens and people of Indian origin including NRI/PIO status with PhD
(in science, mathematics, engineering, pharmacy, medicine, and agriculture related subjects)
from any recognized university in the world are offered contractual research positions in
Indian Institutions / Universities to carry out independent research and emerge as a leader in
future science & technology. In the last 5 years, total number of 589 scientists applied for
INSPIRE Faculty Award out of them 170 were selected, 116 accepted the proposal and finally
55 scientists were absorbed.
(iv) Four scientists have been supported under National Jawaharlal Nehru Science Fellowship
Programme.
(v) Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) has a scheme to attract Scientists/
Technologists of Indian Origin (STIO) under which they are appointed at an identified CSIR
laboratory so as to nurture a research field in their area of expertise. Total of 667 scientists
have been offered the award letter in the last 5 years, and 396 have accepted the offer. They
are working in cutting edge research areas in various national laboratories and academic
institutions in the country. 232 of these scientists have been absorbed as a faculty or as a
Scientist in our institutions.
18.3 The Committee takes note of the initiatives taken by the Ministry of Science & Technology
that have resulted in the inflow of accomplished researchers back to India. Measures taken by
the three Departments have led to the increasing reversal of flow of researchers. The Committee
recommends that further measures should be taken to retain bright Indian scientists coming
back to India and attract the young talents so that they find it more appealing to stay in India.
For that purpose, the Department should increase the scholarships and stipends provided to
researchers. The Committee also recommends that the research funding and grants should be
linked to the potential and performance of the research undertaken. The research undertaken
should be incentivised, based on its utility and performance.
18.4 The Committee notes with serious concern the decline in the number of research publications
in journals and publications of national and international repute in various areas of scientific
research. The Committee also believes that there is no incentive or concrete action plan to
promote such publications by our scientists and researchers. The Committee is not satisfied with
the policies pursued by the Department to encourage the commercialisation of patents registered
by the innovators. Necessary incentives to researchers/innovators and scientists for the purpose
should be put in place and purposively implemented.
19. INCREASING PRIV ATE SECTOR INVESTMENT IN R & D
19.1 As stated in the 'Research and Development Statistics 2011-12', brought out by DST, the National
expenditure on R&D has been registering a consistent rise in the past few years. India's expenditure on
R&D as percentage of GDP has increased from 0.81 percent in 2004-05 to 0.8 percent in 2009-10. In
absolute terms, the total national R&D expenditure increased by more than 50 percent from ` 24,117.24
crore in 2004-05 to ` 53,014.3 crore in 2009-10, representing a significant increase considering the
overall resources of the country. The Government intends to raise the national R&D expenditure, as

20
percentage of GDP, to 2 percent by the end of XII plan period through various measures including but
not confined to increase in plan allocations for scientific departments, setting up of new institutions for
science education and research, creation of Centres of Excellence and facilities in emerging and frontline
areas in academic and national institutes, induction of new and attractive fellowships, strengthening
infrastructure for Research and Development (R&D), and encouraging public-private R&D partnerships.
Further, setting up of new S&T institutions on the lines of All India Institute of Medical Sciences and
Indian Institute of Technology's have been envisaged in the recent budget for the year 2015-16.
19.2 According to the Department steps are being taken to achieve 2% percent target by the end of the
XII Plan. It was also stated that the Department of Science and Technology (DST) has been consistently
pressing on the need for increasing the allocations for Research and Development with the erstwhile
Planning Commission.
19.3 The percentage share of Private sector in national R&D expenditure has increased from 19.3
percent in 2001-02 to 25.9 percent 2005-06 and further to 28.9 percent in 2009-10. Providing the details
of efforts made by the Department to motivate private sector to increase their share of investment into
the R&D voluntarily in XII Five Year Plan, the Department apprised that it has taken several steps to
encourage research and development with enhanced participation of the private sector in the country.
Steps being taken include: Policy advocacy, increase in investment in R&D including by industry and
strategic sectors, expansion of basic science infrastructure including sophisticated analytical instruments
and lab facilities for the usage of both public and private research, evolving new models of public-private
partnership in scientific research in the fields of drug research, instrumentation, clean energy, etc.
Further, a White Paper on stimulation of investment of private sector into R&D envisages building of
large pool of quality professionals suited for industrial R&D, well designed incentive mechanisms to
trigger commercialization of R&D outputs, simplification and rationalization of entire value chain of
industrial R&D and technology commercialization processes.
19.4 The Department also informed that it offers several incentives to the private sector for R&D,
e.g. Cent percent write-off of revenue and capital expenditures in R&D, weighted tax reduction on in-
house R&D, income tax exemption to donation made to approved non-commercial scientific and industrial
organizations, custom duty exemption to R&D institutions, etc. The Department is also encouraging
private sector to engage in some of the R&D programmes of the Department. It is expected that, over
the years, private sector investment would increase in a gradual manner.
19.5 The Committee notes that the Department is striving to synchronise the efforts made by
the public sector with the private sector in the scientific research domain. However, such syncing
process must take into account the security of the 'common goods' and environmental concerns.
Rather than focussing on exemptions at the input levels, outputs should be incentivised. The
partnership should be result oriented and the benefits should be linked with the performance.
20. NATIONAL MISSION FOR SUSTAINING THE HIMALAYAN ECOSYSTEM
20.1 The National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC) has enunciated the launch of a National
Mission for Sustaining the Himalayan Ecosystem (NMSHE). The Mission needs to deliver better
understanding of the coupling between the Himalayan ecosystem and the climate factors and provide
inputs for Himalayan Sustainable development while addressing also the protection of a fragile ecosystem.
This will require the joint effort of climatologists, glaciologists and other experts.

21
20.2 Recogn izing the importance of scientific and technological inputs required for sustaining the fragile
Himalayan Ecosystem, the Ministry of Science and Technology has been charged with the nodal responsibility
of coordinating this mission. However, the mission requires valuable cooperation of Indian Himalayan
States, the planning commission and the Ministry of Environment and Forests to achieve its goals.
20.3 The primary objective of the Mission is to develop in a time bound manner a sustainable national
capacity to continuously assess the health status of the Himalayan Ecosystem and enable policy bodies
in their policy-formulation functions as also to assist States in the Indian Himalayan Region with
implementation of actions selected for sustainable development.
20.4 The mission attempts to address some important issues concerning
(a) Himalayan Glaciers and the associated hydrological consequences,
(b) Biodiversity conservation and protection,
(c) Wild life conservation and protection,
(d) Traditional knowledge societies and their livelihood and
(e) Planning for sustaining of the Himalayan Ecosystem.
20.5 Under the National Mission for Sustaining the Himalayan Ecosystem [NMSHE] as part of the
National Action Plan for Climate Change (NAPCC), six major research programmes have been initiated
/ supported. It includes vulnerability assessment, sustainability and to enhance strategic knowledge in
Climate Change. A number of detailed Technical reports about the R&D work were brought out on
Climate Change.
20.6 The Mission has been allocated an outlay of ` 550.00 crore during the XII Five Year Plan period.
Informing about the progress made in National Mission the Department informed that a major initiative
of establishing 6 Thematic Task Forces anchored around key knowledge institutions in the Himalayan
region as outlined in the Mission document was taken up. The same has been finalised. Following are
six task forces:-
(1) Natural and Geographical wealth by Wadia Institute of Himalayan Geology, Dehradun;
(2) Forest Resources and Plant biodiversity by GB Pant Institute on Himalayan Environment and
Development, Almora;
(3) Micro flora and fauna and wild life and animal population by Wild Life Institute of India,
Dehradun ;
(4) Traditional Knowledge systems by Jawaharlal Lal Nehru University;
(5) Water, Ice, snow and glaciers by National Institute of Hydrology, Roorkee and
(6) Himalayan Agriculture by Indian Council for Agriculture Research.
20.7 The Department further informed that an Inter-University Consortium on "the Himalayan Cryosphere:
Science, and Society" was also launched wherein four universities viz., JNU, Kashmir University, Jammu
University and Sikkim University participated. A major programme for building human capacity in glaciology

22
and related areas under Indo-Swiss S&T cooperation was also launched. Under this programme, it was
proposed to impart training to 30 students annually through a three level training programme jointly by
Indian and Swiss faculty. It was also informed that DST also initiated discussion with International
Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), Kathmandu for developing a Regional Cooperation
framework for multi-lateral cooperation in the areas of Himalayan Ecosystem.
20.8 The Committee hopes that National Mission for Sustaining Himalayan Ecosystem, a part of
National Action Plan for Climate Change, will follow the Mission Document and its task forces
will accomplish the targets of the Mission. The Committee recommends that considering the
enormous challenges of Climate Change and fragile Himalayan ecology, this Mission should be
adequately funded.
20.9 The focus of the Ministry of Science and Technology should be on endeavouring to acquire
a global leadership position in the frontier areas of sciences including material sciences, synthetic
biology, genetics and astrophysics, etc. International partnerships in these areas should be
established with countries and companies with known expertise and leadership in these and other
areas of big ticket sciences.
20.10 The Department should consider sharing their research and innovations with the state governments
and their instrumentalities so as to ensure a useful dissemination of knowledge throughout the country.
The Committee also recommends that special efforts should be made to disseminate information and
knowledge of the schemes of the Department in far-flung districts and particularly in the states of North
East.

23
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS — AT A GLANCE
TREND OF UTILISATION IN THE LAST THREE YEARS
The Committee finds that though utilisation of allocated resources by the Department
improved considerably in the last three years, the allocation to some of the schemes was reduced
due to delay in seeking administrative approval. The Committee is of the view that grounds cited
by the Department are of routine administrative nature which could have been avoided by the
Department as delay in completion of infrastructure projects leads to time and cost overrun and
affects research & development work. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the loopholes
which led to underutilisation of funds should be plugged and delay in seeking administrative
approval should be avoided, and also responsibility for delay should be fixed. (Para 7.6)
MECHANISM TO MONITOR AND REVIEW THE ONGOING SCHEMES
The Committee is of the opinion that a robust monitoring mechanism is essential for
ensuring timely completion of various projects to avoid time and cost overrun and to ensure full
utilisation of the allocated funds. The Committee notes the performance of the Department of
Science & Technology evaluated by third party under Result Framework Document and finds
that there is a considerable scope for improvement in the performance and the Department
needs to further strengthen its monitoring mechanism to make it more robust for timely
completion of projects and optimum utilisation of funds in the year 2015-16. (Para 8.3)
BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2015-16
The Committee takes strong exception to the fact that despite Department's request for
allocation of more funds, the Ministry of Finance has not paid any heed to the matter in the past
two years. Such constraints only circumscribe the functioning of important projects undertaken
by the Department. The Committee, therefore, recommends that in future the Ministry of
Finance should give a favourable response to the request of the Department. (Para 9.6)
MEGA FACILITIES FOR BASIC RESEARCH
It is noted that the Department has adopted and implemented the principle of reciprocity
and parity with regard to the use of mega-facilities in the basic research undertaken by our
scientists. This much-appreciated initiative of the Department is likely to work as an enabler in
injecting greater confidence in our scientists and would also lead to the acknowledgement of our
scientific expertise at an international level. The Committee values the partnership between the
DST and the Department of Atomic Energy and feels that such efforts would develop the much-
needed capacity building in the university and academic sector for building mega facilities for
basic research. It will enable the Department to explore possibilities of collaboration with other
reputed scientific departments such as the Departments of Biotechnology, Scientific Research,
Space and Ministry of Earth Sciences. The Committee feels that such initiatives need systematic
attention and financial nurturing so that the perennial neglect of basic research in the country
is duly addressed and the systemic pitfalls are avoided. (Para 11.9)
23

24
INDIA-BASED NEUTRINO OBSERV ATORY PROJECT (INO)
The Committee takes note of the joint initiative taken by the Departments of Science &
Technology and Atomic Energy in setting up the India-based Neutrino observatory for cutting-
edge research in Neutrino studies. The Committee wishes all the success to "Asia's first state-
of-the-art facility" to provide research facility in particle physics. Furthermore, the Committee
recommends that necessary budgetary provisions should be made available for the observatory.
(Para 12.5)
The Committee hopes that in the years to come, the observatory will transform into an
Observatory Par Excellence setting international standards and provide high quality research
facility to science students across the country, and help them develop sophisticated detectors and
electronics using their own hands and producing new insights in Neutrino studies. (Para 12.6)
THIRTY METER TELESCOPE
The Committee believes that the proposed Thirty Meter Telescope has tremendous potential
to unravel the myriad mysteries of the universe. It is likely to become a tool for the Indian
astronomy in keeping up the level of excellence in research in astronomy and astrophysics of
the country. The Committee hopes that the TMT project would help the country to embark on
world class, international science collaborations and also help develop the required human resources
in the field. (Para 13.7)
NATIONAL SUPERCOMPUTING MISSION
The Committee finds that India was a leader in Supercomputing till 2005 but it has now
slipped down in the global ranking to 14th place. The Committee is of the view that boosting
indigenous efforts in Supercomputing capability is in strategic interests of India, more so when
Information Technology capabilities of the country are recognised worldwide. The Committee
hopes that the mission will help India attain leadership and self-reliance in the field of
Supercomputing. The Committee recommends that considering the significance of Supercomputing,
the Department should make every possible effort including establishment of requisite ecosystem
for the success of the Mission to successfully imp)emcnt the project in a time-bound manner. The
Committee further recommends that the Department must ensure that the allocated outlays for
the scheme are fully utilised. (Para 14.10)
THE NATIONAL MISSION ON NANO SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
The Committee finds that fund utilisation under the Mission has been satisfactory in the
last eight years. However, the Committee recommends that the Department should inject the
qualitative parameters in terms of utilization of resources of the National Mission on Nano
Science & Technology. (Para 15.3)
The Committee notes with satisfaction that India holds the third rank in terms of publications
of papers on Nano science & technology. The Committee also takes cognisance of the performance
of the Department in the first phase of Nano Mission especially in fundamental sciences and
human resources. The Committee believes that the Department would take necessary steps to

deprived of requisite basic infrastructure and necessary wherewithal to undertake quality research.
International collaboration may be encouraged in such cases, both in terms of developing
infrastructure and capacity building of the personnel. (Para 16.7)
The Committee notes the improvement in the performance of some major universities/
colleges. However, the Committee is of the view that qualitative improvement is needed to make
Indian universities and research institutes at par with the international standards. International
Best Practices need to be inculcated in the tertiary education and higher research in India. It
is, therefore, recommended that the Ministry should take steps to meet these objectives. Financial
support, technical and technological know-how and R&D support should not be confined to a few

areas of the country as it would help capture the untapped knowledge resources in the country.
The Ministry needs to bring about uniformity in the quality of research conducted in institutions

The Committee finds that many of the top universities have research Centres in collaboration

universities and research institutes. (Para 16.9)

technologies. (Para 17.6)
The Committee hopes that scheme for empowerment of women in its new form will not only

26
women and encourage them to pursue a career in scientific research as also for augmenting the

INTRODUCTION
The Department of Biotechnology was initially set up as an Independent Board in 1982 and thereafter
became a full fledged Department under Ministry of Science & Technology in 1986. The main mandate
of the department is given below:
(i) To evolve policies and integrated programmes in biotechnology and ensure their implementation
and monitoring.
(ii) To identify specific programmes of Research and Development and manufacturing in biologicals
and biotechnology and oversee the initiation and pursuit of related research and manufacturing
activities.
(iii) To identify, set up and support Centres of Excellence for Research and Development in
biotechnology and ensure proper dovetailing of their activities as per national priorities and
objectives.
(iv) To act as a screening, advising and approving agent of the Government with regard to import
and transfer of new technologies for the manufacture of biologicals, biotechnological products
and their intermediates.
(v) Evolve safety guidelines for biotechnology Research and Development and manufacturing in
India.
(vi) To act as the central agency for the import of genetically manipulated materials, culture, cells,
specimens, tissues and biotech products including DNA and RNA of any type or size and for
promoting their production in the country.
(vii) Serve as the inter-ministerial and interagency nodal point for all specific international bilateral
and multilateral Research and Development collaborations and agreements in the area of
biotechnology; act as the nodal point for all technology transfers in the area of biotechnology.
(viii) Manufacture and ensure application of recombinant, cell-based and DNA vaccines, diagnostics
and other biotechnological products.
(ix) To evolve programmes for Human Resource Development in the area of biotechnology.
(x) Serve as an administrative and implementing Department of agencies, commissions, boards,
etc. specifically formed by the Government for fulfilling the national objectives in biotechnology
and also to serve as the nodal point for Bio-informatics including training and creation of
infrastructure, collection, dissemination and exchange of information relating to biotechnology.
(xi) Establishment of National Biotechnology Regulatory Authority

4.3 The Committee feels that although the Department of Biotechnology had been able to spend
97.76 percent and 99.19 percent of the allocations made during 2012-13 and 2013-14, the allocations
of the Department were not only allocated on pro-rata basis during first three years of the
Twelfth Plan period but it has been reduced at RE stage in each of the first three years of the
Plan period. The Committee is of the considered view that the Biotechnology will play a very
important role in the development of the nation in the years to come and reduction in the
allocations of the Department at the RE stage, when the Department has demonstrated capability
to utilise the allocated amounts, results in avoidable delay in the implementation of programmes
and achievement of the targets fixed, thereby adversely affecting the scientific and technical
advancement of the country. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the budgetary allocation
of the Department should be increased at the RE stage during the current financial year and the
Department should be provided the full amount as it is capable of utilising the same during the
remaining period of the Twelfth Plan.
5. MONITORING MECHANISM OF THE DEPARTMENT
5.1 The Committee enquired about the mechanisms devised by the Department to monitor and review
the progress of its ongoing schemes and programmes. The Committee was informed that the Department
has put in place several mechanisms for monitoring the progress of implementation of its projects. The

4
Department implements various types of schemes broadly classified as (a) Scientific research and
infrastructure development through Competitive Research Grant system open to individual scientists/
Professors or network of scientists (b) Technology development through public private partnership
schemes (c) implementation of programmes in the autonomous R&D institutions; and (d) International
S&T cooperation. For all S&T schemes, there are about 20 subject specific task forces consisting of
about 250 experts engaged in monitoring of the progress of the project on 6 monthly or annual basis
including site visits etc. An elaborate monitoring mechanism has also been put in place for all public
private partnership schemes such as site visits by Project Monitoring Committee (PMC) comprising of
two area experts, one DBT officer and one financial person, every six months at the project implementation
site to review the progress of the project. The review of the project is also done by Technical Steering
Committee (TSC) every year and the annual financial releases are made based on the successful completion
of milestones/targets specified. To strengthen the system further, the Department is implementing online
project registration and monitoring system namely "e-promis" where all periodical progress reports are
available for scrutiny and review at all permitted levels.
5.2 The Committee is of the view that a strong and potent monitoring mechanism is extremely
important for achieving the set objectives and implementation of the schemes and, therefore,
recommends that the Department should continue with its monitoring mechanisms to ensure
that there are no time and cost overruns in respect of its schemes/programmes.

7. PRIV ATE SECTOR INVESTMENT IN RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
7.1 The Committee desired to know the details of action initiated by the Department to augment private
sector investment in Research and Development and public private partnership schemes to promote
biotechnology ventures and whether any international collaborative ventures had been signed with major
non-governmental scientific and technology establishments. The Committee was informed that the
Department has set up the Biotechnology Industry Assistance Council (BIRAC) with the approval of the
Cabinet, as a public sector, 'Not-for-Profit' company on 20th March, 2012. BIRAC is an interface agency
of the Department of Biotechnology, Ministry of Science & Technology, and has the mandate of fostering
and nurturing the Biotech Enterprises specially start-ups and Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) for
enhancing their innovation research capacities and promoting affordable product development. BIRAC
provides funding support for the various components of Product Development Chain from Discovery,
Innovation, Early and Late Stage validation upto pre-commercialization. Various funding schemes are
being handled by BIRAC. So far nearly 250 start-ups and SMEs and over 100 young entrepreneurs have
been supported. 17 Products, 11 new technologies and 24 IP have been generated. Through this support,
there is a commitment of funds of ` 550 crores from Government and as a part of the company
contribution approximately ` 650 crores have been committed. Various Public Partnership schemes for
healthcare, agriculture and industrial biotechnology are operational as listed below:
Biotechnology Ignition Grant (BIG):  To support and nurture high risk and novel concepts for
potential entrepreneurs from Academia start up or an Incubatee who have an exciting idea.
Small Business Innovation Research Initiative (SBIRI): To strengthen those existing private industrial
units whose product development is based on in-house innovative R&D, encourage smaller businesses
to increase their R&D capabilities. Support is provided for Discovery to Proof of Concept and Early
Stage Validation.
Biotechnology Industry Partnership Programme (BIPP):  It is a partnership with Industrie(s) for
support on a cost sharing basis for path-breaking research in frontier futuristic technology areas
having major economic potential and making the Indian industry globally competitive.

6
Contract Research Scheme (CRS):  This scheme facilitates the academia-industry interaction to take

translation by industry.
7.2 BIRAC has a major focus on International partnerships to leverage the strengths of the organization
and bring in best practices and also to encourage collaboration between Indian startups /SMEs with the
partners globally. Some important International collaborations are (i) an agreement with Bill and Melinda
Gates Foundation (BMGF) to collaborate on mission directed research and to build a 'Grand Challenges
India' to support health research and innovation; (ii) United States Agency for International Development
(USAID) has also joined hands with DBT-BMGF-BIRAC to collectively promote innovation for affordable

7.3 The Committee takes note of the initiatives taken by Biotechnology Industry Assistance

actual role of experts in the field of biotechnological advance and also the need for the best
minds to provide a leadership role in the area, the challenges outlined above need to be proactively
and imaginatively dealt with. Hence retaining and engaging the best minds is of critical importance.
10. INDIA'S RANKING IN INTERNATIONAL RESEARCH PUBLICATIONS
10.1 The Committee enquired from the Department as to what was India's position/ranking in international
research publications on biotechnology and what efforts have been made by the Department to improve

10
the said position/ranking. Department informed the Committee that Biotechnology is a multidisciplinary
area involving foundational sciences such as biochemistry, genetics, microbiology, immunology and
molecular biology techniques for understanding basic biology in terms of structure and function so as
to develop biotechnological processes and products beneficial in agriculture, healthcare, industry and
environmental aspects. Therefore, performance in the foundation sciences, as measured by the number
of publications over a period of 5-10 years, citable documents, scientific citations, self citations, citations
per document and H index (total publications/citations), are important ranking parameters of scientific
performance across countries. Among several agencies, SCImago Journal & Country Rank portal, which
analyses information of a large database of publications namely 'Scopus' is one of the most referred
sources. 10.2 The Department provided the following comparative ranking in the above foundation

10.3 Between 1996 and 2013, India improved its global ranking from 14/15 to 7/8 immediately after
advanced countries. Increased investments in science & technology in general and biological sciences
and biotechnology in particular have been the major contributing factors. Several initiatives by the
Department of Biotechnology with a primary mandate to promote basic and applied research in foundational
biological sciences such as integrated human resource development, establishment of research resources,
technology platforms, incubators, high-end equipment, large scale extramural competitive R&D grants in
universities and institutions, establishment of new institutions in cutting edge areas for global competence
have been largely responsible for the phenomenal performance. Several recent initiatives particularly
international collaborations, establishment of Centres of Excellence and human resource development
schemes from graduate colleges to young scientists in biological sciences is expected to further enhance
the international performance in future years.
10.4 The Committee notes the improvement in the global ranking of the country in various fields
of Biotechnology but expresses its concern over India lagging behind China in the field of
foundational sciences. The Committee also notes that the Department has not let the budgetary
constraints come into the way of its excelling in the field of biotechnology and earning India a
place in the top countries of the world. The Committee exhorts the Department to attain

11
excellence and improve India's global ranking in Biotechnology and must specifically endeavour
to be amongst the first five countries as per established parameters. A time frame for achieving
the milestone should be fixed and a purposive/concrete Action Plan be formulated to achieve this
ambitious national aspiration. The Committee feels that Department should adore the number
of patents granted to its scientists as one of the measures to judge the quality of research. This
area requires a special focus. Commercialisation of patents is a weak area. The reasons therefore
need to be identified and suitable correctives should be applied.
11. STEPS TO CONTAIN BRAIN DRAIN
11.1 Brain drain is a major concern for our country. A majority of the country's skilled workforce goes
abroad in search of greener pastures keeping this in view, the Committee sought to know from the
Department as to what steps have been taken by the Department to attract talented people into the field
of research/study of Biotechnology and the result achieved thereby. The Committee was informed that
the Department is implementing an integrated human resource development programme to create trained
manpower in the field of biotechnology by providing hands on experience to UG science students under
star college scheme, supporting M.Sc. /M.Tech. teaching programmes in 71 universities in the country,
industrial training for B.Tech./M.Sc./M.Tech. biotech students and finishing schools for bridging skill
gaps and enhancing employment prospects, re-training of existing faculty and scientists in advanced
areas for upgrading their skills by conducting short term training courses, providing fellowships for
doctoral and post-doctoral research. Emphasis is laid on selection of students on an All India entrance
test basis, framing of model course curriculum, provision for regular faculty positions in gap areas and
inviting guest faculty, scholarships for all selected students, liberal grants for laboratory equipment,
maintenance and recurring grants for consumables, thesis grants to provide quality all round training as
well as industrial training to ensure employability of students.
11.2 Further, the Department has instituted Ramalingaswami fellowships for encouraging Indian scientists
working in overseas laboratories to return to the country as well as DBT Wellcome Trust fellowships
for outstanding scientists to pursue research in Indian laboratories. Opportunity for conducting advanced
research or undergoing specialized training CREST (Cutting Edge Research Enhancement and Scientific
Training Awards) for Indian scientists in leading overseas laboratories is also provided. Department has
launched DBT-BUILDER (DBT-Boost to University Inter-disciplinary Departments of Life Sciences for
Education and Research) for advanced education and research by upgradation/re-engineering/remodelling/
creation of Life science departments in universities. These programmes have resulted in attracting,
retaining and training to meet the needs of quality trained manpower in the country.
11.3 The Department has also implemented biodesign programmes focused on innovation and
entrepreneurship in area of medical devices and implants and an indigenous international biodesign
fellowship i.e., i-Fellowship at AIIMS, New Delhi and IIT, Delhi in collaboration with Stanford University,
USA and Queensland University, Australia.
11.4 The Department further informed that Star College scheme has resulted in attracting young students
to take up undergraduate science courses, provide hands-on experience resulting in retaining students in
science which is evident from increase in cut off percentage for admission, number of applications

12
received with reference to number of seats, decline in drop out rates, better performance in UG results,
increase in PG admissions in science courses. Biotech Industry Training Programme provides opportunity
for skill development for industry needs; yearly about 600 students are placed in biotech industries.
11.5 The Committee notes the steps taken by the Department for attracting the required talent
available with the country in the field of Biotechnology through various fellowships/schemes,
both for students and scientists. The Committee feels that there is no dearth of talent in the
country. The need is to tap this talent and provide all necessary wherewithal for achieving
excellence in the field of Biotechnology. The Committee, therefore, recommends that there
should be no let up in the efforts of the Department to attract talented people in the field of
Biotechnology. The Department should spearhead an accelerated effort not only to woo the talent
available in the country but also attract top Indian talent in other countries to the field of
Biotechnology in India. Apart from initiatives already in place, the Department should explore
other meaningful initiatives to establish strong foundations for an onward and long journey to
achieve a leadership role in the various areas of biotechnology. The Committee feels that excellent
leadership has been provided in the past by the Department of Biotechnology but for the Department
to play its rightful role in meeting challenges of the future, it must inspire the best minds to
join the Department and continue with various schemes. Allocating fiscal and career progression
related incentives should be put in place for the purpose.
12. BIOTECHNOLOGY FOR SOCIETAL DEVELOPMENT
12.1 The mandate of the Societal Programme is to promote use of biotechnological processes and tools
for the benefit of the disadvantaged sections of society comprising women, rural population and SC/STs
in ecologically compatible manner. The programme aims to create a platform for self-employment
generation among the target population and diffusion of proven and field-tested technologies through
demonstration, training and extension activities. The focused areas are bio-fertilizer production,
vermicomposting, apiculture, poultry, fish production and rearing, artificial insemination, mushroom
cultivation, goat rearing, fruit plant nurseries, sericulture, post-harvest processing technologies, hybrid
seed production, use of quality planting materials and women and child health care.
12.2 The BE and RE allocation made and actual expenditure incurred in respect of this programme during
2013-14 and 2014-15 and budgetary allocation made during 2015-16 are as under:

12.3 The Committee was informed that under this programme, the impact has been assessed in the
participating community with skill development activities by Training and Demonstrations conducted in
various parts of the country. The Committee sought to know the details of the activities undertaken and
the impact of the above programme and how it had actually benefitted the society in terms of employment

13
and entrepreneurship. The Committee was informed that the proposals supported during the year
2013-14 & 2014-15 were on various aspects such as promotion of quality planting material, mushroom
cultivation, sericulture, production and use of bio-agent/bio-fertilizers, floral craft technology for physically
& mentally challenged children, value-added product preparation, piggery, turkey and quail farming,
hygienic drying of fish through solar dryer, new born screening for genetic disorders, artificial insemination
for improving the animal breeds, introducing improved variety of crops etc.
12.4 As regards t he benefit to the society in terms of employment and entrepreneurship, the Committee
was informed that large number of women, both rural and urban, have benefitted directly through biotech
packages for floriculture, horticulture, cultivation of mushrooms, medicinal and aromatic plants,
biofertilisers, organic farming, vermicomposting, sericulture, aquaculture, animal husbandry, poultry
farming and making of bio-crafts. Several training modules have been prepared for creating awareness
on health, nutritional food preparations and agricultural practices. One of the example of innovative
scheme supported under Biotechnology based Programme for Women was "Network Project on Prasad
Kit" which has been successfully completed benefitting around 7000 women. Emphasis was on the
utilization of locally available and nutritionally rich raw material for preparation of edible items used as
Prasad in different religious shrines/temples. Some of the projects supported under the scheme resulted
into sustainable model of income generation in the region and are still continuing. Various projects have
also been supported under a new initiative to improve the health, hygiene and nutritional aspects with
respect to women community.
12.5 In the Rural Bio-resource complexes supported by the Department, the integration of 2-3 interventions
Agri/Horticulture/Animal Husbandry would fetch good income generation. Some of the interventions
adopted by entrepreneurial activities by the youths and Self Help Groups (SHG's) have resulted in good
earning and annual income of ` 30,000/- to ` 50,000 per acreage land area. This programme is addressed
to cover the grass root level community farmers, youths, villagers and SHG's to utilize local resources
for their sustainable livelihoods. Other activities like health intervention, environment and sanitation are
also addressed to provide good socio economic condition to the community for their holistic development.
12.6 The Committee had earlier been informed by the Department that a survey will be undertaken, based
on primary and secondary data collection, to assess the impact of the above programme. When enquired
about the details of the survey so conducted, the Department informed that although the survey could
not be undertaken, the special Task Force of multidisciplinary experts have been monitoring the progress
of the projects implemented under the scheme.
12.7 The Committee notes the contributions made by the Department in the field of bio-fertilizer
production, vermicomposting, apiculture, poultry, fish production and rearing, artificial
insemination, mushroom cultivation, goat rearing, fruit plant nurseries, sericulture, post-harvest
processing technologies, hybrid seed production, use of quality planting materials and women and
child health care for societal development through biotechnology. The Committee recommends
that the Department should ensure greater involvement of Civil Society organisations, NGOs,
local representatives at the Panchayat level in the implementation of its schemes/programmes
so that the benefits of the programme percolate to the rural areas and weaker and lower sections
of the society in real terms.

14
12.8 The Committee notes that although the Department has outlined the multifarious benefits
of the programme, the fact remains that, in spite of its earlier assurance to the Committee to
undertake the survey to assess its impact as to how it actually helped/benefitted society in terms
of employment and entrepreneurship, the survey has not been conducted so far. The Committee
recommends that the Department should institute a survey to assess the impact of its societal
benefit programmes/schemes in actual terms and report the results to the Committee.
12.9 The Committee also recommends that special efforts should be made to disseminate
information and knowledge of the schemes of the Department in for flying districts and particularly
in the states of North East.

only if the recommendations of the Committee are implemented in their true spirit and not

implemented proactively and within a stipulated time frame.

FINANCIAL ACHIEVEMENTS OF THE DEPARTMENT
The Committee feels that although the Department of Biotechnology had been able to spend
97.76 percent and 99.19 percent of the allocations made during 2012-13 and 2013-14, the allocations
of the Department were not only allocated on pro-rata basis during first three years of the
Twelfth Plan period but it has been reduced at RE stage in each of the first three years of the
Plan period. The Committee is of the considered view that the Biotechnology will play a very
important role in the development of the nation in the years to come and reduction in the
allocations of the Department at the RE stage, when the Department has demonstrated capability
to utilise the allocated amounts, results in avoidable delay in the implementation of programmes
and achievement of the targets fixed, thereby adversely affecting the scientific and technical
advancement of the country. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the budgetary allocation
of the Department should be increased at the RE stage during the current financial year and the
Department should be provided the full amount as it is capable of utilising the same during the
remaining period of the Twelfth Plan. (Para 4.3)
MONITORING MECHANISM OF THE DEPARTMENT
The Committee is of the view that a strong and potent monitoring mechanism is extremely
important for achieving the set objectives and implementation of the schemes and, therefore,
recommends that the Department should continue with its monitoring mechanisms to ensure
that there are no time and cost overruns in respect of its schemes/programmes. (Para 5.2)
RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
The Committee notes that inspite of making utilisation of its allocated funds in respect of
Research and Development scheme, the allocation under R&D had been considerably reduced
during the 2014-15. The apparent increase in allocation during 2015-16 is actually due to merger
of 'International Collaboration" under R&D scheme. The Committee is of the view that for
facilitating R&D and encouraging young scientists in the extremely important area of
biotechnology, increased allocations to this sector are in order. Genomics, synthetic biology and
chemical biology are frontier areas of big ticket science and for India to establish itself as a
global leader in these areas, funds should never be an issue. We need to invest in our future
now. Biotechnology holds the key to some of the critical challenges that we face.
(Para 6.4)
PRIV ATE SECTOR INVESTMENT IN RESEARCH & DEVELOPMENT
The Committee takes note of the initiatives taken by Biotechnology Industry Assistance
Council (BIRAC) to encourage and involve the private sector in the field of Biotechnology. The
Committee is of the view that involving/facilitating private sector is extremely important for
accelerating the growth of biotechnology in the country and recommends that BIRAC should
accelerate its efforts to attract/facilitate private sector participation and increase global
competitiveness of Indian biotech industry. International partnership should be entered in the
frontier area of biotechnology and the results thereof should be clearly verifiable.
(Para 7.3)

REPORT
The holistic understanding and study of the Earth and its processes is vital for the mankind. The
Earth, being a single, interlinked and self-regulating system, together with its components i.e. atmosphere,
oceans, cryosphere, geosphere and biosphere exhibit complex interactions. The scientific understanding
of the Earth system becomes necessary in order to provide greater accuracy in the forecast of weather,
climate and hazards. Moreover, the exploration of polar regions, sea bed and optimum use of resources
is significant for the sustenance of life on earth and developing services for societal benefit.
1.2 The Ministry of Earth Sciences was established in 2006 by the Government of India for better
understanding the complex processes of the Earth system namely ocean, atmosphere, cryosphere and
solid work. To monitor and give an overall policy direction to the Ministry, the Earth System Science
Organisation (ESSO) was also established in the year 2007.
1.3 The Ministry is mandated to provide weather and climate services in varied sectors of agriculture,
aviation, shipping, disasters (cyclones, earthquakes, tsunamis), marine resources, coastal and marine
ecosystem, climate change and under water technology. The Ministry also deals with Antarctica/Arctic
and Seismological research in an integrated manner.
2. OBJECTIVES AND FUNCTIONS OF THE MINISTRY
2.1 The Ministry of Earth Sciences has the following objectives and functions:
• Improving weather forecast and provide advisory to agriculture, aviation, shipping, sports
including the Extended Long Range Seasonal Monsoon forecast;
• Providing a wide range of ocean information advisories including fishery information;
• Improving the understanding of Polar Science and its implications for climate change;
• Developing technology for harnessing marine resources;
• Conducting survey for assessing non-living resources;
• Assessing coastal marine productivity and Marine Ecosystems;
• Improving understanding of Clime Change Science;
• Providing early warning of natural hazards viz. cyclone, tsunami, sea level rise; and
• Promoting basic research including capacity building in the Earth Systems Science.
3. ORGANISATIONAL STRUCTURE OF THE MINISTRY
3.1 The Ministry of Earth Sciences functions through the Earth Commission. The executive arm of the
Ministry i.e. 'The Earth System Science Organisation (ESSO)' is responsible for implementing its policies
and programmes. It has four major branches of earth sciences viz., (i) Ocean Science and Technology
Services; (ii) Atmospheric and Climate Science Services; (iii) Geoscience and Technology; and (iv) Polar
Science and Cryosphere. The policies/programmes of the ESSO are being pursued through its autonomous

2
bodies and subordinate offices. The institutions, under the ESSO includes, India Meteorological Department
(IMD), National Centre for Medium Range Weather Forecasting (NCMRWF) and Indian Institute of
Tropical Meteorology (IITM), National Centre for Antarctica and Ocean Research (NCAOR), National
Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT), Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS),
Centre for Marine Living Resources (CMLRE) and Integrated Coastal and Marine Area Management
(ICMAM).

Earth Commission, on the lines of Space Commission and Atomic Energy Commission, was submitted

Earth Sciences.
4.2 After carrying out inter-ministerial consultations with relevant Ministries/Department only the
Department of Expenditure did not support the proposal and raised certain observations which were

8. POLAR SCIENCES AND CRYOSPHERE
8.1 The Committee was informed that the programme of Polar Sciences and Cryosphere entails the
study of Antarctica, Arctic, and glaciers of Himalayas and the impact of climate and climate change in
these regions and its variability over the Indian region. The study of Antarctica and Arctic regions are
important as these regions not only govern the earth's climate but are also the storehouse which archive
its past climatic history.
8.2 The Ministry informed the Committee that India had successfully commenced operations at 3rd
Indian Permanent Station, Bharati, in the Larsemann Hills, East Antarctica which would give a major
thrust to study in the field of glaciology, atmosphere, paleoclimate and Polar biology. India has been
accorded observer status in the Arctic Council in recognition of India's scientific contribution and
endeavour in Polar research. For the first time, a Multi-sensored Moored Observatory off the Kingsford,
Norway about 1100 km away from the North Pole, to understand interaction between fjord and sea as
well as the response of the Arctic to climate variability was installed. The design, development and
installation of this underwater moored observatory have been executed by ESSO-NIOT (National Institute
of Ocean Technology), in collaboration with ESSO-NCAOR (National Centre for Antarctic and Ocean
Research), Goa. A team of scientists from ESSO-NIOT and ESSO-NCAOR successfully executed its
deployment on 23rd July 2014.
8.3 The Committee desired to know the reasons for increase in the budgetary allocation to the programme
from ` 200.00 crore in B.E. 2014-15 to ` 294.00 crore in B.E. 2015-16 and the details of additional
activities proposed to be undertaken by the Ministry with the enhanced allocation in this scheme. In its
response, the Ministry informed that the Polar Science & Cryosphere Scheme comprises the following
major activities:
• Expedition to Antarctica
• Project on cryosphere and Climate
• Paleoclimatic studies
• Himalayan cryosphere studies
• Indian Arctic Programme
• Southern Ocean studies

6
• National Centre for Antarctic and Ocean Research (NCAOR) -Manpower, Operation and
Maintenance
• Construction and commissioning of the Polar Research Vessel
8.4 While the outlay for all the activities at (a) to (g) above for 2015-16 has been kept at almost the
same level in 2014-15, the enhanced outlay of ` 94.00 crore is primarily to cater to the requirements
related to the construction of the polar research vessel.
8.5 The Ministry further informed the Committee that 34th Expedition was initiated in December 2014
for Maitri and Bharati - the two permanent stations in the Antarctica and, under the biogeochemistry and
Paleo-environmental studies, a 70 cm sediment core was drilled including the drilling of sediment cores
measuring 95cm and 140cm. The Ministry also informed that a Polar Remotely Operated Vehicle (PROVe)
was indigenously developed and deployed in Antarctica during February - March 2015. PROVe recorded
the scientific data such as bottom imagery, Irradiance, Temperature, Conductivity, Dissolved Oxygen,
etc.
8.6 On being required about initiation of any project to undertake cryosphere/glaciological studies in the
Himalayas, the Ministry informed that NCAOR is undertaking a major research project entitled "Cryosphere
and Climate" during the 12 Five Year Plan. One of the major components of the project is the study of
Himalayan glaciers. As part of the Himalayan Glaciology Project, NCAOR has undertaken major field
based studies during 2013 and 2014 on six glaciers of the Chandra basin in Lahul-Spiti in Himachal
Pradesh. The major glaciers that are being studied include: Samudra Tapu, Sutri Dhaka, Batal, Bara Sigri,
Nal Kanal and Gepang. In the study, observation was made on the melting of glaciers (in Ctype - debris
free and D-type - debris covered glaciers).
8.7 The Committee is of the view that the programme is one of the most important programmes
of the Ministry and the activities pursued in the Antarctica, Arctic and Himalayan region is of
extreme use for better understanding of Indian Climate and other societal benefits. The Committee
also observes that the programme is of strategic importance and in order to make our country's
presence in Arctic and Antarctica felt, this programme is of utmost importance. The research
undertaken in polar regions will help understand the fragile Himalayan region. The Committee
recommends that the programme should be undertaken diligently and in a well-planned manner.
9. POLAR RESEARCH VESSEL
9.1 The Committee was informed that the Polar Research Vessel will help sustain two Indian research
bases in Antarctica (Maitri and Bharti); dovetail research initiatives in the Southern Ocean domain with
those in the proximal regions of the Antarctic continent; widen the thrust on Arctic research disciplines
undertaken through Indian Station Himadri, and provide a suitable research platform for other tropical
sea programmes. Such a vessel can not only perform the dual functions, research and logistics, in the
polar region but also serve as a research platform for scientists undertaking scientific research in the
ocean realm including Southern Ocean contributing substantially and fruitfully for the polar research of
the world community. Indian scientists have been having a sustained presence in the Arctic since 2007.
With India's entry into the Arctic Council as an Observer along with China, Singapore, Japan and South
Korea, it has become strategically important to enhance our scientific investigations endeavour, in line

7
with our shared international commitments towards understanding of the global climate change phenomenon,
to have an increased visibility in the Arctic too, facilitating India to assume a lead role among the Asian
Nations active in the Polar Regions. In the context of India having expanded its scientific presence to
the Arctic as well and the country's growing strategic interests in the polar and ocean domain, a polar
research vessel would serve as the perfect vehicle for building up on our sustained presence and for
enhanced understanding of ocean processes and their linkages.
9.2 The Committee desired to know the progress made so far in procuring Polar Research Vessel. In
response, the Ministry informed that the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) in its meeting
held on 29th October 2014 approved the proposal of Ministry of Earth Sciences for acquisition of Polar
Research Vessel (PRV) at a cost of `1051.13 crore for a period of 34 months from the date of the
approval. An administrative order in favour of the implementing agency National Centre for Antarctic &
Ocean Research (NCAOR), Goa for acquisition of PRV was issued on 14th November 2014. The
Ministry further informed that more funds are needed for the acquisition of Polar Research Vessel. On
an enquiry the Ministry informed that an amount of ` 315 crore would be required for the vessel in
2015-16 (May 2015 to February 2016) However, the funds available is only ` 140 crore. Thus, additional
funds required by the Ministry for the vessel during the current financial year are ` 175 crore.
9.3 The Committee observes that the progress of the research activities on the polar regions
depends upon the infrastructure that includes Polar Research Vessel. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the vessel be acquired expeditiously. The Committee notes that the amount for
the vessel had been approved but more funds to the tune of ````` 175 crore are required to acquire
the vessel. The Committee, therefore, also recommends that adequate funds be made available
to the Ministry for acquisition of the vessel.
10. SEISOMOLGICAL  AND GEOSCIENCE (SAGE) PROGRAMME
10.1 This programme aims to undertake research relating to solid-earth and geoscience including the
study of earthquakes and to generate inputs for earthquake disaster mitigation. The Ministry informed
the Committee that the Seismological and Geoscience programmes have been clubbed together in view
of the close inter linkages and also in compliance with the directive from Ministry of Finance regarding
rationalization of schemes. The Committee enquired from the Ministry about the clubbing of the two
programmes of different magnitude, one related to Seismology and earthquakes and other with ocean and
deep see drilling. In response, the Ministry informed that the Geosciences is not related to only ocean
and deep sea drilling, it encompasses, geodynamics of the Indian sub-continent and earthquake hazard
assessment, deep imaging of Indian lithosphere, studies related to Andaman-Nicobar subduction zone,
active faults, climate and tectonics etc. In a broader sense, the Geoscience covers the activities related
to Seismological application and vice-versa. The main activities under seismological and Geoscience
(SAGE) programme proposed to be undertaken during 2015-16 are:-
• Drilling and instrumentation of pilot bore hole in Koyna.
• Procurement of broadband seismometer (BBS) systems to augment the existing systems.
• To initiate construction activities related to National Centre for Seismology (NCS).
• Active fault mapping research.

8
• To support existing observational network including Multi-parametric Geophysical Observatory
(MPGO).
• R & D programmes including procurement of small equipments and payment of salary to
National Centre for Earth Science Studies (NCESS).
• Payment of annual contribution to International Ocean Discovery Programme (IODP) and
International Continental Deep Drilling Programme (ICDP).
• To initiate creation of Geochronology facility.

10.4 The Ministry has undertaken deep drilling project which includes deep drilling, establishment of a
borehole observatory in the Koyna - Warna region and a Bore-Hole Geophysics Research Laboratory in
Karad (Maharashtra). When the Committee enquired about the status of setting up of the lab in the
Koyna-Warna region which faces regular occurrence of earthquakes, the Ministry informed the Committee
that the scientific deep drilling programme in Koyna -Warna region of Maharashtra is being implemented
by Ministry in close association with National Geophysical Research Institute (NGRI) as per the Cabinet
approval.
10.5 As part of the 'Preparatory Phase', various studies/investigations were taken up which included
Broadband Seismology, Magneto-Tellurics (MT), Land-based Gravity-Magnetics, Airborne Gravity and
LIDAR surveys, etc. These studies were supplemented by the exploratory boreholes at a depth of ~ 1.5
km surrounding the seismic zone. Out of the 10 planned boreholes, 8 have been completed to depths
of 1522.5m (Rasati), 1196m (Udgiri), 1134m (Kundi), 1211.6m (Nayari), 1500m (Panchgani), 1503m
(Ukhalu), 1500m (Paneri), 1103m (Khadi) with logging and heat flow measurements. One more borehole
at Phansavale (Warna) has been drilled upto 891 m. The studies helped to delineate the sub-surface
structure around the seismic zone most prospective for scientific deep drilling and fault zone investigations.
The Committee was informed that the main phase has now been started and the activities initiated in
preparatory phase viz. monitoring of seismic activity using borehole and surface seismographs, have been
subsumed in the main project which includes drilling of two 2-3 km pilot boreholes in the next one and
half years followed by drilling of deep boreholes of 5-7 km each. A proposal for construction of office
and core repository in Karad is under consideration of finance division.
10.6 The Ministry informed the Committee that for drilling 1 - pilot bore hole and for setting up of
Research Laboratory, total funds required is ` 52 crore out of which only a meagre amount of ` 4 crore
is available to the Ministry. The additional funds required by the Ministry is ` 48 crore for both the
activities.
10.7 The Committee takes note of the activities undertaken in the preparatory phase which is
relevant for collecting seismological data and for continuing the seismological research activities
in the main phase. The Committee recommends that the main phase of the programme be
carried on taking inputs from preparatory phase and to complete the deep drilling of the bore
holes essential for understanding the regular occurrence of the earthquakes in the region.
10.8 The Committee takes serious note of the fact that additional ````` 48 crore is required and only
meagre amount of ````` 4 crore are available to the Ministry for such an important programme
which is critical in nature seeing the regular occurrence of earthquakes in the region. The
Committee recommends that ensuring funds to the programme should be a high priority as the
research on earthquakes will serve two purposes of monitoring critical parameters in the "near
field" of earthquakes and providing India a unique opportunity to take global leadership role in
this important scientific issue.

12. MICROZONATION OF CITIES
12.1 On the progress of the seismic hazard Microzonation of metro cities of India, the Ministry informed
the Committee that the Seismic microzonation of Delhi on 1:10,000 scale has been completed and various
thematic maps prepared including, Site classification, Liquefaction susceptibility, Peak Ground Acceleration
at 2% and 10%, Probability of Exceedence, Design spectra and Integrated Hazard index, etc. The
Committee was informed that the Microzonation of Bangalore on 1:20000 scale was completed in 2009.
Microzonation of Kolkata is expected to be completed in the next one year. As a part of 12th Microzonation
of 30 selected cities, falling in seismic zone V , IV and III with 0.5 million population and State capitals,
has also been initiated and Base maps of targeted cites available with Survey of India have been procured
and remaining are in process. Also, an MoU between NCS and GSI has been signed on "General
framework for sharing of geological, geophysical and other data/information for enrichment of Geoscientific
knowledge base for sustainable development" on 25-7-2014. Under provisions of this MoU, digital
geological and other related maps for targeted cities are being acquired.
12.2 The Committee takes note of the importance of microzonation of cities on account of
vulnerability of India's land to severe earthquakes and recommends to Government to take such
purposive measures in consultation with State Governments and stakeholders as would mitigate
the consequences of a potential earthquake in the vulnerable areas. The Committee also
recommends that microzonation of cities particularly those falling in seismic zone V , IV and III
should be taken up expeditiously and necessary geophysical, geological and other information/
data should be acquired from Geological Survey of India so that delay in microzonation of cities
is avoided.
