14. In view of the foregoing, the Committee makes the following observations/
recommendations:
(i) The Committee notes that the quantum of e-waste is not only huge but
is increasing at a staggering pace and thus the issue needs to be
addressed in a purposive manner and on urgent basis. There is a yawning
gap between the e-waste generated and the capacity developed to deal with
it. The Committee feels that the number of 126 E-Waste recyclers/
dismantlers is abysmally inadequate to treat the quantum of nearly 8 lakh
tonnes of e-waste generated in the country. The Committee, therefore,
recommends the Central/State Authorities to take immediate remedial
measures to suitably and efficiently address the issue by enlarging the
infrastructure in place to deal with the issue. The Committee believes
that there is an immediate need to increase the number of dismantlers/

5
recyclers/collection centres specially in States generating large quantum of
e-wastes and the gap between the e-waste generated and the capacity to
deal with it should be bridged at the earliest possible.
(ii) The Committee feels the need to increase the coverage of Extended
Producer’s Responsibility to involve more producers in the management of
e-wastes.  The Committee feels that EPR has not been adequately
enforced nor is the present legal and policy architecture adequate to
enforce the same. Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
should immediately set in motion steps to address the issue.
(iii) The Committee is constrained to note that the e-waste rules are still at
a nascent stage of implementation despite the fact that generation of
e-waste had crossed 8 lakh tonne way back in the year 2012. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should bring forward
necessary amendments in the e-waste rules incorporating the best
practices and incentive schemes prevailing internationally for encouraging
recycling.
E-RADIATION
15. The effects of electromagnetic radiation on health of human beings, animals, birds and
honeybees  through  radiations from mobile phone towers is  a matter of concern and intense
public discourse. The Committee feels that the issues arising therefrom, needed to be flagged.
16. Electromagnetic fields are part of the electromagnetic spectrum which extend from
static electric and magnetic fields, through radio frequency (RF), infrared radiation, and visible
light to X and gamma-rays. Part of the electromagnetic spectrum extending from 3 KHz
frequency to 300 GHz is referred as radio frequency (RF). Television and radio transmitters,
mobile telephones, radars, baby monitors and radio-controlled toys etc. use RF. Radio
frequency fields are non-ionizing radiation i.e. they lack the energy to liberate electrons, i.e.
ionize or effect changes in atomic structure.
17. The Committee was informed by the Secretary, Department of Telecommunication that
Electromagnetic Radiation (EMR) may also occur from natural sources like ultraviolet light
from the sun and lightning. EMR may also be generated by man made sources like power
(electricity) lines, TV/Radio broadcast, fixed and mobile radio communication, radars, medical
devices, satellite communications, X-rays, radioactive material, etc.
18. The Committee was also informed by the Department of Telecommunication that World
Health Organisation (WHO) has referred to approximately 25,000 articles, published around the
world over past 30 years, and based on an in-depth review of scientific literature, has
concluded that current evidence does not confirm the existence of any health consequences
form exposure to EMF radiation. World Health Organization (WHO) in its fact sheet No-304,
May 2006 on Electromagnetic Fields and Public Health (Base Stations and Wireless
Technologies) has concluded that “considering the very low exposure levels and research
results collected to date, there is no convincing scientific evidence that the weak RF signals
from base stations and wireless networks caused adverse health effects. From all evidence

6
accumulated so far, no adverse short or long term health effects have been shown to occur
from the RF signals produced by based stations.” The fact sheet No-304 is at Annexure-I.
19. In respect of EMF radiations from mobile handsets, WHO in its publication in June
2011 had concluded that “a large number of studies have been performed over the last two
decades to assess whether mobile phones pose a potential health risk. To date, no adverse
health effects have been established as being caused by mobile phone use”. Since the effects
on human being are to be studied over a long period of time, further studies are going on
around the world. The WHO study thus felt that the effects of EMF radiations from mobile
handsets needs to be studied further.
20. To further the international research on the subject, World Health Organisation (WHO)
established the International EMF Project in 1996 to assess the scientific evidence of possible
health effects of EMF in the frequency range from 0 to 300 GHz. While summarizing the key
points on health effect of EMF radiation, WHO website mentions the following i.e.  “WHO’s
International EMF Project was launched to provide scientifically sound and objective answers
to public concerns about possible hazards of low level electromagnetic fields. Despite extensive
research, to date there is no evidence to conclude that exposure to low level electromagnetic
fields is harmful to human health.”
21. The Committee was further informed by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and
Climate Change that an ‘Expert Committee’ with the following mandate to study the possible
impacts of communication towers on wildlife including birds and bees, was constituted by the
Ministry on 30th August 2010.
(i) To review all the studies done so far in India and abroad on aspects of ill
effects of mobile towers on animals, birds and insects.
(ii) To assess the likely impacts of the growth in the number of mobile towers in
the country.
(iii) To suggest possible mitigatory measures.
(iv) To formulate guidelines for regulating the large-scale installation of mobile
towers in the country.
(v) To identify the gap areas for conducting further detailed research.
22. After considering all aspects, the Expert Committee made the following
recommendations :-
(i) EMF should be recognised as a pollutants/regular auditing of EMF should be
conducted in urban localities/educational/hospital/industrial/residential/recreational
premises and around the protected areas and ecologically sensitive areas.
(ii) Introduce a law for protection of urban flora and fauna from emerging threats
like ERM/EMF as conservation issues in urban areas are different from forested
or wildlife habitats.
(iii) Bold signs and massages on dangers of cell phone tower and radiation which
is emitted from it are displayed in and around the structures where the towers

7
are erected. Use visual daytime markers in areas of high diurnal raptor or
waterfowl movements.
(iv) To avoid bird hits, security lighting for on-ground facilities should be minimized
and point downwards or be down-shielded.
(v) Independent monitoring of radiation levels and overall health of the community
and nature surrounding towers is necessary to identify hazards early. Access to
tower sites should be allowed for monitoring radiation levels and animal
mortality, if any.
(vi) Procedure for removal of existing problematic mobile towers should be made
easy, particularly in and around protected area or urban parks and centres
having wildlife.
(vii) Strictly control installation of mobile towers near wildlife protected areas,
important Bird Areas, Ramsar Sites, turtle breeding areas, bee colonies, zoos,
etc up to a certain distance that should be studied before deciding and should
also be practical. Ecological assessment/review of sites identified for installing
towers before their installation also may be considered in wildlife/ecologically/
conservational important areas.
(viii) The locations of cell phone towers and other EMF radiating tower along with
their frequencies should be made available in the public domain. This can be at
city/district/village level. Location-wise GIS mapping of all cell phone towers be
done by DOT. This information will help in monitoring the population of birds
and bees in and around the mobile towers and also in and/or around wildlife
protected areas.
(ix) Public consultation to be made mandatory before installation of cell phones
towers in any area. The forest Department should be consulted before
installation of cell phone towers in and around Protected Areas and zoos. The
distance at which these towers should be installed should be studied case by
case basis.
(x) Awareness drive with high level of visibility in all forms of media and regional
languages should be undertaken by the Government to make people aware about
various norms in regard to cell phone towers and dangers from EMR. Such
notices should be placed in all wildlife protected areas and in zoos.
(xi) To prevent overlapping high radiations fields, new towers should not be
permitted within a radius of one kilometre of existing towers.
(xii) If new towers must be built, construct them to be above 80ft and below 199
ft. tall to avoid the requirement for aviation safety lighting. Construct  towers
with platforms that will accommodate possible future co-locations and build
them at existing ‘antenna farms’, away from areas of high migratory bird
traffic, wetlands and other known bird areas.

view of unrestricted location of mobile towers/antennas in cities and smaller towns, cell
towers are having a concentrated effect. The Committee, therefore, recommends that
the Department of Telecommunications consider framing suitable regulations and
guidelines regarding the location and inspection of the mobile towers. The number of
qualified inspectors to carry out inspections to check the effects of EMR from cell
towers be increased.
31. The Committee is aware that Indians are more vulnerable and prone to risk from
radiations as compared to European countries because of their low body mass index and
low fat content.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that comprehensive scientific
studies need to be undertaken to conclusively establish the level of risks and adverse
health effects of EMR of cell towers. The Committee presently working on the issue
should be directed to expedite their reports which should be given within a stipulated
time-frame.

constituted to study the impact of Mobile Towers on Birds and Bees should be
implemented so that the harmful effects of EMF radiation on birds, bees, insects etc.
may be minimized.

that apart from self-certification, random checking and inspection reports should be
made public so that public at large is aware of the issue. Stringent penalties for
violation of norms and guidelines be prescribed and these should go beyond fiscal
penalties.

ANNEXURE -I
Electromagnetic fields (EMF)
Electromagnetic fields and public health
Base stations and wireless technologies
Backgrounder May 2006
Mobile telephony is now commonplace around the world. This wireless technology
relies upon an extension network of fixed antennas, or base stations, relaying information with
radiofrequency (RF) signals. Over 1.4 million base stations exist worldwide and the number is
increasing significantly with the introduction of third generation technology.
Other wireless networks that allow high-speed internet access and services, such as
wireless local area networks (WLANs), are also increasingly common in homes, offices, and
many public areas (airports, schools, residential and urban areas). As the number of base
stations and local wireless networks increases, so does the RF exposure of the population.
Recent surveys have shown that the RF exposes from base stations range from 0.002% to 2%
of the levels of international exposure guidelines, depending on a variety of factors such as the
proximity to the antenna and the surrounding environment. This is lower or comparable to RF
exposures from radio or television broadcast transmitters.
There has been concern about possible health consequences from exposure to the RF
fields produced by wireless technologies. This fact sheet reviews the scientific evidence on the
health effects from continuous low-level 31 human exposure to base stations and other local
wireless networks.
Health concerns
A common concern about base station and local wireless network antennas relates to
the possible long-term health effects that whole-body exposure to  the RF signals may have, to
date, the only health effect from RF fields identified in scientific reviews has been related to
an increase in body temperature (> 1 °c) from exposure at very highfield intensity found only
in certain industrial facilities, such as RF heaters. The levels of RF exposure from base
stations and wireless networks are so low that the temperature increases are insignificant and
do not affect human health.
19


20
The strength of RF fields is greatest at its source, and diminishes quickly with
distance. Access near base station antennas is restricted where RF signals may exceed
international exposure limits. Recent surveys have indicated that RF exposures from base
stations and wireless technologies in publicly accessible areas (including schools and hospitals)
are normally thousands of times below international standards.
In fact, due to their lower frequency, at similar RF exposure levels, the body absorbs
up to five times more of the signal from FM radio and television than from base stations -
This is because the frequency used in FM radio (around 100 MHz) and in TV broadcasting
(around 300 to 400 MHz) are lower than those employed in mobile telephony (900 MHz and
1800 MHz) and because a person’s height makes the body an efficient receiving antenna.
Further, radio and television broadcast stations have been in operation for the past 50 or more
years without any adverse health consequence being established.
While most radio technologies have used analog signals, modern wireless
telecommunications are using digital transmissions. Detailed  reviews conducted so far have not
revealed any hazard specific to different RF modulations.
Cancer: Media or anecdotal reports of cancer clusters around mobile phone base
stations ha\€ heightened public concern. It should be noted that geographically, cancers are
unevenly distributed among any population. Given the widespread presence of base stations in
the environment, it is expected that possible cancer clusters will occur near base stations
merely by chance. Moreover, the reported cancers in these clusters are often a collection of
different types of cancer with no common characteristics and hence unlikely to have a
common cause.
Scientific evidence on the distribution of cancer in the population can be obtained
through carefully planned and executed epidemiological studies. Over the past 15 years, studies
examining a potential relationship between RF transmitters and cancer have been published.
These studies have not provided evidence that RF exposure from the transmitters increases the
risk of cancer. Likewise, long-term animal studies have not established an increased risk of
cancer inform exposure to RF fields, even at levels that are much higher than produced by
base stations and wireless networks.
Other effects: Few studies have investigated general health effects in individual exposed
to RF fields from base stations. This is because of the difficulty in distinguishing possible
hearlh effects from the very low signals emitted by base stations from other higher strength
RF signals in the environment. Most studies have focused on the RF exposures of mobile
phone users. Human and animal studies examining brain wave  patterns, cognition and behavior
after exposure to RF fields, such as those generated by mobile phones, have not identified
adverse effects. RF exposures used in these studies were about 1000 times higher than those
associated with general public exposure from base stations or wireless networks. No consistent
evidence of altered sleep or cardiovascular function has been reported.
Some individuals have reported that they experience non-specific symptoms upon exposure
to RF fields emitted from base stations and other EMF devices. As recognized in a recent WHO
fact sheet “Electromagnetic Hypersensitivity”, EMF has not been shown to cause some symptoms.
Nonetheless, it is important to recognize the plight of people suffering from these symptoms.

21
From all evidence accumulated so far, no adverse short or long-term  health effects
have been shown to occur from the RF signals produced  by base stations since wireless
networks produce generally lower RF signals than base stations, no aderse health effects are
expected from exposure to them.
Protection standards
International exposure guidelines have been developed to provide protection against established
effects from RF fields by the International Commission on Non-Ionizing Radiation Protection
(ICNIRP, 1998) and the Institute of Electrical and Electronic Engineers (IEEE, 2005).
National authorities should adopt international standards to protect their citizens against
adverse levels of RF fields. They should restrict access to areas where exposure limits may
be exceeded.
Public perception of risk
Some people perceive risks from RF exposure as likely and even possibly severe.
Several reasons for public fear include media announcements of new and unconfirmed
scientific studies, leading to a feeling of uncertainty and a perception that there may be
unknown or uncovred hazards. Other factors are aesthetic concerns and a feeling of a lack of
control or input to the process of determining the location of new base stations. Experience
shows that education programmes as well as effective communications and involvement of the
public and other stakeholders at appropriate stages of the decision process before installing RF
sources can enhance public confidence and acceptability.
Conclusions
Considering the very law exposure levels and research results collected to date, there
is no convincing scientific evidence that the weak RF signals from base stations and wireless
networks cause adverse health effects.
WHO initiatives
WHO, through the International EMF Project, has established a programme to monitor
the EMF scientific literature, to evaluate the health effects from exposure to EMF in the range
from 0 to 300KHz. to provide advice about possible EMF hazards and to identify suitable
mitigation measures. Following extensive international reviews, the International EMF Project
has promoted research to fill gaps in knowledge. In response national governments and
research institutes have funded over $250 million on EMF research over the past 10 years.
While no health effects are expected from exposure to RF fields from base station and
wireless networks, research is still being promoted by WHO to determine whether there are
any health consequences from the higher RF exposures from mobile phones.
The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), a WHO specialized agency, is
expected to conduct a review of cancer risk from RF fields in 2006-2007 and  the
International EMF Project will then undertake an overall health risk assessment for RF fields
in 2007-2008.

4. PPS to Addl. Director (CP), MoEF
5. The Member Secretary, Central Pollution Control Board.
6. The Director, Wildlife Institute of India
Advisory on use of mobile towers in a way minimize their impacts on
wildlife including birds and bees
An ‘Expert Committee to Study the possible Impacts of Communication Towers on Wildlife
including Birds and Beet ‘ was constituted by the Ministry of Environment and Forests,
Government India on 30th August 2010. The report of the expert  committee has been submitted
to the Ministry of Environment and Forests.
The review of the available scientific  information by the Expert Committee in the report
indicates that the Electro–magnetic Radiations (EMIR) interfere with the biological systems. On
the basis of the report of the Expert Committee and subsequent deliberations with the
stakeholders, a list of actions to be undertaken by various agencies involved in providing,
regulating, and at along in any other manner with, the EMR based services, has been prepared.
Main objective of the listed actions is to avoid and mitigate the impacts of EMR. The Ministry
of Environment and Forests accordingly requests the concerned departments, State
Governments, user agencies, ane the public at large to rake following actions:
I. Ministry of Environment and Forests:
1. The Electro Magnetic Radiations from the communication towers may have
varying . negative impacts on wildlife especially birds and bets; Accordingly, the
information on the impacts related to different forms of wildlife as well as
humans, should be provided to the concerned agencies for regulating the norms
for notification of standards for safe limits of EMR taking into consideration the
impacts on living beings.
II. State/Local Bodies;
1. Regular auditing and monitoring of EMR should be conducted in urban
localities/educational/hospital/industrial/residential/recreational premises and
especially around the Protected Areas (PAs) and ecologically sensitive areas
w.r.t. notified norms of Department of Telecommunications. Problematic towers
from EMR point of view should be got suitably relocated/removed.

25
2. Bold signs and messages on the dangers of cell phone towers and associated
radiations are displayed in and around the structures of the towers. In addition
to these signs, use of visual daytime markers in areas of high diurnal raptor or
waterfowl movement, should also be promoted.
3. Before according permission for construction of towers, ecological impact
assessment and review of installation sites will be essential in wildlife and/or
ecologically important areas. The Forest Department should be consulted before
installation of cell phone towers in and around PAs and zoos.
III. S tate Environment and Forest Departments:
1. Regular awareness drive with high level of visibility through all forms of media,
and in regional languages should be undertaken by the State Governments and
concerned Departments to make people aware about various norms and
standards with regard to cell phone towers and dangers of EMR from the same.
Such notices should also be placed in all wildlife protected areas and zoos by
the Forest Department.
IV. Department of  Telecommunications:
1. To prevent overlapping of high radiation fields, new towers should not be
permitted within a radius of one kilometer of the existing towers. Sharing of
passive infrastructure if made mandatory for Telecom Service Providers can
minimize need of having additional towers. If new towers must be built, these
should be constructed with utmost care and precautions so as not to obstruct
flight path of birds and also not to increase the combined radiations from all
towers in the area.
2. The location and frequencies of cell phone towers and other towers emitting
EMR, should be made available in public domain. This can be at city/district/
village level. Location-wise GIS mapping of all cell phone towers should be
maintained which would,  inter alia,  help in monitoring the population of birds
and bees in and around the mobile towers and also in and/or around wildlife
protected areas.
3. There is an urgent need to refine the Indian standard on safe limits of exposure
to EMR, keeping in view the available literature on impacts on various life forms.
Till such time the Indian standards are reformed, a precautionary approach shall
be preferred to minimize the exposure levels and adopt stricter norms possible,
without compromising on optimum performance of the networks.
V . All concerned agencies:
1. Security lighting for on-ground facilities be minimized, and as far as possible,
point downwards or be down-shielded to avoid bird hits.
2. Any study conducted on impact of EMF radiation on wildlife needs to be shared
with Forest Department and Department of Telecommunications to facilitate
appropriate policy formulations.

REPORT
Concerned with the unprecedented floods in the context of climate change in Srinagar
and failure of warning and forecasting of floods system, the Department-related
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology, Environment & Forests
decided to visit inter-alia  to Srinagar, Leh, Jammu and Pathankot from 24
th to 29 th May, 2015
to interact with the concerned Central and State Government agencies as well as members
of Civil Society/NGOs.
SRINAGAR
2. In Srinagar on 24
th May 2015, the Committee held an interaction with civil society
organizations and NGOs on the reasons for unprecedented floods in Srinagar and failure of
warning and forecasting of floods in the context of climate change.  The Chairman, while
initiating the discussion, stated that the idea behind having a meeting of the Committee with
civil society and non-governmental organizations was to have a firsthand information of the
ground reality.  He further stated that though floods of the magnitude that occurred in
Srinagar were unprecedented but with the technological advancement in India particularly in
weather forecasting, it should not have been impossible to forecast and forewarn the people
so that damage could have been minimized, more so when we had the experience of
torrential rain and its aftermath in Uttarakhand not too long ago.  He asked the members of
Civil Society/NGOs to express their views frankly and without hesitation so that their views
could be factored in for the future. A list of Civil Society Organisations/NGO and individuals
is at Annexure I.
3. Representatives of NGOs/Civil Society raised a number of points pertaining to the
subject under discussion, some of main ones are summarized as under:-
(i) Ms. Maria Hearty, a representative of an environmental group stated that
services of environmental experts should be obtained and their input taken into
consideration on every aspect of planning to avoid recurrence of floods that
caused heavy damages.
(ii) Ms. Shahala Ali Sheikh, a representative of an environmental group stated that
due to bad planning and illegal constructions/ encroachments which have taken
place on wet lands/agricultural lands, the space for water bodies had shrunk to
a great extent. The State Government had prepared a Detailed Project Report
for providing water transport from Pampore to Chattabal but it had not been
made fully operational. She further informed the Committee that dredging/
desilting of waterbodies had not been done to the desired level even though
these wetlands function as water sponges/water storage structures. She also
suggested forming of a committee on wetlands. She also expressed concern
over the degradation of high forests and grass lands through continuous heavy

2
deployment of security forces especially in Dachigam National Park and
demanded its mitigation.
(iii) Ms. Jyoti Singh, social/environmental activist, suggested that youth should be
taken into confidence and involved in the efforts to conserve Dal Lake. She also
stated that people’s involvement in development and management of resources
was extremely important.
(iv) Shri Vijay Dhar, a prominent native of the city, informed the Committee that
eight Cement factories were functioning in Khrew Khonmoh areas of the Valley
which was a matter of concern from environmental point of view. He stated
that 60% to 70% of the solid/liquid waste of the hotels and house boats in Dal
Lake in the city goes into the Dal Lake. He suggested that an improvised
technology for disposal of solid/liquid waste costing Rs.2.00 lacs per unit can
be adopted for proper management of the sewage. He further suggested that
intensive measures should be undertaken for dredging of water bodies and
rivers on priority basis. He emphasized upon the need of Master Plan for
development of Pahalgam, Sonmarg and Gulmarg.
(v) Justice (Retd.) Muzaffar Hussain Jan stated that some Civil Society members
had filed a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) in the Hon’ble High Court of J&K
during his tenure as a Judge of the High Court wherein he passed orders for
preservation of Dal Lake, which was implemented to a large extent. Directions
were passed that no construction should be permitted to come within radial
distance of 200 metres from the periphery of the Dal Lake. He also stated that
he had passed orders for putting a stop to all constructions in flood prone
areas.  Unless there was a effective drainage of water, floods were bound to
occur.
(vi) Shri Javed Makhdoomi, retired Inspector General of Police, was of the view
that despite lapse of eight months after floods of September 2014, only minor/
nominal remedial measures have been taken up by the Government with no
tangible results on the ground. He informed that effective steps need to be taken
by the Government for improvement/construction of infrastructure without any
further delay. Large scale engineering works should be immediately taken up so
that no breach of banks of River Jehlum takes place again. He also suggested
that the Government should take immediate steps for providing weather
forecasting system in the valley as there are apprehensions of recurrence of
floods and that can be worst since no life saving  machinery / equipments have
been put in place till date. He also said that training should be provided to the
concerned staff of Govt. agencies for effective delivery in times of exigency.
(vii) Shri Mohammed Ishaq Qadri, Ex-Advocate General, disagreed that there was no
Master Plan of Srinagar city. He said that the Master Plan for Srinagar city was
under review, because the building permission authorities had miserably failed to

3
check illegal constructions.  He stated that a number of water bodies had been
encroached upon and the administration had not been able to remove them.
Thus floods were inevitable since there was no channel for passage of water.
He also stressed that Government should initiate dredging work of Dal Lake,
River Jehlum and other water bodies, especially Wullar, on war footing basis so
that their existing water capacity is enhanced. These waterbodies have got silted
up and their carrying capacity reduced to 10% to 20% only. Shri Qadri
suggested dredging work should be undertaken upto two to three meters depth
in the aforesaid water bodies.
(viii) Shri Mohammed Shafi Pandit, Ex-Member PSC, suggested that Government of
India should install weather forecasting machinery in the Valley. He also
suggested that dredging work of rivers and flood spill channels should be taken
up on war footing basis. He also impressed on the improvement work on
embankments to prevent any chances of breaches during high water levels.  He
further observed that the Master plan was not being implemented in letter and
spirit.
(ix) Shri Shakeel Qalender was of the view that main reasons behind the floods of
September 2014 were devastation of wetlands, soil erosion, lack of dredging
work of rivers, Dal lake and other water bodies.  He stated that the presence
of security forces had destroyed the eco-fragile areas, which was wreaking
havoc on environment.  He also brought out that J&K does not have a disaster
management  authority and the government machinery evaporated into thin air
during September 2014 floods.
(x) Shri Nazir-be-Nazir stated that all wetlands had gone into oblivion and there was
an urgent need for plantation.   He further suggested that a solid waste
management plant with modern technology should be installed at Achan dumping
site where Srinagar Municipal Corporation was dumping garbage of entire
Srinagar city.
(xi) Dr. R. Kundangar stated that there was  no visible improvement in Dal
conservation as the basic proposals for conservation of Dal are faulty. A
Detailed Project Report (DPR) amounting to Rs. 199.00 Crores for conservation
of Dal Lake was framed and submitted to the Government of India, but the
same was pending for the last three years. He demanded expediting the same.
He further informed that three Sewerage Treatment Plants were defunct, as
chemicals required for functioning of these plants were not available because of
non-availability of funds with the LAWDA. He requested that an amount of Rs.
100 lakh may be sanctioned for maintenance of these defunct plants.
(xii) The representative of Kashmir Chamber of Commerce was of the view that
dredging work of water bodies should be taken up immediately so that water
carrying/holding capacity of these water bodies could be enhanced.  He also

4
requested for expediting the financial package of  Rs. 44000 crore to the State
Government by the Government of India so that compensation/relief could be
provided to the flood victims of  Kashmir Valley without any further loss of
time.  He pointed out that a partly some of Rs.3800/- was paid to those whose
houses had been damaged upto 90%.  It was also brought out that contractors
in Kashmir Valley, who had executed works after floods of September 2014,
have not received payments despite cheques issued by the Government
functionaries which were pending in various treasuries of Kashmir Valley due to
cash crunch.
(xiii) Shri Afaq Qadri stated the Central Government should issue a white paper for
cause of devastating floods in September 2014. He stated that no dredging has
been carried even after 8 months of the floods.  He was surprised when he
received Income Tax notices at a time when his office was in 20 feet deep
water.
4. Sympathizing with the people of Kashmir valley, the Chairman assured to take up the
issues with the concerned authorities.
5. On 25
th July 2015, the Committee visited some of the areas critically affected by floods
such as G.B. Pant Contentment General Hospital, Hotel Management Institute, Amar Singh
College, Craft Museum School of Designs, DAV Institute, Lal Chowk etc. and apprised itself
of the devastation caused due to the floods. The Committee also interacted with the local
populace at these places.  The Committee witnessed that some building and houses had been
thoroughly devastated by the floods and there were watermarks upto 12-15 feet on houses and
buildings.
6. Thereafter, the Committee met with the representatives of Union Ministries of
Environment Forests & Climate Change, Earth Sciences, India Meteorological Department,
Department of Scientific and Industrial Research and local administration of Government of
J&K on unprecedented floods in Srinagar and failure of Warning and Forecasting of Floods
systems in the context of Climate Change and strengthening relief and rehabilitation work and
remedial/preventive measures.
7. Initiating the discussion, the Chairman stated that vagaries of weather, erratic and
unpredictable climatic behavior with discernible and debilitating impact on human life and
livelihood, has been manifesting at regular intervals.  He desired to know as to how far
ecological degradation caused by unplanned development and urbanization alongwith reckless
encroachment on the wetlands leading to shrinking of water bodies-wetlands, drainage
channels, etc. were responsible for the calamity in Kashmir. The Chairman also brought out
various issues raised by members of Civil Society/NGOs etc. before the Committee to the
notice of Chief Secretary, J&K and sought his response.
8. The Chief Secretary informed the Committee that State Government had issued warning
well in time to the people in the affected areas of Kashmir, Jammu and in some parts of

5
Ladakh Region through press, electronic media and various NGOs etc. but they had not
anticipated floods of such a gigantic magnitude. He added that almost all the people were
rescued and brought to the safer places.  He gave brief of the measures taken by the State
Government in providing timely relief /compensation to flood victims. The Chief Secretary
informed the Committee that relief has been provided to the flood victims in light of policy
framed by the State Government and according to the available resources and donation
received from various State Governments/NGOs and volunteers.  Replying to the Chairman’s
observation that business community have not been provided with any relief by the State
Government, the Chief Secretary informed the committee that there was no provision in the
existing rules wherein business community can be provided compensation. However, State
Government has framed a relief package of Rs. 44000 crores which had been submitted to
the Government of India for approval wherein provision for relief to the business community
has also been kept but sanction to the aforesaid relief package was pending with Government
of India. The Principal Secretary to Chief Minister, J&K informed the Committee that the
Chief Minister, accompanied a team of State Government Officers, to Delhi where it had
been assured by the Central Government that the package shall be processed for sanction at
the earliest. The Principal Secretary to the Chief Minister, Jammu and Kashmir also informed
the Committee that various Insurance Companies had also settled the insurance claims of
flood victims.
9. The Chairman desired that that State Government must come up with a short term
proposal which would be beneficial for providing immediate relief to the people who have not
got any type of relief / compensation.  In this regard, the Committee was informed that an
amount of Rs.75,000/- and Rs.1,00,000/- had been given to those whose house had been fully
damaged from State Disaster Relief Fund and Prime Minister Relief Fund respectively.  It was
also informed that with the representative of Government of India, World Bank had been roped
in to help in the housing sector.
10. The Chairman brought to the notice of State administration that Members of Civil
Society / NGOs, during interaction with the Committee, complained that garbage is being
dumped at Achan site and there is no provision of its scientific disposal. The Principal
Secretary to the Chief Minister informed the Committee that latest technology is in place at
Achan dumping site which has been designed by a reputed consultant engaged by Economic
Reconstruction Agency (ERA) and the said technology was functioning satisfactorily.  The
Chairman also raised the issue of non-functioning of three Sewerage Treatment Plants (STPs)
around the Dal Lake. The Vice Chairman, Lakes and Waterway Development Authority
(LAWDA) informed the Committee that Sewerage Treatment Plants were functioning
satisfactorily. He gave a brief account of various activities being carried out by the LAWDA
which includes dredging of Dal Lake and other water bodies, shifting of dislocated people from
Dal Lake, their rehabilitation in Rak-I-Arch and eviction of encroachments etc. The Divisional
Commissioner, informed the Committee that State Government has submitted a DPR amounting
to Rs.23000 crores to Central Water Commission, Government of India for conservation of Dal
Lake in the year 2006 approval of which was still awaited although all the observations raised

6
by the CWC have been replied by the State Government from time to time. The Committee
assured that the issue shall be taken up with the concerned Ministry in the Government of
India for its early approval.
11. Thereafter, the Chairman raised the issue of eight Cement factories in the suburbs of
Srinagar city. The Chairman, J&K State Pollution Control Board informed the Committee that
these Cement plants were located 13 Kms away from Srinagar city and have been installed in
Khrew area in distant past. Proper checking of pollution is being conducted by the Board
through its functionaries. It was also stated that some increase in pollution level was noticed
in summer months.
12. The Chairman also asked the Director General, Meteorological Department to intimate
the Committee whether any warning had been issued to the State Government in time. The
Director General, India Meteorological Department informed the Committee that they had issued
flood forecast warning on 6 th  September 2014 in Jammu and Kashmir through State
Government in view of unprecedented rains for the last so many days in Kashmir Valley and
in some Districts of Jammu and Ladakh Region.
13. Taking all the interaction in view, the Committee is of the opinion that action
on following points should be taken at the earliest to check the occurrence of similar
floods in J&K in future.
(i) Dredging/desilting of waterbodies should be undertaken on war-footing so
that carrying/holding capacity of their water bodies could be enhanced.
(ii) Old Drainage system of Srinagar should be replaced with new drainage
system that could cope up with future exigencies.
(iii) Central Govt. should sanction a suitable and adequate relief package to
the State Government and actively engage with the State Administration
to bring relief to the people.
(iv) The State Government should look into the issue of providing relief to
those people who have not got any type of relief/compensation.
(v) Compensation for partially/fully damaged houses should be suitably
revised.
(vi) Central Water Commission, Government of India should process the
Detailed Project Report submitted by the State Govt. for conservation of
Dal Lake expeditiously.
(vii) Effect of cement factories in Khrew area on environment should be
examined and a detailed project with all facts be prepared and submitted
to CPCB as well as the Committee.
(viii) Ministry of Earth Sciences and India Meteorological Department should
coordinate and integrate their effort with the State Govt. and ensure
timely warning and forecasting for such calamities particularly floods.

7
Leh
14. On 27 th May, 2015 at Leh, the Committee interacted with representatives of NGOs/Civil
Society Organisations and Deputy Commissioner of Leh and other officers of Ladakh
Autonomous Hill Development Council, Union Ministry of Environment, Forest & Climate
Change regarding pollution control measures and effects of Climate Change.
 15. Initiating the discussion, the Chairman enquired about the environmental status of Leh
and Ladakh and pollution mitigation measures adopted in Leh as it was one of the most pristine
and ecologically sensitive part of the country. The Committee felt that pollution by growing
number of vehicles had been affecting Ladakh and Leh and the ever growing number of
tourists visiting the city are causing heaps of polybag and garbage all over the area. He desired
to know as to whether any time frame has been fixed for achieving the pollution mitigation
goals. Chairman invited representatives of civil society/NGOs to inform the Committee about
the issues of environmental pollution and effects of climate change being felt in Leh. A list of
Civil Society Organisations/NGOs is at Annexure II.
16. Thereafter, representatives of civil society/ NGOs made the following points before
the Committee:-
(i) There was selective and myopic approach to deal with ecological imbalances
in Leh.
(ii) Instead of targeting the tourists, a comprehensive well thought out action plan
should be devised to mitigate environmental pollution caused by tourists.
(iii) There was scarcity of water in the area and climate change had an adverse
impact on water scarcity, life stock and agriculture.
17. The Chairman emphasised that awareness among the general public about environmental
issues needs to be increased. Leh District had a fragile ecology and global warning was having
its effect on Leh too.
18. Thereafter, the Committee desired to know from the officers representing the local
administration, about the status of bio-medical waste, municipal solid waste, plastic waste
management etc. In response, the Committee was informed that Leh District was among top
tourist destination on the tourist map of India and during summers tourist influx is at its
peak. Therefore, the number of Hotels, Guest Houses, and Restaurants was growing. The
Committee was informed that the District Forests Officer, Leh acts as Nodal officer for JK
Pollution Control Board to have a check on the Development activities, growth of hotels etc.
As regards status of Bio-Medical Waste, Leh has 04 Health Care Facilities (HCFs) including
02 clinical laboratories catering to 360 beds and generating 240 Kgs/day of biomedical waste.
All the  04 HCFs have applied and have been granted authorisation under Bio-Medical Waste
(Management & Handling) Rules. No Common Bio-Medical Waste Treatment Facility exists in
Leh. Out of the 240 kgs/day bio-medical waste generated, 50 kg/day is incinerable, 40kg/day
is recyclable and 150kg/day is disposed via secured landfill. Only one on-site incinerator of
capacity 25kg/hr is available for waste treatment. In order to create awareness regarding the

8
need for proper handling of the infectious bio-medical waste, a training was organized in
collaboration with a team from CPCB.
19. Regarding status of Municipal Solid Waste, the Committee was informed that for the
collection of municipal solid waste, door to door collection mechanism is in place but
segregation of waste is not carried out. However, the recyclable segment of the waste was
collected manually by rag-pickers. Both the bio-degradable and non-bio-degradable waste are
stored in a single bin. Transportation of the waste is carried out by tippers and transported
to an open dumping site, as Leh does not have a designated engineered landfill site for the
disposal of the waste. Although, Leh District Master Plan in the year 2009 had earmarked a
land approx. 28 kms from leh for setting up of sanitary landfill site.
20. Regarding status of Plastic Waste Management, it was informed that to control the
menace of polythene carry bags and the other non-biodegradable products in the state, J&K
State Pollution Control Board presented a draft bill to the Government which was finally
enacted as J&K State Non-Biodegradable material (Management, Handling & Disposal) Act,
2007. Later, ban had been imposed on polythene carry bags under the said Act in 2008.
However, the enforcement of the Act became possible only after notification of J&K Non-Bio-
degradable (Management, Handling & Disposal) Rules in May, 2009. The Committee was also
informed that a proposal had been sent to State Pollution Control Board for monitoring of
Water Pollution by six new stations at Leh Nalla, Indus River, Pangong Lake, Tsomoriri Lake,
Niddar Nallah and Hunder Tokpo.
21. It was also informed that out of 23 stone crushers operating in Leh, 08 stone crushers
have been granted permission by the Pollution Control Board while notices were served to 13
operating illegally and closure order had been issued against 02. Further, under national Air
Quality Monitoring Programme (NAMP), 03 stations for Leh viz Leh, Zanskar and Nubra had
been sanctioned which were not operational.
22. Considering all the points, the Committee feels that to mitigate the
environmental pollution of Leh, action on following needs to be undertaken on
priority:-
(i) The State Government should constitute an expert group to study ways
and means to reconcile the growth of tourism in the district with the
imperatives of preserving the ecology.
(ii) Concerned municipal agencies must ensure that solid waste is disposed off
in a environmentally friendly manner.
(iii) Action is required to be taken for the setting up of a sanitary landfill for
disposal of municipal solid waste for which Leh District Master Plan 2009
had earmarked a land approximately 28 km from Leh.
(iv) Three stations under National Air Quality Monitoring Programme (NAMP)

Jammu
23. On 29
th May, 2015, the Committee held interaction with members of civil society,
NGOs and the concerned central and state govt. authorities on the problems of Tier-II cities
of J&K in general and Jammu in particular.
24. In the beginning, the Chairman highlighted that the pace and process of economic
growth has put environment under great stress. The need of the hour was to make
environment and development supplementary and complementary to each other in a way that
the two sustain each other. He stated that there were formidable environmental challenges such
as rising population, haphazard urbanisation, growing industrialisation, ever increasing number
of vehicles plying on the roads, depleting natural forest cover; inadequate facilities for disposal
of sewerage and solid waste, e-waste, biomedical waste, etc., which were common to all the
towns and cities and Jammu was no exception to it. He asked the representatives of civil
society organisations/NGOs to present their views on environmental problems in Jammu so that
the Committee could get a clear picture of actual state of affairs. A list of Civil Society
Organisations/NGOs is at Annexure- III.
25. The members of civil society organisation/NGOs raised a number of points, some of
which are as under:-
(i) Shri Bhushan Parimoo brought out that in Jammu, the forest cover was only
about 2.78%. He also stated that a large number of wetlands had shrunk and
the position seemed to be irreversible now.
(ii) Shri Om Prakesh Thakur stated that in Doda, areas which were once a jungle,
have transformed into industrial areas. The forestry and wildlife of these areas
has been destroyed.
(iii) Dr. Seth stated that attention should be paid for increasing the number of oak
trees and nurseries in the region.
(iv) The representatives of Tawi Bachao Andolan impressed upon the need for
creation of State Green Tribunal and Tawi Development Tribunal. He also
wanted bringing River Chenab under National River Conservation Plan. He
suggested plantation activities on both sides of the National Highway in a time
bound manner.
(v) Shri Vikram Gaur stated that residential areas had become commercial hubs in
the city and vehicular traffic mismanagement and increasing number of vehicles
were adding to the pollution. Disposal of medical waste was not being done

10
properly. He also stated that some areas near Jammu Railway station had
become dumping grounds.
(vi) Shri Anil Raina stressed upon the need for an action plan for saving River Tawi
which had become a dumping point for solid waste and debris. He stated that
there was a acute shortage of drinking water in Jammu. He wanted rain water
harvesting to be made compulsory for all.
(vii) Shri Rakesh Gupta, representative of Chamber of Commerce and Industry,
Jammu stated that the nallahs in the city had been encroached not only by
people but also by Govt agencies. He also alleged that nallah sites had been sold
by the govt for constructing shops there.
26. The Chairman raised the issue pertaining to encroachment on forest land in
compartment No.1 to 35 Ramban (Narparistan) of Ramban Forest Division falling under the
jurisdiction of Jammu region. The Principal Chief Conservator of Forests informed the
Committee that this forest land is on upper hills. Out of 317 hectares of forest land, 150 kanals
have been evicted. He further stated that eviction process shall be completed within a period

encroached forest land and asked if encroached land can be evicted within a period of three
months. He desired that the reply from the PCCF should reach the Committee through Chief
Secretary, J&K in the shortest possible time.

th June, 2015, forwarded a Status report on the ‘Forests of Neel,

28. The Committee feels that action on following points needs to be taken to

(ii) Nurseries should be set up on large scale to meet the requirement of

(iii) Action against encroachment of forest land should be intensified and there

heart and lungs. Roads and streets are full of garbage. Because of smell

school and colleges.
(iii) The representative of  Paryas Sanstha highlited that 17 people had been injured

for environment protection and nandishala for providing shelter to stray bulls.
He stated that inspite of meetings with the district administration, no solution
for the problem had come out.

and local authorities on the points raised by various members of civil society etc.  The

PWSSB that there were three disposal points for discharge of treated domestic effluent of
Pathankot City, of which two disposal points shall be made functional by 31-08-2015 for
discharge of treated domestic effluent of Pathankot City and the third disposal point shall be
made operational only after getting clearance from Railway Authorities, Govt. of India.
Regarding solid waste management project, the Committee was informed by the Mayor,
Pathankot that a solid waste management project was proposed to be set up in and around
Pathankot. Land has been identified at Deriwal village. Final steps for identification were in
progress and within next one month, collection points for garbage would be identified. The
Chairman desired that the garbage should be removed from the city at the earliest and report
be sent to the Committee. As regards the place for dumping carcasses, the Committee was
informed by the concerned authorities that a case had been filed against the culprits and the

(i) Deputy Commissioners of Pathankot and Gurdaspur should from a citizens
Committee under their chairmanship to take care of environmental issues
such as cleanliness, menace of stray animals, wastes, garbage, cleaning of
roads and streets and removal of debris etc. and the meetings of the

and strict and better enforcement of provisions regarding stray animals
for disposal of excreta discharged by the animals, concerned municipal

Corporation, Pathankot should submit a comprehensive report/plan

(v) The existing site for dumping carcasses should be shifted elsewhere
outside at the earliest.  Chairman, PPCB should prepare a report

(vi) For smooth functioning of public transport, Deputy Commissioner,

unlawful plying of autos.
(vii) Unauthorized vehicles, auto rickshaws, should be banned as they are a big
source of pollution.
(viii) Provision to provide more parks, path for pedestrians/morning or evening
walkers should be explored, planned and executed in a time bound
manner.
(ix) The problems of drainage system and the resultant menace of mice in

(xiv) Deputy Commissioner, Pathankot in consultation with Sewerage Board
should initiate action for getting funds from the Govt. of Punjab to
enhance the capacity for sewerage system.

Present Status of the Forests:-
With the increase in human population as well as cattle population the forests
of these catchments have come under tremendous biotic pressure. Not only
this, the forests of these catchments have also borne the brunt of militancy.
During the militancy period the forest areas of these catchments along with
other forest areas of Chenab Valley remained inaccessible which resulted in poor
control of the field staff over the forests. This coupled with increasing biotic
pressure has led to damages to the forests. These damages are visible in the
form of unauthorized removal of trees, especially during the militancy period,
and encroachments on certain portions of the forest land. As per the available
data 6359 Kanals (318 Ha) of forest land have been encroached upon in the
aforementioned forest compartments. At certain locations soil erosion has also
occurred. Incessant rains and snow avalanches have caused landslides in
different areas over the past few years.

35
Issues of concern:
The Forest Department is grappling with the following issues as on today.
i. Prevention of illegal removal of trees:
With the growing demand of timber due to increase in human population there
has been a tremendous pressure on the forests for timber and firewood. At
times people resort to unauthorized felling and removal of trees from the forests
to meet their requirements. This is becoming difficult to deal with because of
unwieldy beats/blocks and inadequate man power.
ii. Removal of encroachments:
Encroachment removal is another uphill task for the department in view of
increasing demand for the land resource.
iii. Rehabilitation of degraded forests:
It is an important aspect of forest management/development. About 27% of
the forest area is degraded in the aforementioned catchments. Rehabilitation of
these degraded forests is also not that easy in view of topography, distance
from road head, refractory edaphic conditions in certain areas and unfavorable
weather at times.
Steps taken by the Department so far:
Though inadequacy of funds and field staff has been an impediment, the
department hastried its best to address the above mentioned issues within
available human/financial resources. Following measures have been taken by the
department so far.
i. Afforestation:
An area of 208 Ha has been brought under plantation under various schemes
like State Plan, District Plan and CAMPA during the last 5 years.
ii. Prevention of damage to the forest crop:
Sincere efforts are being made to prevent illegal removal of trees from the
forests. The field staff do frequent rounds of their respective areas of
responsibility. On detection of a damage case, immediate action is taken as
required under rules. During the last few years 59 damage cases have been
booked and 500 cft of illegal timber has been seized/confiscated.
iii. Eviction of encroachers:
The Forest Department has initiated action to prevent/remove encroachment of
the forest land. During the last 2 years 155 Kanals of forest land has been
retrieved.

36
Measures proposed for future:
To treat the degraded forest areas and prevent! remove the encroachment of forest
land, effective steps are required to be taken. Demarcation work and removal of
encroachments has to be undertaken by the Forest Department with the assistance of Revenue
and Police Department. The development works shall be executed with the involvement of
people of the area as people participation is important for sustainable management and
development of forests. Accordingly, following measures are proposed to be undertaken in the
aforementioned catchment.
i. Demarcation and removal of encroachments:
The old boundary pillars are either damaged or missing’. To make the boundary
line clearly visible on ground, recently approved newly designed boundary pillars
have to be erected in place of the old ones. This is possible only after carrying
out demarcation of the forest land. The main boundary line of the forests of
these catchments consists of 304 boundary pillars. The boundary line around
the Chaks has 1265 boundary pillars. All these boundary pillars are to be erected
afresh in order to have newly designed Boundary Pillars in place. expenditure
of Rs. 70.70 lacs.
After carrying out the demarcation, encroachment on the forest land would
become clearly visible and accordingly the eviction process would’ ‘be initiated.
As on today, record indicates encroachment on 318 Ha of forest land in Neel,
Pogul and Paristan catchments. It is proposed to retrieve this encroached forest
land within a period of 5 years. After removal of encroachments, the retrieved
area would be fenced followed by plantation of coniferous and broad leaved
plants. The fencing of and plantation in the retrieved forest area would involve
an expenditure of Rs. 90.70 lacs.
Monitoring of demarcation works and encroachment removal:
As the demarcation work and subsequent removal of encroachments requires assistance
of Revenue and Police Department, it is proposed to have following monitoring committees for
the above said purpose.
a. District Level Monitoring Committee:
The District Level Monitoring Committee is proposed to be headed by Deputy
Commissioner Ramban with SSP Ramban as its member and Divisional Forest
Officer Ramban Forest Division as member secretary.
b. Provincial Level Monitoring Committee:
The Provincial Level Committee is proposed to be headed by Divisional
Commissioner Jammu with IGP Jammu Zone as its member and Chief
Conservator of Forests Jammu as its member secretary.

37
ii. Rehabilitation of Degraded Forests:
The record shows that 3745 Ha of forest area is degraded in the aforementioned
compartments which includes very steep/difficult area in the upper most.
reaches of the compartments as well besides the snow-clad peaks. Therefore,
practically about 2000 Ha of degraded forest area only is treatable. It is
proposed to rehabilitate the treatable degraded forest area in two phases of 5
years each i.e. phase- I from 2015-16 to 2019-20 and phase-
ii ITom 2020-21 to 2025-26. In Phase-I 1,000 Ha of degraded forest area is
proposed to be treated. Annually about 200 Ha of degraded forest area will be
treated. The above said target shall be achieved by incurring an expenditure of
Rs. 320.00 lacs in 5 years. Rehabilitation of degraded forests would involve
fencing of the area being treated, plantation of conifers/broad leaved species in
the fenced area and minor soil/moisture conservation works. Treatment to the
degraded forest areas will be given in two ways - i) by assisting the natural
regeneration (ANR) of the indigenous species to get established and ii) by
promoting artificial regeneration (AR) of the indigenous species. Apart from
this, silvi- pasture development is also proposed to be a component of
rehabilitation programme in certain areas adjacent to habitation where demand
for forage/fodder is high and people meet their fodder requirement substantially
from forest areas.
iii. Soil Conservation measures:
Soil conservation measures are proposed to be carried out in landslide lerosion
prone areas of the aforementioned compartments. The landslides have taken
place at various locations in the forest areas of aforesaid catchments which
need to be treated! arrested. The soil conservation measures to be undertaken
in such areas would involve mechanical method and vegetative method. In
mechanical method gabionic structures, retaining walls and check dams would
be constructed at appropriate places in the eroded areas, whereas vegetative
method entails plantation of soil binding species in the inter check dams/inter
retaining walls/inter gabionic structures spaces. The soil conservation works
would involve a financial implication of Rs. 28.20 lacs in the 1st phase.
Landslide in Co.30/Rbn.

38
The total project cost is estimated to be Rs.509.60 lacs. Statement showing
year:-wise physical and financial targets from 2015-16 to 2019-20 is enclosed
as annexure-A to this report. The requisite funds shall be arranged by pooling
the resources under different schemes.
Steps to be taken immediately:
The process of demarcation, encroachment removal and rehabilitation of degraded
forests has to be started in a well planned and resulted oriented manner. It is deemed proper
to start this process from Paristan catchment and conclude it in Neel catchment. Therefore,
first compartment to be dealt with would be compartment No. 35/Rbn falling in Paristan
catchment and last compartment to be treated would be compartment No. l/Rbn falling in the

No. 35/Rbn to begin with.
i) Demarcation work and removal of encroachment: d
As per record total forest area of this compartment is 350 Ha, out of which

ii) Treatment of retrieved forest land:
