INTRODUCTION 
 
 I, the Chairman of the Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Science & Technology, Environment & Forests, having been authorised by the 
Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this Two Hundre d Seventy-sixth 
Report on the Action Taken by the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research on 
the recommendations contained in the Two Hundred Fifty -seventh Report  of the 
Committee on Demands for Grants (201 5-2016) of the Department of  Scientific and 
Industrial Research, which was presented/laid in the both the Houses of Parliament on 5 th 
May, 2015. 
 
2. There were twelve  recommendations contained in the Two Hundred Fifty-
seventh Report of the Committee.  Action Taken Notes on the recommendations o f the 
Committee were received from the Department on  5th August, 2015.   
 
3. In the meeting held on 15th January, 2016 , the Committee considered the draft 
Report and adopted the same. 
 
  
  
 
 ASHWANI KUMAR 
New Delhi: Chairman 
January 15, 2016 
25 Pausha, 1937 
         Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Committee on Science & Technology, Environment & Forests 
 Rajya Sabha 
  
  
  
 
 
 

REPORT 
 
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Department of 
Scientific and In dustrial Research on the recommendations contained in the Two 
Hundred fifty-seventh Report of the Department -related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Science & Technology, Environment & Forests on the Demands for 
Grants (2015-16) of the Department of Sc ientific and Industrial Research,  (Ministry of 
Science and Technology)  presented to both the Houses of Parliament on 5th May, 2015. 
There were twelve recommendations in the Report of the Committee. Action Taken note 
on the recommendations of the Committee were received from the Department on 5 th 
August, 2015.  The Committee, on e xamination of Action Taken Note , however is not 
satisfied with action taken by the Department in respect of seven recommendations (Para 
nos. 3.13, 4.6, 6.5, 7.6, 8.2, 9.11 and 13.2)  and would like the Department to take further 
action in respect of such recommendations as indicated in the Report. 
The Committee's recommendations, action taken note thereon and comments of 
the Committee on the Action Taken by the Department of Scientifi c & Industrial 
Research, are set out in the subsequent paragraphs:- 
FINANCIAL ACHIEVEMENTS OF THE DEPARTMENT  
Recommendation (Para 2.2) 
 The Committee notes that in spite of utilizing more than 99% of the allocation 
during 2012-13 and 2013-14, the budgetary allocation of the Department was reduced at 
RE stage during the last three financial years. The Committee is of the view that 
investments in scientific research are extremely important for the development of the 
nation and that reduction in budgetary all ocation at RE stage results in delay in 
implementation of schemes/ programmes of the Department. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that since the Department has potential of fully utilizing its budgetary 
allocation, reduction in allocation at the RE should not be resorted to. 
Action Taken by Government 
The Department thankfully acknowledges the observations of the Committee. The 
observations are being forwarded to the Department of Expenditure, Ministry of Finance, 
for appropriate action as deemed fit.  
Comments 
  The Committee takes note of the reply. 
SCHEMES OF THE DEPARTMENT OF SCIENTIFIC AND INDUSTRIAL 
RESEARCH 
Recommendation (Para 3.13 ) 
In all the above cited four schemes viz Promoting Innovations in Individuals, 
Start-ups and MSMEs, Patent Acquisit ion and Collaborative Research and Technology 
Development, Building Industrial R&D and Common Research Facilities and Access to 
Knowledge for Technology Development and Dissemination of the Department, there 
has been gross underutilisation of allocated res ources. The reasons cited for the same are 
administrative and in a way were avoidable. Because of underutilisations, allocation at 
BE stage for 2015 -16 for all the said schemes was reduced quite drastically. The 
Committee, therefore, strongly recommends th at the Department should strengthen its 
administrative and monitoring mechanism for utilising the allocated resources in each 
quarter. Not utilising the allocated fund during first three quarters of the year and then 
using one third allocation during last quarter as an explanation for underutilisation, is 
untenable.  
Action Taken by Government 
 The SFC memorandum and guidelines of the schemes had to go through several 
iterations within the department and were approved only during the 3rd quarter of 2013 -
14. Even after approval, release of funds were linked to complying with certain pre -

conditions, such as 3rd party appraisal of the scheme, independent evaluation of the 
financial health of companies, etc. which could be complied with by the department, only 
by the 3rd quarter of 2014 -15. Furthermore, releases were affected since a condition was 
imposed that beneficiaries should spend their share in the project before availing DSIR 
support as opposed to earlier practice of releasing the first instalment at the time of 
commencement of project and releasing subsequent instalments upon receipt of 
utilization certificate from the beneficiary. Finally, in February -March, 2015, financial 
approvals even for the projects recommended by the inter -departmental committees were 
put on hold.  
In order to improve fund utilization, inter -alia, it is proposed that Guidelines or 
Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for processing of proposals for financial 
approvals are framed, which remain stable over a period of time. Also, the  roles of 
program heads, inter -departmental committees, financial advisers etc. need to be clearly 
defined. Newer compliances to be introduced in Guidelines/SOPs should be discussed at 
appropriate forums and approved by the competent authority. 
Comments 
The Committee does not find reasons stated for delay as cogent.  Moreover 
while framing the memorandum and guidelines, the Department should have 
visualized the time needed for granting approval.  The Committee reiterates its 
recommendation and hopes that th e Department would inform the Committee 
about the concrete steps taken to grant approval on time.   
RESULT FRAMEWORK DOCUMENT (RFD) 
Recommendation (Para 4.6 ) 
The Committee notes the performance of DSIR evaluated by third party under 
Result Framework Docum ent (RFD) and finds that performance is declining 
continuously. From a score of 96 % in 2010 -11, it has nosedived to 80% in 2014 -15. The 
Committee strongly disapproves such a trend. What is more appalling is the excuse of 
enforcement of model code of conduct in March, 2014 as reasons for under -performance. 
The Committee understands that model code of conduct prohibits only new 
schemes/programmes but it is applicable to ongoing schemes/projects, is a news to it.  
Action Taken by Government 
 The department notes of the Committee’s concern over the declining RFD score.   
In view of the introduction of Model Code of Conduct in March 2014, files being 
processed for support to private industries were put on hold, affecting performance of the 
scheme during 2013-14.  
Comments 
 The Committee does not find reasoning for the declining RFD score tenable 
in as much as that t he Department should have foreseen the situation causing out of 
operation of  Model Code of Conduct.  The Committee, therefore,  reiterates its  
recommendation.  
Recommendation (Para 4.7) 
 In view of the above, the Committee recommends that the Department should find 
out the reasons for its continuous decline under RFD and prepare a time bound action 
plan to improve its RFD score.  
Action Taken by Government 
 Reasons for continuous decline in RFD score have been, delayed approval of XII 
plan schemes and their slow implementation because of imposition of a number of pre -
compliance requirements.   Speedy implementation of the schemes with adequate 
guidance, advice and support from all concerned will help in improvement of the RFD 
score.  
 
 

Comments 
 The Committee takes note of the reply and hopes that the Department would 
come out with concrete steps to plug the loopholes.  
AUTONOMOUS INSTITUTIONS 
COUNCIL OF SCIENTIFIC AND INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH (CSIR) 
Recommendation (Para Nos.  6.5 & 6.6) 
  The Committee observes that the number of patents granted to CSIR during 2014-
15 both in India and abroad has been way behind the target set for grant of patents. CSIR 
has been granted only 60 patents as against the target of 150. CSIR has itself admitted 
that the activities in the area could not be pursued at the desired level due to paucity of 
funds. The Committee observes that in the years 2013 -14 and 2014 -15, Rs 40.00 crores  
were allocated for the scheme at BE stage which was reduced to Rs. 35 crores at RE. In 
BE 2015-16, again an amount of Rs. 40 crore has been allocated. As such, the allocation 
made to CSIR for Intellectual Property and Technology Management has remained 
constant, with little margin to offset even the inflationary cost over the years.  
The Committee recommends that increased funds should be provided to CSIR for 
Intellectual Property and Technology Management scheme so that fund constraint does 
not come in the way of achieving progress in this sector. Since patent filing is one of the 
major indicators of the scientific and technological advancements of a country, the 
Committee also recommends that CSIR should further intensify and galvanise its efforts 
and try to improve upon its performance in terms of filing and grant of patents.  
Action Taken by Government 
 Department would like to submit the updated data on Patent filing and granted 
during 2014-15. 
 
 Filed  Granted  
Target  Achieved  Target Achieved 
India 170 308 150 64 
Abroad 250 392 250 282 
The above table shows that target for ‘patents to be granted’ in India during 2014 -
15 could not be achieved. As stated earlier Department would like to submit that it is 
because of pendency of work in Indian Patent Office.  
Department appreciates Committee’s concern that fund constraint for the Scheme 
should not come in way of achieving progress in the area of Intellectual Property. 
Department would take up the issue with Ministry of Finance at the stage of ‘Revised  
Estimate’ discussion as recommended by the Committee. Department will make all out 
efforts to exceed the target in filing and getting patents granted in India and Abroad.  
Comments 
 The Committee takes note of the reply.  
WORLD RANKING OF CSIR 
Recommendation (Para 7.6) 
The Committee is extremely disappointed to note that the world ranking of CSIR 
has dipped from 73 in 2011 to 84 in 2014. The Asia ranking of CSIR has also gone down 
from 15 in 2011 to 17 in 2014. Budgetary constraints and inadequate manpower  are not 
potent reasons to justify the decline of CSIR in world ranking during the last three years. 
CSIR may be holding No. 1 position in the country but its 17th rank in Asia again is 
indeed a matter of concern. The Committee is of the view that CSIR's c ontribution in the 
fields of research, innovation and technology development to improve its world ranking 
can bring laurels to the country and therefore, reiterates the recommendation made on this 
issue in its 244th Report that in order to fulfil the aspir ations of modern India, CSIR 
should aim to become amongst at least first 10 global organisations in its field and it 
should strive hard to achieve that ranking within next 5 years.  

Action Taken by Government 
 Department would put all efforts so that the C ommittee’s recommendation for 
CSIR to strive placing itself in top 10 global organizations be achieved. There are certain 
factors which influence the endeavour however and these are beyond the control of the 
Department. 
Comments 
 While taking note of the r eply, the Committee expect that some concrete 
action plan would be chalked out to improve ranking of CSIR. 
BUS MOUNTED REVERSE OSMOSIS (RO) WATER FILTER  
Recommendation (Para 8.2) 
The Committee appreciates the bus mounted Reverse Osmosis water filter 
developed by CSIR. However, the Committee is appalled to know that instead of 
commercialising such a path breaking innovation at least to States/State agencies, at 
present there is only one such RO unit with the Department. The Committee is at a loss to 
understand as to why, in the current climatic scenario, when natural disasters are on the 
rise in the country, no thought has been given to increasing the number of such mobile 
RO units or the commercialisation of this technology. At a time when the country is 
making preparations for meeting the challenges of disasters, the availability of such RO 
units has great relevance during disaster times. 
Action Taken by Government 
 Department appreciates the Committee’s concern about providing potable water 
to people in disaster-affected areas. As recommended by the Committee, Department will 
make all out efforts to draw a road map for the purpose.  
Comments 
 The Committee takes note of the reply and would like to be apprised of the 
progress made in this regard.  
NATIONAL S&T HUMAN RESOURCES DEVELOPMENT PROGRAMME  
Recommendation (Para 9.10) 
  The Committee takes note of the reasons advanced by CSIR for not being able to 
achieve the targets set in respect of number of scholarships/fellowships/associateships 
awarded under Nati onal S&T Human Resource Development (Research Scheme). The 
Committee is of the view that financial constraints apart, lack of proper planning and 
methodology for grant of awards also played a pivotal role in CSIR not being able to 
achieve its targets in re spect of award of scholarships/fellowships/associateships, as a 
result of which a large number of bright students were denied opportunity of these 
scholarships/fellowships. Creating a bank of well trained researchers is extremely 
important for the developm ent of science and technology in the country. The 
fellowship/scholarships under this scheme provides motivation and encouragement to the 
personnel pursuing/engaged in scientific fields. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that in future, CSIR should set a  realistic target for award of its fellowships/scholarships 
so that it does not fall short of the targets set by it. 
Action Taken by Government 
Department through CSIR has been trying to create a pool of well -trained 
researchers which is extremely important for the development of Science and Technology 
in the country, as kindly pointed out by the Committee. As recommend ed by the 
Committee CSIR would try to set a realistic target for award of Fellowships/Scholarships.  
Comments 
 The Committee takes note of the reply. 
Recommendation (Para 9.11) 
The Committee also observes that the allocation made for S&T Human Resources 
has remained almost the same since the last three years despite the fact that the 
emoluments for research personnel have been revised. A numbe r of sanctioned posts are 

also lying vacant. These need to be filled up urgently. CSIR has also highlighted the need 
for additional funds under this head. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the 
budgetary support to this scheme should be adequately i ncreased so that lack of funds 
does not come in the way of incentives devised to encourage scientific research in the 
country  
Action Taken by Government 
 During 2015 -16, an amount of Rs. 288 crore has been allocated to the Scheme 
“National S&T Human Resou rce Development Programme”. Department has already 
requested Ministry of Finance to allocate additional funds of Rs. 220 crore to meet the 
expenditure on account of revision of rate of emoluments to research scholars w.e.f. 01-
10-2014 so that lack of funds  does not come in the way of incentives devised to 
encourage scientific research in the country, as directed by the Committee.  
Comments 
 The Committee takes note of the reply.  
NATIONAL CIVIL AIRCRAFT DEVELOPMENT PROGRAMME (NCAD)  
Recommendation (Para 10.4) 
The Committee is extremely disappointed to note that a programme of great 
national importance such as National Civil Aircraft Development Programme (NCAD) 
Programme has made very little, rather no progress, at all during the last three years. The 
Committee is constrained to state that although our country has mastered space 
technology, we are yet to develop technology for developing a commercial aircraft. The 
Department has inter alia indicated financial constraints for non -approval of the 
programme duri ng the last three years. The Committee recommends that the 
administrative approvals for the fresh initiatives taken in collaboration with Hindustan 
Aeronautics Ltd. may be obtained at the earliest so that the actual work on the 
programme could be initiated  in right earnest. The Committee also recommends that 
adequate financial allocations be made for the above programme so that its execution is 
not delayed any further. A comprehensive review of the causes of delay of the project 
needs to be undertaken and responsibility fixed for the delay alongwith an action plan for 
successfully implementing the project within a stated time-frame considering the strategic 
importance of the project.  
Action Taken by Government 
 CSIR, in 2008, took up a pilot study for devel opment of a 50 to 70 seater 
Turboprop Civilian Transport Aircraft for Regional Connectivity. A ‘High Powered 
Committee’ was formed in May 2010 under the Chairmanship of Dr. Madhvan Nair, Ex. 
Chairman, Indian Space Research Organization to oversee the activ ity related to detailed 
feasibility study (report) for development of a 70 -seater Civilian Transport Aircraft for 
regional connectivity in consultation with all the stakeholders. The Feasibility Study 
Report recommended 70 to 90 seater Turbo Fan configurat ion. In 2012, Dr. Kelkar 
Committee was formed to explore the possibility of a Public -Private Partnership model 
for development of the Aircraft. The Committee found that there was lack of enthusiasm 
in the Indian Private Sector companies for participation i n the programme. It was mainly 
due to lack of clarity in identifying a launch customer, number of aircrafts to be 
manufactured, competition from several existing established players/ Original Equipment 
Manufacturer of the sector. The domain is complex and ecosystem for aerospace 
technology deployment does not exist in the country. CSIR has made all efforts necessary 
for the endeavour under reference.  
Recommendation was made for setting up a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) 
between M/s Hindustan Aeronautics Li mited and CSIR -NAL. Department is making all 
efforts to make the project operational.  
 
 

Comments 
 The Committee takes notes of the efforts and complexities invo lved with 
National Civilian Airc raft Development Programme and would like Department to 
keep making earnest efforts at the earliest for operationalisation of programme.  
CSIR 800 
Recommendation (Para 11.4) 
The Committee is at a loss to understand as to why a scheme launched to augment 
the incomes and improve the quality of lives of one million rural  citizens geographically 
spread across the country, was merged with another scheme, the objectives of the new 
merged scheme have no direct relation whatsoever with CSIR -800 scheme. The 
Committee hopes that with the merger of the CSIR -800 scheme with the Na tional 
Laboratories scheme, the objectives of the original CSIR -800 scheme will not be lost. 
The Committee recommends that there should be no let up in the activities of the 
Department on this front and adequate financial support should be provided to the 
Department for achieving the objectives of the scheme in the new merged scheme.  
 
Action Taken by Government 
 Department would like to submit for the kind consideration of the Committee that 
CSIR has reviewed and merged the CSIR-800 scheme with National Laboratories scheme 
in pursuance of the direction of Government of India to rationalize the implementation of 
schemes. The department would adequately fund CSIR 800 program and make all efforts 
to fulfill the objectives of the approved CSIR 800 projects/ activities. 
Comments 
 The Committee takes note of the reply.  
TREATMENT OF MUNICIPAL, URBAN WASTE ETC. 
Recommendation (Para 12.1, 12.2  and 12.3) 
 During the meeting of the Committee held on 9th April 2015, the Committee was 
informed by the Department about t he CSIR's involvement and contribution in clean 
Ganga Mission. One of the points highlighted by the Department was demonstration 
project on Phytorid Technology for treatment of sewage to avoid pollution load to River 
Ganga. It was informed that the project  was a single solution to treat municipal, urban, 
agricultural and industrial effluents. Further, it was a low cost project with facility for 
reuse of treated water.  
The Committee desired to know whether the above project was successful in practical 
terms and whether the technology had actually been applied to treat municipal and city 
waste. In response, the Committee was informed that extensive research work on the 
project had been done at National Environment Engineering Research Institute, Nagpur. 
In response to a further query as to whether the application of the technology could be 
actually seen at the ground level, the DG, CSIR failed to provide a categorical reply to 
the Committee.  
The Committee is of the view that treatment of municipal, urban, ind ustrial 
effluent etc. is one of the major problems not only of municipal authorities but of Town 
Planners also, which is also responsible for the increasing pollution load of our rivers. 
The Committee recommends that the Department should take immediate ne cessary steps 
to test the Phytorid technology at the ground level and, if required, further researches on 
the above technology should be carried out on urgent basis to make it a successful model 
in a time bound manner.  
Action Taken by Government 
Department would like to elaborate further on Phytorid technology as under:  
The technology is useful for treatment of municipal sewage both for urban and 
rural as a stand -alone system as it involves constructed wetland to tackle both organic 
carbon and nutrients v iz. nitrogen and phosphorous. This system is nature based and has 

been through R&D studies structured into technology. The technology is not a single 
solution for treating domestic, agriculture and industrial effluent. Particularly industrial 
effluents may cause toxicity due to heavy metals or other organic compounds which are 
not degradable. Agriculture runoff however can be treated as the system has both 
physical and biological component for treating the pollutants in agriculture runoff. The 
control of flow will be a major issue in case of runoff, as phytorid will require a properly 
controlled and designed hydraulic flow with proper retention time. However, as 
envisaged this project definitely can be deployed in Clean Ganga Mission particularly for 
the Nallah which are contributing Ganga pollution by way of conveying sewage into it. 
One such demonstration plant has been put up in Nagpur at the Nallah which flows with 
domestic sewage. The capacity is 0.1 MLD and results are very satisfactory. The capital 
cost of sewage treatment plant is almost equivalent to conventional technology provided 
the land cost is not added and is applicable wherever there is a land available for putting 
constructed wetland. But the major saving is on the operation and maintenance a nd 
therefore the technology is more sustainable. Treated water can be used for irrigation and 
other non-potable purposes. However, if the treated water is used for some other uses, 
select tertiary technologies such as filtration, disinfection can be combin ed for getting 
better water quality.  
Phytorid technology has been applied in the field successfully for treatment of 
domestic sewage at colony level and also for some of the municipal colonies. First plant 
was commissioned in 2006 at Kalina Campus at Mumb ai with the help of Mumbai 
University. About 40 such treatment systems are in operation in various places. One such 
demonstration unit is available in Nagpur which already has been mentioned in response 
to para 12.1. R&D for further improving the engineeri ng design vis -à-vis targeting high 
organic load is also in progress as continuous improvement in the technology is required 
to cater to specific problems.  
Action Taken by Government 
 The technology has already been provided in the municipal and urban town ships. 
CSIR-NEERI is proposing Dewat technologies as well as low cost technologies using 
combination of technologies where phytorid is one of the components to address the 
problems faced by municipalities / town planners. Though the present capacity of the  
plant at various places is not more than 100 M3 / day, higher capacity plants can be 
designed particularly for deployment in urban areas provided land is not the constraint. 
Land constraint will be addressed through combined technologies which are being 
developed by CSIR -NEERI. These include natural systems as well conventional and 
advance systems for delivering good water quality product. Institutes planning to use the 
technology plus combination of technologies in the Clean Ganga Mission at select places  
to provide solution to pollution in Ganga.  
Comments 
 The Committee takes note of the reply.  
ROBOTICS TECHNOLOGY  
Recommendation (Para 13.2) 
The Committee feels that Robotics is the technology of the future as the future 
management of human civilisation was going to depend heavily on robotics. Already, in 
countries like USA and Japan, robots were being used for treating and taking medical 
care of the aged people. Compared to these countries, India was way far behind in this 
critical field. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should make 
an action plan to make rapid progress in the field of robotics so as to be able to compete 
with advanced countries in this field in a given time frame. The Committee also 
recommends that required budget ary support should be provided to the Department to 
make rapid strides in this field.  
 

Action Taken by Government 
 Department would like to submit that during the current XII Five Year Plan, CSIR 
is executing following four projects wherein various forms of Robotics are being 
developed.  
• Technology Solutions for Micro Air Vehicle Development;  
• Robotics and Micro Machines; 
• Autonomous Underwater Robotics; and ;  
• Advanced Instrumentation Solutions for Health Care; 
 
The Department will make all efforts  to make available the approved budget to 
these projects in remaining period of the plan. 
Comments 
 The Committee , while taking note of  the reply , feels that the Department  
should chalk out an action plan to make rapid progress in the field of robotics to 
compete with advanced countries like USA and Japan in the field of robotics in a 
given timeframe.  The Department has only provided the names of projects it is 
executing in the XII Five Year Plan. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its 
recommendation and desires that an action plan to make rapid progress in robotics 
to be submitted to the Committee at the time of Demand for Grants 2016-17.

REPORT
The Chairman, Rajya Sabha, in consultation with the Hon'ble Speaker, Lok Sabha, referred* "The
Compensatory Afforestation Fund Bill, 2015" (Annexure-I) as introduced in Lok Sabha on 8th May, 2015
and pending therein, to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and
Technology, Environment and Forests for examination and report.
2. The Bill seeks to provide for the establishment of funds under the public accounts of India and
the public accounts of each State and crediting thereto the monies received from the user agencies
towards compensatory afforestation, additional compensatory afforestation, penal compensatory
afforestation, net present value and all other amounts recovered from such agencies under the Forest
(Conservation) Act, 1980; constitution of an authority at national level and at each of the State and Union
territory Administration for administration of the funds and to utilise the monies so collected for undertaking
artificial regeneration (plantations), assisted natural regeneration, protection of forests, forest related
infrastructure development, Green India Programme, wildlife protection and other related activities and
for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.
3. The Ministry of Environment, Forest & Climate Change through a background note on the 'The
Compensatory Afforestation Fund Bill, 2015' submitted to the Committee gave an outline for the need
of the Bill, summary of which is as follows:
(a) The principal objective of "Compensatory Afforestation Fund Bill, 2015" is the establishment
of the National Compensatory Afforestation Fund (NCAF) and the State Compensatory
Afforestation Fund (SCAFs) to credit amounts collected by State Governments and Union
territory administrations to compensate loss of forest land diverted for non-forest purpose.
The bill also provides for constitution of a National Authority and a state Compensatory
Afforestation Fund Management & Planning Authority in each State and Union Territory to
manage and utilize the amounts credited to the National Compensatory Afforestation Fund
and State Compensatory Afforestation Funds respectively. The Bill also establishes a
Monitoring Group to assist the National Authority in Monitoring and Evaluation of activities
undertaken from amounts released from NCAF and SCAFs.
(b) Under Section-2 of the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, the Central Government accorded
approval to the State Government for realizing funds from the user agency for creation and
maintenance of the Compensatory Afforestation to mitigate impact of diversion/dereservation
of forest land for non-forest purpose.
(c) Observing the considerably slow and poor progress in some of the states for raising money
for compensatory afforestation, Ministry of Environment, Forest & Climate Change placed
the same before the Supreme Court of India in the form of a statement. The Supreme Court
treated the statement as an I.A. No. 566 and issued notices to the defaulting states. The
*Rajya Sabha Parliamentary Bulletin Part II, dated 21 st May, 2015.

2
Supreme Court in its order, further stated that large sums of money were realized by various
states but the utilization of the money for reforestation represents only about 83 per cent
of the funds (shortfall is of nearly Rs. 200 crores) actually realized by the State Governments.
The Supreme Court in its order stated that the Ministry of Environment, Forests & Climate
Change should formulate a scheme to ensure that if the permission granted for use of forest
land for non-forest purposes has the condition for compensatory afforestation, then the
responsibility for the same should be of user agency to set apart a sum of money for doing
the needful and the scheme formulated by the Ministry should have no shortfall in respect
thereto. Further, the State Governments concerned will have to provide or make available
land on which reforestation can take place and this land may have to be made available
either at the expense of the user agency or of the State Governments as the State Governments
may decide.
(d) The Supreme Court, for implementation of the orders, constituted the Central Empowered
Committee (CEC) which placed a Report regarding Compensatory Afforestation. The Report
stated that:-
(i) Funds in the states of Chhattisgarh, M.P., Uttrakhand (erstwhile Uttaranchal) and
Uttar Pradesh for the compensatory afforestation is readily available as the money is
directly deposited by the user agency with the forest Departments as 'Forest Deposit'
and do not form a part of consolidated funds.
(ii) In the other states, the funds received from the user agencies for compensatory
afforestation are deposited as revenue receipts with the State Government which are
made available to the forest Department only through budgetary provisions because
of which all the states, except Karnataka, are facing problems in the timely release
of funds for compensatory afforestation and until the present system of release of
funds through budgetary provisions is changed, the pace of quality of compensatory
afforestation cannot be increased significantly.
(iii) The practice of artificial regeneration which is envisaged by the present compensatory
afforestation scheme does not adequately compensates the loss of forest cover and
should be replaced by assisted natural regeneration as per the general consensus
among the States/UTs. Also, as per the unanimity of views the assisted natural
regeneration and other forests conservation and development activities in addition to
plantations should be a site specific plan wherein assisted natural regeneration should
be given due importance.
(iv) At present, net present value for forest land being diverted for non-forest use is being
recovered from the user agency in the states of M.P., Chattisgarh and Bihar. It is
desirable that such norms for recovering money from the user agency which could
be utilized for undertaking specific activities may be laid down for all the states.

3
(e) The Central Empowered Committee, after considering the views of State Governments as
well as Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, was of the view that the
present system of compensatory afforestation is neither being implemented effectively nor
does it adequately compensate the loss of natural forests.
(f) The Central Empowered Committee recommended that a 'Compensatory Afforestation Fund'
should be created in which all the monies received from the user-agencies is deposited
subsequently released directly to the implementing agencies as and when required. The
rules, procedure and composition of the body for management of the CAF shall be finalized
by Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change with the concurrence of Central
Empowered Committee within one month. The Committee also recommended that funds
received or yet to be received from user agencies and amount received on account of
compensatory afforestation but not spent or any balance amount lying with the States/Union
Territories shall also be deposited in this Funds.
(g) In response to the Report of the CEC, the Union of India field an affidavit in the Supreme
Court of India. In the affidavit, the Ministry of Environment, Forest & Climate Change
accepted the recommendations of the Central Empowered Committee in principle and mentioned
that major institutional reorganization of the present mechanism needs to be done. The
affidavit proposed framing of comprehensive rules which will inter-alia also relate to the
procedure and compensation and a body for the management of the Compensatory
Afforestation Funds.
(h) The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change vide Notification dated 23rd April,
2004 constituted Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management and Planning Authority
(CAMPA) as an authority under sub-section (3) of section 3 of the Environment (Protection)
Act, 1986. Supreme Court in their judgment dated 26.09.2005 suggested certain amendments
in the CAMPA notification dated 23.04.2004 issued by the Ministry of Environment Forests.
The MoEF vide notification dated 13.03.2007 incorporated these amendments in the CAMPA
notification dated 23.04.2004. The Supreme Court in their order dated 05.05.2006 took note
that the CAMPA had not become operational and directed for constitution of an ad-hoc body
consisting of Director General of Forests and Special Secretary, MoEF as Chairman and
Inspector General of Forests (FC), a representative of the Comptroller and Auditor General
and a nominee of the Chairman of the CEC, as members, till CAMPA becomes operational.
Consequent to the said order dated 5th May, 2006 passed by the Supreme Court, the ad-
hoc CAMPA became operational and the funds have, since the year 2006, started flowing
into the State wise accounts operated by this body.
(i) The Compensatory Afforestation Fund Bill, 2008 was introduced in the Parliament in 2008.
It was passed by the Lok Sabha on 23rd December, 2008. However, the Bill, taken up for
discussion in Rajya Sabha, could not be passed and lapsed on dissolution of the 14th Lok
Sabha.

4
(j) After the Compensatory Afforestation Fund Bill, 2008 lapsed, there were persistent requests
from Members of Parliament, Chief Ministers, Forest Ministers and Chief Secretaries for
release of funds to the States/UTs from Ad-hoc CAMPA for carrying out compensatory
afforestation activities urgently. Accordingly, Ministry of Environment, Forest & Climate
Change formulated guidelines dated 2.7.2009 for State-CAMPA and placed before the Supreme
Court for approval on which the Supreme Court gave the following directions, vide their
order dated 10.07.2009:-
(i) The guidelines and structure of the State CAMPA may be notified/implemented and
all previous orders of the Supreme Court would stand modified to the extent necessary
for implementation of state CAMPA.
(ii) Funds received by the Ad-hoc CAMPA would be released not all at one time but the
sum of about Rs.1000 crore per year, for the next 5 years in proportion of 10% of
the principal amount pertaining to the respective State/UT provided that the details of
the bank account opened are intimated to the Ad-hoc CAMPA and the schemes for
which amount is released towards NPV and protected areas would be reviewed by
the State Level Executive Committee and the Annual Plan of Operation is approved
by the Steering Committee of the State CAMPA. Also, the site specific works for
which amount may be released towards the compensatory afforestation, additional
compensatory afforestation, PCA and the Catchment Area Treatment Plan must be
approved by MoEF&CC while granting prior approval under the FCA, 1980.
(iii) 5% of the amount released would be utilized by the National CAMPA Advisory
Council whether directly or through the Ad-hoc CAMPA for monitoring, evaluation
and implementation of various schemes. Recommendation from time to time would
be made for the release of funds seeing the progress of state CAMPA and the
effectiveness of the accounting, monitoring and evaluation systems.
(iv) Till an alternative system is put in place (after obtaining permission from this Court)
the money towards CA, NPV and Protected Areas (National Parks, Wildlife Sanctuaries)
shall continue to be deposited in the Ad hoc CAMPA and its release will continue to
be made as per the existing orders of this Court. Also, the funds would be utilized
by the work as per the broad guidelines adopted by the NREGA and work if possible
may be allotted mostly to the unemployed rural people.
Following the order, State CAMPAs were constituted in each State/Union Territory
and funds limited to Rs.1000 crore p.a. were released to various State CAMPAs
during 2009 to 2014. Supreme Court in their judgment dated 12th March 2014
permitted the Ad-hoc CAMPA to release annual amount equal to 10% of the principal
amount lying to the credit of each State/Union Territory, out of the interest receivable
by it with effect from financial year 2014-15 onwards.

5
(k) The Comptroller and Auditor General (C&AG) in their report entitled "Compensatory
Afforestation in India (21 of 2013)" recommended that the Ministry needed to review the
existing paradigm of CAMPA by approaching the Supreme Court, where considered necessary
and in a way that enhances transparency, bringing CAMPA within the broader focus of both
Parliament and State legislatures and in greater public view so as to ensure the largest
possible stakeholders participation. The C&AG further recommended that the amounts lying
in Ad-hoc CAMPA are to be transferred into the Public Account of India as per compensatory
Afforestation Fund Bill, 2008 and transfers to individual states could be made transparent
which would ensure that budgetary financial and performance related indicators/information
on CAMPA are suitably reflected in public documents at the Centre and State level for
income and outflows from CAMPA.
Earlier, the C&AG in his D.O. No.13-CAG/ Rep (C)/CAMPA/13 dated March 4, 2013
requested the Hon'ble Finance Minister to examine the entire issue of maintaining a fund
outside Government Accounting System and also suggested to move to the Supreme Court
for reviewing its decision to transfer the Ad-hoc CAMPA fund into Public Account of India.
(l) The MoEF&CC in consultation with the concerned Ministries formulated the draft CAMPA
order 2014 with a view to utilize unspent amounts to provide for constitution of an
Authority, as provided in sub-section (3) of the section-3 of the Environment (Protection)
Act, 1986 in the Union of India and in each State and the UT to be known as National
CAMPA and the State CAMPA respectively and to provide for establishment of a non-
lapsable, non-alienable, dedicated, interest bearing fund under the Public Accounts of Union
of India and of states to be managed by the National CAMPA and the concerned state
CAMPA respectively.
The cabinet in its meeting held on March 27, 2014 approved the proposal of draft CAMPA
order, 2014 and the MoEF filed I.A. No. 3797 of 2014 in the writ Petition (Civil) No. 202
of 1995 in the matter of T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad vs. Union of India before the
Supreme Court that the MoEF may be allowed to publish the said order in the official
gazette and to implement the draft CAMPA order, 2014 as per modifications to be made by
the Hon'ble Supreme Court. The said I.A. was listed before the Green Bench of the
Supreme Court several times and the last time on 16th January, 2015.
The learned Attorney General for India in his D.O. letter dated 22nd January, 2015 informed
the Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Environment, Forest & Climate Change that
the Attorney General before Hon'ble Supreme Court pleaded that the matter needs to be
heard at the earliest since more than Rs.37,000 crores is available in the said fund and also
advised that the Government of India may consider introducing a new Bill in line with the
CAMPA Draft Order, 2014 in the Parliament and the bill would have to address the judgment
of the Supreme Court dated 26/9/2015 wherein the Supreme Court had stated that the
CAMPA fund do not come within the fold of Article 266 or Article 283 of the constitution

6
and therefore the Court had not allowed transfer of these funds to the Consolidated Fund
of India or the Public Account of India due to two reasons i.e. (i) The fund is for
regeneration of forests and maintenance of ecology and will not fall in constitutional provisions,
and (ii) It is a 'fee' and not a 'tax'.
However, according to the Attorney General, the reasons are not tenable as the funds come
well within the constitutional provisions and would at least be public revenue and therefore
amounts could be spent. According to him, if the judgement of the Supreme Court could
not be reversed by introducing a legislation, its effect could be nullified by removing the
basis of the judgment. The Bill therefore, must address itself to the judgement of the
Supreme Court dated 26/9/2005 and it would be in the nature of a validation Act which
would state that law is being enacted not withstanding anything contained in any judgment
or order of any court. It is informed that in pursuance to advice of the learned Attorney
General for India, The Compensatory Afforestation Fund Bill, 2015 had been introduced in
the Parliament.
4. The Committee held a preliminary discussion on the Bill and heard the views of Secretary, Ministry
of Environment, Forest and Climate Change on 24th June, 2015. Considering the significance of the Bill,
the Committee directed to issue a Press Release, in national dailies and other regional newspapers on 27th
June, 2015 inviting memoranda from the public, experts, organizations etc on the Bill. In response the
Committee received a number of memoranda. The said memoranda are at ANNEXURE-II. The Committee
sought the comments of the Ministry on the memoranda received from various experts/organizations.
5. The Committee also wrote to States/Union Territory Governments/administrations for seeking their
views/comments on the provisions of the Bill and also undertook study visits to Udhagamandalam (Ooty),
Shimla, Kochi, Nagpur, Pench, Bengaluru and Goa to hear the views of concerned State Governments.
The views of the State Governments on the Bill received by the Committee are at Annexure III. The
Committee also heard the views of some experts/NGOs in its meetings held during the study visits and
also on 17th September, 2015 and on 14th January, 2016 in Delhi.
6. The Committee held detailed deliberations on views/suggestions of experts, NGOs and State
Governments on various provisions of the Bill and took up clause by clause consideration of the Bill in
its next meeting. After taking into account the suggestions received on various clauses, the comments/
recommendations of the Committee are as follows in seriatim:-
6.1 Long Title
Plantations of indigenous/native species needs to be encouraged since it has long term impact on
environment. Further, Green India Programme is a separate programme of Government and has its own
budgetary allocation. The funds under Compensatory Afforestation are not meant to finance Green India
Programme.
Therefore, the Committee recommends that in Para 1, line 8, the words particularly of
native species, may be added after the word 'plantations' and in line 9, the words "Green India
Programme" may be deleted.

7

The Committee adopts the Clause without any modification.

The Committee adopts the Clause without any modification.
6.4 Clause 2(e)
An indicative list of 'environmental services' has been given in this clause which is not exhaustive.
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the words "environmental services means" may be
substituted by the words "environmental services includes".
6.5 Clause 2(e) (iv)
Pollination & Seed Dispersal are critical ecosystem services for forest regeneration and must find
their place in any definition of environmental services.  Therefore, the Committee recommends that
the words "including pollination and seed dispersal" may be added at the end of the clause.

"Prescribed" means prescribed by rules made by the Central Government in consultation

The Committee adopts the Clause without any modification.

7. In its report of September 2013 on Compensatory Afforestation, the CAG has put forth some
startling facts. It computes that between 2006 and 2012, the State environmental departments were to
get 103,382 hectares of non-forest land for afforestation from revenue departments. Instead, all they got
was 28,086 hectares out of which afforestation was carried out on "an abysmal 7280.84 hectare
constituting seven per cent of the land which ought to have been received". Both the CAG and the
Government have noted that it is difficult to procure land for Compensatory Afforestation. The 'land for
land' requirement as stipulated by the FCA 1980 is difficult to satisfy as land is a limited resource.
Further, several issues arise with regard to the purchase of land such as lack of clear land titles, difficulty
in complying with procedures for land use etc. Also, land for compensatory afforestation cannot be
acquired under the Land Acquisition Act 2013. In 2014, a High Level Committee reviewing environmental
laws noted that while forest and tree cover has increased, the quality of this cover has significantly
decreased. The High Level Committee observed that one of the reasons behind this decline is the poor
quality of Compensatory Afforestation plantations. The Supreme Court in its order dated 26.9.2005
directed collection of these funds because States had utilized only 83% of the funds collected. The
Compensatory Afforestation Fund Bill, 2015 seeks to unlock these funds that are currently under "Judicial"
Overview and create a structure so as to place them under "Parliamentary/Legislative" oversight.
8. The Committee, therefore, recommends that in order to meet the situation where enough
land is not available for Afforestation, specific provisions should be made in the bill for encouraging
densification and revitalization of available forests closest to areas where deforestation is considered
unavoidable on account of critically important national projects. Thus the bill should contain
provisions emphasizing the same.

9. The Committee deliberated on the main issues of Bill and views of state Governments and experts
thereon. The Committee then first took up the long title of the Bill and felt that plantations of indigenous/
native species needed to be encouraged since it has long term impact on environment. Further. Green
India Programme being a separate programme of Government and had its own budgetary allocation and
need not be part of the afforestation under the Bill. The Committee decided to recommend the inclusion
of the words particularly of native species after the word 'plantations' and deletion of the words "Green
India Programme" from the Long Title.
10. The Committee then considered Clause 2(e) and was of the view that the indicative list of
'environmental services' given in the Clause was not exhaustive. The Committee, therefore, decided to
recommend that the words "environmental services means" may be substituted by the words "environmental
services includes" in the Clause.
***Relate to other matters.

36
11. As regards Clause 2(e)(iv), the Committee felt that Pollination & Seed Dispersal, (III) being
ecosystem services for forest regeneration, must find their place in any definition of I environmental
services. The Committee decided that the words "including pollination and seed dispersal" may be added
at the end of the clause.
12. As regards Clause 2(1), the Committee observed that the Bill contained many provisions for
making rules which will have a bearing on States/Union Territories and that the views of States should
be taken on board before rules are framed. The Committee therefore decided that "Prescribed" appearing
in the Clause should mean rules made by the Central Government in consultation with the State Governments/
Union Territory Administrations under the Act.
13. The Committee then considered Clause 3(4) and formed the view that most of the State Governments
were of the view that crediting 10 percent of the funds to National Authority is on the higher side and
it must be lowered. The Committee therefore decided to recommend the reduction of the share of the
National Authority to five per cent instead of ten per cent proposed in this Clause. The Committee also
decided to recommend the share of the Central Government and Stale Governments/Union Territories to
five per cent and ninety-five per cent respectively, as envisaged in Clauses 5(a) and 5(b).
14. As regards Clause 4(3)(iii), the Committee felt that the words "receipt of all monies", may be
substituted by the words "all monies realized" for the sake of uniformity. Further, the Committee
observed that since "State Authority" was defined in clause 2, the words "constituted in such State"
appearing in sub-clause 4 (4) (i), (ii) and (iii) were redundant and may thus be deleted.
15. The Committee then took up Clause 6(b) and was of the view that the phrase "infrastructure
development, supply of wood and other forest produce saving devices and other allied activities" needed
to be elaborated and clearly defined to avoid any ambiguity and to ensure that money is used only for
activities related to forest restoration, protection and management. Further, the Committee felt that the
word "money" may be substituted by the word "monies" and the words "particularly of native species"
be added after the words "artificial regeneration (plantation)".
16. The Committee found that the words Administrations' and 'Sate' appearing in Clause 6(c) and 6(g)
respectively have been spelled wrongly may therefore be read as Administrations' and 'State'.
17. As regards Clause 6(d), the Committee was of the view that there was a need to facilitate
relocation of people residing in critical wildlife habitats to achieve long term conservation goals. Accordingly,
the Committee decided that in Clause 6(d), the words "including facilitating voluntary relocation from
and" may be added after the word "activities".
18. On clause 8, the Committee was of the view that the nomenclature of ministries are changed quite
often and sometimes ministries are merged/bifurcated and therefore the word "of in line 1 of-Clause
8(4)(ii) may be substituted by the words "dealing with". Further, Ministries of Space and Earth Sciences
have important role to play in forest mapping including remote sensing, satellite imagery and monitoring
forest cover etc. and decided to recommend the inclusion of the these Ministries in the Governing Body
of the National Authority.

37
19. The Committee then considered Clause 8(4)(x) and was of the view that the Governing Body of
the National Authority needed to be expanded and one expert each of the fields mentioned in the sub
clause should be included and decided to recommend accordingly.
20. As-regards Clauses 9 (2) (ix) and 11(3), the Committee was of the view that an expert on tribal
matters or a representative of tribal community should be co-opted in the Executive Committee of the
National Authority and the Steering Committee of the State Authority and decided to recommend accordingly.
21. The Committee then considered Clause 15(1) and was of the view that the approval of Annual Plan
Operations of the State Authorities by the National Authority should be within a definite time frame.
Accordingly, the Committee decided to recommend that the National Authority should approve Annual
Plan Operations submitted by the State Authorities within three months from the date of receipt.
22. As regards Clause 16(1)(i), the Committee felt that monitoring and evaluation of the works
implemented in the States and Union Territories by the monitoring should be based on the use of scientific
methods and recommended that the words "including remote sensing" may be added at the end.
23. The Committee also felt that no periodicity of the meetings of the steering Committee of the State
Authority had been mentioned in the Bill and decided to recommend that a clause stating that the Steering
Committee of a State Authority shall meet at least once in every three months be added as Clause(18)(2).
24. The Committee then considered Clause 19(1)(i) and observed that the Steering Committee of the
State Authority was proposed to send the Approved Annual Plan of Operations to the Executive Committee
of the National Authority for final approval in Clause 18(i) and, therefore, decided to recommend that
the Executive Committee of the State Authority may formulate and submit Annual Plan of Operations to
the Steering Committee of the State Authority for its concurrence.
25. As regards Clause 33(1) to 33 (3), the Committee felt that there was an overlapping in the
provisions of sub-clause (1) and (2) and decided to amend the two Clauses as under:
(1) The Central Government may, if it finds necessary or expedient in public interest, issue such
policy directives to the National Authority or any State Authority, in writing, and such policy
directives shall be binding upon the National Authority or the State Authority, as the case may be.
Further, the Committee recommended that sub-clause (3) may be renumbered as sub-elause (2).
26. The Committee then adopted the draft 277th Report of the Committee on 'The Compensatory
Afforestation Fund Bill, 2015", with the above amendments.
27. The Committee also decided to present/lay its *** 277th Report on 'The Compensatory Afforestation
Fund Bill, 2015' to both the Houses of Parliament on 26th February, 2016. The Committee also decided
to lay a copy of the evidence tendered before the Committee in relation to its 277th Report in both the
Houses of Parliament.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
As the diversion of forest land for non-forestry purposes was causing loss to the valuable forests,
the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 was enacted to maintain a rational balance between the objectives
of conservation and development. The Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 makes provision for conservation
of forest and provide for the basic framework for regulating indiscriminate diversion or use of forest
for the developmental needs of a State. It intends to harmonize development with that of conservation
of forests and forest eco system. The compensatory afforestation envisages additional plantation activities
by utilising the money deposited by the user agency for the purpose.
2. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in its order in TN. Godavarman Thirumulpad V . Union of India
[Writ Petition (C) No. 202 of 1995], dated 30th October, 2002, observed that a Compensatory Afforestation
Fund may be created in which all the monies received from the user agencies shall be deposited. The
Court directed that the Fund shall be utilised for plantations, protection of forests, wildlife protection and
other related activities. Presently, in compliance with the direction of the Supreme Court, all monies
collected under the scheme has been placed under an ad hoc Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management
and Planning Authority (CAMPA) and deposited in the nationalised banks.
3. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in its Judgment dated the 26th September 2005 in the aforesaid
case observed that the fund generated for protecting ecology and providing regeneration should not be
treated as a fund under article 266, article 283 or article 284 of the Constitution. Funds are therefore;
kept outside the Consolidated Fund of India or Public Account of India. In the absence of proper
institutional mechanism with adequate statutory backup amount of unspent funds has increased to more
than rupees thirty eight thousand crorers.
4. The Comptroller and Auditor General in its report on Compensatory afforestation in India (21
of 2013) observed that given the substantial amounts of funds being collected under the compensatory
afforestation, the expenditure therefrom, the overall objectives of conservation, protection, regeneration
and management of forests, conservation, protection and management of wild life and its habitats and
compensatory afforestation; the clear public purpose involved in the work relating to CAMPA, there is
need to review the existing paradigm of CAMPA. The Comptroller and Auditor General recommended
that this should be done in a way that enhances transparency, brings CAMPA within the broader focus
of both Parliament and State Legislatures and in greater public view so as to ensure the largest possible
stakeholders' participation. Towards this end it would be appropriate if the amounts lying in ad hoc
CAMPA are transferred into the Public Account. The Comptroller and Auditor General has also observed
that the receipts accruing into the ad hoc CAMPA are essentially payments being made for the acquisition
of public assets, namely, forest land for non-forest purposes by user agencies. The receipts, so arising,
in essence are non-tax revenue, as are forest receipts.
5. Accordingly, to ensure safety, security and expeditious utilisation in a transparent manner of
funds accumulated with the ad hoc CAMPA and the funds to be collected by the State Governments and
Union territory Administrations it is proposed to enact a legislation, namely, the Compensatory Afforestation
Fund Bill, 2015 to provide for the establishment of a Statutory Fund and a Management Authority at the
National level and at each State and Union territory.
73

74
6. The Bill will provide the required legal backing for setting up of required institutional mechanism
both at the Government of India and in each State and Union territory for expeditiously, and utilisation,
in a transparent manner, of amounts realised in lieu of forest land diverted for non-forest purpose.
7. The Bill seeks to achieve the above objectives.

of a State Authority in performance of its functions for a period not exceeding five years. Sub-clause

Memorandum received from S/Sh. Praveen Bhargav and Shekar Dattatri
PLANTING TREES IS NO ANTIDOTE TO FOREST LOSS
"The Compensatory Afforestation Fund Bill 2015, which is pending approval in Parliament,
is anchored on the flawed and unscientific premise that loss of natural forests due to development
projects can be 'compensated' by planting trees elsewhere."
While vigorously pursuing a slew of reforms to ease forest clearances, the Prime Minister and his
Environment Minister have repeatedly averred that development will not be pursued at the cost of India's
last remaining forests. Welcome as these statements are, there is cause for apprehension in the form of
the Compensatory Afforestation Fund Bill, 2015 (CAF Bill), which was introduced in the Lok Sabha on
8th May, 2015.
'Compensatory Afforestation' is a convenient Indian concept that has been in place since 1980.
Whenever development projects seek land inside a Reserved Forest, or a Protected Area (PA), such as
a Sanctuary or a National Park, certain levies are imposed on the project proponent. This money is to
be utilized to plant trees elsewhere, ostensibly to compensate for the loss of forest.
Over the last 10 years, a staggering corpus of 35,000 crore rupees has accrued from such levies
in a fund called Compensatory Afforestation Management Planning Authority (CAMPA). The Central
Government now wants to release 90 per cent of this money to States for carrying out afforestation
projects. On the face of it, this might seem like a progressive step. But given that the Bill is anchored
on a flawed and un-scientific premise, it is only likely to provide a 'fig leaf' for covering up the increasing
diversion of forests in the name of development.
Fragmentation, the greatest threat
When ill-planned development projects are thrust into the heart of PAs, the result is fragmentation,
ie., the breaking up of large forest blocks into smaller and more vulnerable patches. Peer reviewed
scientific research has clearly established that fragmentation is one of the most serious threats to long-
term biodiversity conservation, causing several devastating impacts; among other things, it disrupts
landscape connectivity, affecting dispersal of animals, and creates new edges that expose forests to
exploitation and severe degradation. Sadly, instead of addressing this critical issue, successive Governments
have been pursuing the flawed idea of trying to 'compensate' for forest loss and fragmentation by raising
artificial plantations elsewhere.
Here is just one example of how the compensatory afforestation approach ends up not just being
a 'greenwash', but an ecological disaster as well. From 1980 to 2005, the Kudremukh Iron Ore Company
Limited (KIOCL) strip-mined hill slopes clothed in virgin rainforests in the heart of Karnataka's Kudremukh
National Park. Besides this horrendous damage to the fragile ecosystem, over 150 million tonnes of
tailings - the waste mud left over after extraction of low grade ore - were dumped into a pristine, 100
metre deep, forested valley. To 'compensate' for this loss of natural habitats, KIOCL went on a massive
compensatory afforestation spree, planting millions of trees. The problem with this was twofold: the trees
87

88
were non-native species with zero biodiversity value; and they were planted on adjoining areas of natural
grassland, which are an extremely important component of the Bhadra River's watershed. Thus, apart
from the forested hill slopes and the valley that were destroyed by mining activities, a third natural
habitat, in the form of ecologically important grasslands, was destroyed through mindless tree planting.
To add insult to injury, governments and project proponents alike proclaim such travesties-as achievements
towards a 'Green India'.
The CAF Bill 2015, if approved in its current form, would end up repeating such colossal mistakes
all over the country. In order to provide real benefits, the Bill must be modified to allow a major
percentage of CAMPA funds to be utilised for consolidating the remaining large blocks of natural old-
growth forests. This will involve strategic land acquisitions, extinguishment of old leased lands in thickly
forested areas, voluntary resettlement of people from PAs, creation of wildlife corridors and facilitating
natural regeneration of degraded forests.
Missing the woods and the trees
Despite the investment of more than 4600 crores during the last three decades, from international
aid agencies like the World -Bank, USAID, European Economic Commission, Overseas Development
Agency and others, there is ample evidence of the extremely poor results of past afforestation efforts.
In Karnataka, where more than 1500 crore rupees have been spent on afforestation projects over the past
thirty years, data from the Forest Survey of India shows that dense and moderately dense forest cover
in the State went down by 2898 sq kms between 1997 and 2011. In Maharashtra, a recent official
evaluation of ten-year old plantations (2004-2014) in all 11 forest circles has shown that 74% of them
have failed while 13% are partially successful and only 13% successful.
Under the 12th Plan, an allocation of 2500 crores was made for the National Afforestation
Programme, but with little to show on the ground. The Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science
& Technology and Environment & Forests in 2015 has recorded that despite massive budgetary provisions,
40% of forests in the country are still degraded. Currently, Japan International Co-operation Agency
(JICA) has committed 15,000 crores for 22 forestry projects in 13 States. Ignoring all this, the Ministry
of Environment is pushing forward with a poorly conceived CAF Bill that will only trigger massive
corruption in the forestry sector, without providing any ecological benefits to the country.
There is further justification for a review of the CAF Bill. CAMPA is India's sovereign fund, and
is thus the only one available for consolidation of large forest blocks. None of the international aid
agencies funding afforestation projects allow for this ecologically vital activity.
Other than investments to consolidate large Reserved Forest blocks, Protected Areas, and the
creation of wildlife corridors, the other important activity that needs to be funded through CAMPA is
natural restoration or regeneration of degraded forests. The approach must be to first identify degraded
forest areas with existent root stock, and invest only on appropriate protection measures such as
trenching, fencing and fire prevention.' The degraded forests will then recover through a natural process
at a very nominal cost to the exchequer. Funding for artificial plantations should only be considered in
extremely degraded areas with no existing root stock.

89
We are at a critical moment in India's fight to achieve ecological security while ensuring economic
and social progress. If recast on the basis of sound science, the CAF Bill 2015 will form the basis of
a far-sighted, and genuinely beneficial strategy to protect India's forests. However, given the way it is
crafted presently, it will allow thirty five thousand crore rupees to be squandered away on corruption-
ridden 'afforestation' projects involving digging pits, buying polythene bags for raising saplings, and
planting trees that can never become forests.

Memorandaum received from Shri Shankar Gopala Krishnan
The Compensatory Afforestation Fund Bill, 2015, seeks to provide a statutory framework for using
the funds collected from user agencies seeking diversion of forest land for non-forest purposes for
"compensatory afforestation", "net present value" and related activities. In order to understand this Bill,
it is important to understand the legal background to this issue, which is summarised below.
Background - What Are Compensatory Afforestation and Net Present Value?
Under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, a law enacted for protection of forests, no "forest
land" can be used for any non-forest purpose without the permission of the Central government. Such
permission is referred to as "diversion" of the said forest land. Upon such diversion, the Forest
(Conservation)'Rules require that either twice the area of diverted land of'degraded forest' or the same
area of non-forest land be set aside for "compensatory afforestation" - essentially tree plantations. The
user agency is required to pay sufficient funds for such planting to the State government, which is then
required to do the planting.
In 2002, and subsequently, over a period of several years, in the course of hearing the Godavarman
case
1, the Supreme Court issued a series of orders that changed this system. In response to concerns
that compensatory afforestation was not taking place, the court ordered that:
• Henceforth, the funds for compensatory afforestation would be deposited not with the State
governments, but in a specialised central fund;
• This fund would be administered by a central body called the Compensatory Afforestation
Management and Planning Authority;
• Payments would include not only money for various categories of compensatory afforestation,
but also for the "Net Present Value" (NPV) ofthe forest being destroyed calculated as per
an arbitrary figure of Rs 5.8 - 9.6 lakhs per hectare.
The said Authority was notified by the Central government but given no statutory basis. As a result
these funds are now lying unspent, up to a total of over Rs 38,000 crores.
Problems With The Current System
There are some severe problems with the system of compensatory afforestation and net present
value payments as it is currently instituted. These have been made more acute due to the Bill contravening
the legal requirements of the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of
Forest Rights Act), 2006 (FRA for short) unanimously passed by Parliament after the Supreme Court's
order of 2002-creating this special fund. The current Bill not only does not address these problems, but
will make them much worse. The problems include:
• Depriving people of their rights over forests and forest land. A forest is a source of minor
forest produce like fruits, food items, saleable tendu patta or kendu patta, fuelwood, medicinal
herbs, etc., as well as containing water bodies, grazing areas, common lands and other
1 WP 202/95, T.N. Godavarman Thirumalpad and Ors. vs. Union of India and Ors.

91
areas that people depend on for their-livelihood. Even where people in fact own the so-called
"forest land" (a lot of which has never been legally notified), as the community lands in the
hill areas of Manipur, they are paid nothing for its diversion. Instead, the Forest Department
collects the money for NPV as well as for compensatory afforestation for which another
piece of community land is taken. Destruction of the forest deprives adivasis, forest dwellers
and other local communities of some or all of their livelihood or basic resources- for which
they are neither informed, nor consulted, nor compensated. Enactment of the FRA now
makes it illegal to remove forest dwellers from forest land till the process of recognition
of their forest rights has been completed. In the Niyamgiri case, the Supreme Court has
upheld the FRA's requirement that the gram sabha must decide whether their forest land
may be diverted. Despite this, forest diversion, often based on obtaining fraudulent gram
sabha resolutions, is continuing.
• Equating tree planting with compensating the loss of diverse natural forests. The system
implies that, if an equivalent area of land is planted with trees, it is somehow equivalent to
the environmental damage caused by destroying an area of natural forest. In fact a natural
forest has multiple environmental and cultural values - such as providing forest products
and ecosystem services including water, a habitat for wildlife, biodiversity, abode of deities,
etc. These cannot be recreated simply by planting trees in another location, often far away
from the site of forest destruction.
• Encouraging seizure of community and individual lands for plantation purposes. In most
cases, the non-forest land used for such plantations which has to be mutated in the name
of the forest department consists of customary community or individual lands of adivasis
and forest communities on which their rights have not been recognized. Even where so
called 'degraded forest' land is used for compensatory afforestation, the FRA requires prior
completion of the recognition of forest rights in these areas, and where the land is claimed
or recognized as community forest resources (CFRs), the gram sabha is the authority for
its management. Neither the forest department nor the state or central governments have
the right to undertake compensatory afforestation on CFRs or other common lands without
the gram sabha's consent. Even as per official records, tens of thousands of hectares of
people's land have been planted with such trees in recent years. Seizure of land for
compensatory afforestation thus leads to double displacement of communities from their
livelihood resources, the first time for diversion of forest land and the second time for
compensatory afforestation.
• Levying of monetary charges does not compensate for the resulting environmental and
livelihood damage. This approach assumes that, just by requiring companies or the
government to pay money for forest destruction, environmental damage will be contained.
This ignores the multi-faceted impacts and nature of environmental damage caused by
natural forest destruction which are closely inter linked with damaged lives, livelihoods and
cultures.

92
What is needed is a system of environmental regulation that will protect people's interests and the
forests in a democratic and transparent manner. The current Bill
does not achieve this in any sense.
Problems with the Current Bill
The Bill Threatens the Rights of Adivasis and Other Forest Dwellers
As stated above, the most fundamental flaw with the current system is that those most directly
affected by forest destruction - adivasis and forest communities - have no control whatsoever over the
process. The current Bill will make this even worse, as despite enactment of the Forest Rights Act, 2006,
it neither refers to the Act nor the rights of forest dwelling communities on forest land.
This will neither result in any reduction of forest destruction nor in any just spending of this
money. Indeed, the Supreme Court's own expert committee on Net Present Value, the Kanchan Chopra
Committee, had recommended in May 2006 that NPV should be shared as per a tripartite sharing
formula. The formula granted the majority share of NPV money to local bodies and State governments.
Plantations by the forest department have become one of the biggest threats to the lands of
adivasis and forest dwellers - especially with regard to land used for shifting cultivation and other
common lands resulting in frequent conflicts. There is no provision for the local community to have any
voice in deciding where this plantation will take place.
There is no reference whatsoever to the gram sabha or the local community institutions. The Bill
thus violates the spirit and letter of the Forest Rights Act, 2006 as well as of the Panchayats (Extension
to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 (PESA for short) and will encourage further seizure of community
lands.
Further, the Bill Will Legalise an Environmentally Destructive and Ill-Thought Tree Plantation
Programme without any consideration of how the resulting changes in land use will impact local
livelihoods.
The Bill Proposes an Expensive Bureaucratic Structure Placing Effective Control over Huge Funds
in the Hands of the Forest Bureaucracy.
The proposed National Authority is to consist of a Governing Body with representation of the
Environment Minister, Secretaries of different central ministries, several forest officials and two
non-government environmentalists. There is no provision for significant involvement of the Ministry of
Tribal Affairs, the nodal Ministry for the Forest rights Act mandated to ensure recognition of customary
rights on the same forest land. The Executive Committee has only forest officials with no representation
of other ministries, along with 3 non- government forestry experts - once again without any expert on
tribal affairs or a social scientist (sec 9(2)). The Chief Executive Officer of both is to be a forest officer.
It is this Executive Committee which is to approve the annual plans of the State Authorities and to
formulate and implement 'schemes' approved by theGoverning Body under Section — 5(b)(iii). Such
