INTRODUCTION
The Department of Scientific and Industrial Research is one of the three Departments of the Ministry
of Science & Technology. The mandate of Department of Scientific and Industrial Research includes promotion
of industrial research for indigenous technology promotion, development, utilization and transfer.
1.1 The primary endeavour of DSIR is to promote R&D by the industries; support industrial units to
develop state-of-the-art globally competitive technologies of high commercial potential; catalyze faster
commercialization of laboratory-scale R&D; augment technology transfer capabilities; enhance the share of
technology-intensive exports in overall exports; strengthen industrial consultancy and establish a user-friendly
information network to facilitate scientific and industrial research in the country.
1.2  The DSIR has two public sector undertakings viz. National Research Development Corporation
(NRDC) and Central Electronics Ltd. (CEL) and two autonomous organizations viz. Council for Scientific
and Industrial Research (CSIR) and Consultancy Development Centre (CDC).  The Department also provides
host facilities and assistance to Asian and Pacific Centre for Transfer of Technology (APCTT) as the focal
point in the country.
1.3 The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technology, Environment
and Forests considered the Demands for Grants (2016-17) of the Department of Scientific and Industrial
Research in its meeting held on 31
st March, 2016.

6. AUTONOMOUS INSTITUTIONS Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR)
6.1 The Council of Scientific & Industrial Research, constituted in 1942 is an autonomous body. The
detailed functions assigned to the Council are as follows:
(i) Promotion, guidance and coordination of scientific and industrial research in India, including
the institution and financing of specific researches;
(ii) Establishment or development and assistance to special institutions or departments of existing
institutions for scientific study of problems affecting particular industries and trade;
(iii) Establishment and award of research studentships and fellowships;
(iv) Utilization of the results of the researches conducted under the auspices of the Council towards
the development of industries in the country and the payment of a share of royalties arising out
of the development of the results of researches to those who are considered as having contributed
towards the pursuits of such researches;
(v) Establishment, maintenance and management of laboratories, workshops, institutes and
organizations to further scientific and industrial research and to utilize and exploit for
purposes of experiment or otherwise any discovery or invention likely to be of use to
Indian industries;
(vi) Collection and dissemination of information in regard not only to research but also to industrial
matters generally;
(vii) Publication of scientific papers and journals;
(viii) To enter into arrangements with foreign scientific agencies and institutions for exchange of
scientists, study tours, training in specialized areas of science and technology, conducting joint
projects, providing technical assistance in the establishment of scientific institutions and for
other matters consistent with the aims and objectives of the Society;
(ix) To do all other such things as the Society may consider necessary, incidental or conducive to
the attainment of the above subjects, etc.
The CSIR has been striving to perform these functions in accordance with the priorities laid down in
Five Year Plans and perceived needs of the nation from time to time.
6.2 The Council of Scientific & Industrial Research is known for its cutting edge R&D knowledge base
in diverse S&T areas. Having pan-India presence, CSIR has a dynamic network of 38 National Laboratories,

10
39 Outreach Centres, 3 Innovation Complexes and 5 units. CSIR’s R&D expertise and experience is embodied
in about 4000 active scientists supported by about 7000 scientific and technical personnel.
6.3 CSIR covers a wide spectrum of science and technology from radio and space physics, oceanography,
earth sciences, geophysics, chemicals, drugs, genomics, biotechnology and nanotechnology to mining,
aeronautics, instrumentation, environmental engineering and information technology. It provides significant
technological intervention in many areas with regard to societal efforts which include environment, health,
drinking water, food, housing, energy, leather, farm and non-farm sectors. CSIR is the Nation’s custodian
for Measurement standards of Mass, Distance, Time, Temperature, Current etc. CSIR has created and is
the custodian of Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) which is a powerful weapon against unethical
commercial exploitation of Indian traditional knowledge.  CSIR maintains Microbial Type Culture collection
(MTCC) and Gene Bank.
6.4 CSIR has been pursuing cutting edge science and advancing new knowledge frontiers. The scientific
staff of CSIR only constitutes about 3-4% of India’s scientific manpower but they contribute to 9.61% of
India’s scientific outputs. In 2013 and 2014, CSIR published 5086 and 5824 papers in SCI Journals with an
average impact factor per paper of 2.86 and 2.97 respectively. As per preliminary estimates, CSIR has
published 5743 research papers in International SCI journals during 2015.
6.5 The Committee notes and appreciates the efforts of CSIR in publishing large number of
research papers in International SCI journals every year. However, the Committee observes that
5743 research papers published in International SCI journals during 2015 also includes a large
numbers of articles, reviews, proceeding papers, editorial materials, letters etc. In view of this, the
Committee would like to suggest that CSIR’s main focus should be on original research work.

8. WORLD RANKING OF CSIR
8.1 The Committee desired to know the world ranking of CSIR and the various steps taken by CSIR to
improve its ranking and overcome the factors adversely affecting its ranking. In response, the Committee
was informed by the Department that CSIR is a globally benchmarked and positioned organization today. It
has been ranked continuously within the top 100 organizations globally. According to the Scimago Institutions
Ranking World Report 2014, CSIR is the only Indian organization among the top 100 global institutions,
ranked at 84among 4851 institutions worldwide. CSIR holds the 17
th rank in Asia.
From research output perspective, CSIR is ranked 72 in a global context, according to the Nature
Index 2014, published by Springer Nature in December 2015. As per this, CSIR is among the only two
Indian organizations of the top 100 institutions across the world.
8.2 The Department has further stated that CSIR is the pioneer of India’s intellectual property movement.
CSIR today is strengthening its patent portfolio to carve out global niches for the country in select technology
domains. Commercialization of CSIR patents is 13.33% in comparison to 3% global average. In terms of
S&T outputs, besides scientific publications in scholarly journals CSIR is also mindful of protecting its
Intellectual Property through patents. Thus CSIR is consciously and continuously endeavouring to improve
its global ranking.
8.3 The Committee is extremely disappointed to note that the world ranking of CSIR has dipped
from 73 in 2011 to 84 in 2014. The Asia ranking of CSIR has also gone down from 15 in 2011 to 17 in
2014. . CSIR may be holding No. 1 position in the country but its 17
th rank in Asia again is indeed a
matter of concern. The Committee is of the view that CSIR’s contribution in the fields of research,
innovation and technology development to improve its world ranking can bring laurels to the country
and therefore, recommends that in order to fulfil the aspirations of modern India, CSIR should aim

13
to become amongst at least first 10 global organisations in its field and it should strive hard to
achieve that ranking.
9. NATIONAL  S & T  HUMAN  RESOURCE  DEVELOPMENT  PROGRAMME
9.1 The main objectives of the National S&T Human Resources Development Programme (NSHITRDP)
are as under:-
i) To have an integrated approach to the National Human Resource Development for science,
engineering and technology (S&T) in close collaboration with academic institutions;
ii) To invest in basic and interdisciplinary research that is harbinger of the ‘high-tech’ and
technology of tomorrow; and
iii) To promote scientific temper by supporting academic/R&D organisations to hold symposium,
seminars and conferences.
9.2 The Committee desired to know as to what steps had been taken by CSIR for enhancing and nurturing
S&T human resources. The Committee was informed that contribution of CSIR to S&T human resource
development in the country is note-worthy. CSIR scientists pursue cutting edge science and technology
development. CSIR scientists define and pursue research work as per the mandate of the laboratory. CSIR’s
projects that include cluster-specific and trans-cluster project activities for the 12
th Five Year Plan have been
prepared through participative and participatory consultation and involvement of all CSIR scientists. This
process has allowed the younger CSIR scientists to interact and be exposed to National Experts in the
domain as well. Further, CSIR had operationalized a unique initiative called “EMPOWER” -Encouraging and
Motivating Pursuit of World Class Exploratory Research, to encourage young scientists in CSIR to undertake
experimentation with their innovative, risky, imaginative and brilliant ideas.
9.3 The Committee was further informed that the Research Council (RC) of the laboratory comprising
specifically chosen members related to the S&T domain of the laboratory also interact and mentor the CSIR
scientists on their R&D endeavours. CSIR has also enabled recently, Open RC meetings at the laboratories
so as to make the process open and transparent to all the serving scientists of the laboratory. Further, the
CSIR-Human Resource Development Centre imparts training programmes, ranging from skill to leadership
development, to CSIR scientists, thus nurturing not only technical but soft skills as well.
9.4 CSIR has also put in place enabling mechanisms to incentivize innovation which include: Sharing of
the premia & royalty received from the transfer of technology with scientists alongwith proceeds from
contractual R&D and consultancy; Facilitating mobility of researchers between industry and CSIR national
laboratories/institutions; and Allowing the researchers to have an equity stake in scientific enterprises and
also spin-offs while in service.
9.5 CSIR scientists serve as faculty to the students of the Academy of Scientific and Innovative Research
(AcSIR) which was set up as an institution of national importance through an Act of Parliament named the
Academy of Scientific and Innovative Research Act, 2011. The focus of AcSIR is also on very high quality

9.6 Further, CSIR has a mandate to develop and nurture S&T manpower at the national level. It also
promotes scientific research through research grants to scientists/professors working in universities/R&D
institutes. To attract the young science students at early stages of their career towards scientific research,
CSIR opened its CSIR-UGC National Eligibility Test (NET) for Junior Research Fellowship (JRF-NET) to

response, the Department informed that during 2015-16, CSIR allocated Rs 26.04 crore to 22 of its laboratories

with the National Laboratories scheme, the objectives of the original CSIR-800 scheme will not be

16. SCIENTIFIC VISION FOR THE FUTURE AND GENERAL OBSERV ATIONS &
RECOMMENDATIONS
16.1 The Committee during its meeting held on 31
st March, 2016 had opined that development of the
country at any phase is always linked with technology and technology happens when there is advancement
in science. Hence science, technology and development are all proportional to each other. A nation who is
not able to prosper on these grounds would never be able to sustain the lives there and may have to solely
depend on other nations for the basic requirements. Such is the influence of science and technology for the
development of a nation. A nation’s development and prosperity is judged to a large extent by the status of
science and technology of that nation.
16.2 The Committee enquired from the Department about its scientific vision for the future i.e. for
the next coming 10-15 years for making our nation a strong force in the field of science & technology
as compared to the developed nations of the world and making self-reliant in every aspect as the
Committee feels that scientific interventions is the key for societal and overall development of the
nation.

22
16.3 In response, the Department informed the Committee that R&D involves treading the un-treaded
path. It involves risk, more so when the aim is to develop a technology which can be globally benchmarked.
CSIR has been undertaking challenge driven R&D aimed at developing the desired products/technologies
and has thus been continuously striving to address the unmet needs through its unique S&T interventions
and thereby contribute to the socio-economic development in the country. It has been providing significant
technological intervention in many areas which include environment, health, drinking water, food, housing,
energy, specially chemicals & petrochemicals, glass & ceramics, medicinal plants & plants of economic
value, leather, mining, metals & minerals, machinery & instrumentation, strategic sectors including aerospace
etc. The journey of CSIR over the years has been quite satisfying.
16.4 The government is making all efforts to position our country as a global leader and to make Indian
industry globally competitive. In the present scenario of rapid globalizations, when we are facing challenges
nationally and internationally of rapid technological advancements along with an unpredictable obsolescence
of even the recently developed S&T interventions, CSIR is building policy and action interventions focusing
on “Technology Innovation and Translational Research” to achieve National Goals. Some of the initiatives
include:
(a) Leveraging Science, Technology and Innovation (STI): Focused R&D efforts through: CSIR
Mission-mode Projects; Translational Research Projects; etc. It is proposed to earmark 60%
of CSIR budget for translational research and technology innovation and mission mode
projects;
(b) Positioning STI Reward System: in order to encourage, motivate and sustain quality deliverables
emphasis is being laid up on “Responsive Science, Technology and Innovation” and “Outcome
Driven Performance” and giving the achievers “Performance Linked Rewards”;
(c) Enhancing  Industry Partnerships  and  last  mile linkages:  Through innovative PPP models,
Technology Parks and Incubation Centers across CSIR Laboratories, Skill Development
Initiatives; Institutional linkages with stakeholder ministries, MSME Clusters etc. The objective
is to accelerate technology deployment at scales.
(d) Measures to enhance Industry Contribution to Science R&D: Policy interventions to encourage
and broaden incentives to industry spending on R&D. Focus will be on developing seamless
and time bound technology transfer mechanisms.
16.5 Through the aforesaid endeavours, CSIR is committed to deliver on the National Missions for enhancing
Self-reliance, Self-sustainability and thus accelerating Socio-Economic Development in the country.
16.6 The Committee has taken note of the response of the Department and feels that the
Department of Scientific and Industrial Research, Ministry of Science and Technology plays a pivotal
role in the promotion of Science & Technology in the county. New initiatives in the field of S&T play
a significant role in the development of a nation, be it in the field of Aerospace Science & Engineering,
Agro, Food Processing & Nutrition Technology, Biology and Biotechnology, Healthcare, Marine
Sciences & Engineering, Chemicals & Petrochemicals, Ecology & Environment, Energy, Electronics
& Instrumentation, Mining, Metrology and Housing, Road & Construction, etc. All the great scientific
discoveries and technological achievements in our country have brought the societal development
and grown economic status and have created many new ways for the new generations to grow in the
technologically advanced environment. The Committee is of the view that although the Department

23
has undertaken many new initiatives & measures for achieving excellence in the field of Science &
Technology, a lot more needs to be done and achieved in this area. In order to successfully meet the
challenges of the future, the Committee recommends that the Department should undertake
meaningful initiatives to establish strong foundations for a leadership role in the world in various
areas of Science & Technology in order to complete with the developed nations like USA and China.
To achieve this goal, the Committee further recommends that adequate allocation of funds be made
available to the Department in order to fulfil its vision into reality.
16.7 The Committee observes that investment in Research and Development (R&D) is decreasing.
It is only about 0.48% of our GDP whereas in some other countries, it is 2-3%. It is also a matter
of concern that all over the world, as per information available with the Committee, about 66 per
cent of R & D funding comes from the private sector and about 25-33 per cent comes from the
public sector. In India, the ratio is reverse. In view of this, it is essential that representatives of
private sector/industries are get involved in order to contribute more in R & D in the country.
Therefore, the Committee recommends that investment in R&D must be increased so that research
work may be taken up at large scale and more and more representatives of industries/companies
should be motivated for making investment in R&D of the Scientific Ministries/Departments of the
country.
16.8 The Committee also feels that even though good amount of research work is being done, it is
not actually percolating down for the use of society. It is just good on the paper. Further, the
Committee also observes that a large number of patents have been obtained in India and abroad,
but only few of them have been transferred in sustainable technologies. Therefore, the Committee
recommends that efforts should be made by the Department for making use of various research
works for societal development and transferring patents into sustainable technologies.
16.9 The Committee observes that similar kind of research in various fields is going on in the
Scientific Ministries/Departments of the country especially in the Departments of Science &
Technology, Biotechnology, and Space and Ministry of Earth Sciences etc. For example, same type of
devices like electronic machine for checking blood pressure, blood sugar and milk adulteration is
also developed by the Department of Science and Technology (DST) besides Department of Scientific
and Industrial Research (DSIR). In view of this, the Committee feels that this shows some sort of
lack of co-ordination and consultation between the various Scientific Ministries/Departments of the
country. Therefore, the Committee recommends that a mechanism should be evolved for having a
constant and broad consultation/co-ordination amongst the various scientific Ministries/ Departments
about the areas/fields of research so that time, energy, money, manpower and brain of the country
may be utilized optimally.

RECOMMENDA TION/OBSERV ATIONS — A T A GLANCE
FINANCIAL  ACHIEVEMENTS  OF  THE  DEPARTMENT
The Committee notes that despite utilizing more than 99% of the allocation during 2013-14
and 2014-15, the budgetary allocation of the Department was reduced at RE stage during the two
financial years i.e. 2013-14 & 2014-15. The Committee is of the view that investments in scientific
research are extremely important for the development of the nation and that reduction in budgetary
allocation at RE stage results in delay in implementation of schemes/programmes of the Department.
The Committee, therefore, recommends that since the Department has the potential of fully utilizing
its budgetary allocation, reduction in allocation at the RE stage should not be resorted to. Further,
the Committee notes that allocation was enhanced at R.E. stage during the last financial year i.e.
2015-16 from ````` 4031.00 to 4036.70 crore. However, the Department has utilized ````` 3811.43 crore (upto
16.03.2016) only which shows that proper and timely planning for utilization of the allocated fund was
not done. In view of this, the Committee observes that the Department must have proper planning
for utilizing the allocated funds so that optimum utilization of allocated funds may be ensured.
(Para 2.2)
REQUEST  &  JUSTIFICATION  FOR  ADDITIONAL  ALLOCATION  FOR  PLAN  &  NON-PLAN
BUDGET  (2016-17)
In view of the above submissions of the Department, the Committee feels that request for
the enhancement in the budgetary allocation to the tune of ````` 1300 crore ( ````` 500 crore in Plan Budget
& ````` 800 crore in Non-Plan Budget) for the financial year 2016-17 is fully justified and the matter
should be taken up with the concerned Ministry/Department vigorously. The Committee also observes
that investment in R &D activities, core creation of infrastructure for new labs of CSIR/Technology
Parks, recruitment of adequate manpower in CSIR, adequate funding for existing schemes of CSIR
etc. are immensely important for the development of our country and hence adequate and sufficient
allocation of funds must be made. (Para 3.12)
SCHEMES  OF  THE  DEPARTMENT  OF  SCIENTIFIC  AND  INDUSTRIAL  RESEARCH
In all, the above cited four schemes viz Promoting Innovations in Individuals, Start-ups and
MSMEs, Patent Acquisition and Collaborative Research and Technology Development, Building
Industrial R&D and Common Research Facilities and Access to Knowledge for Technology
Development and Dissemination of the Department, there has been gross underutilization of allocated
resources. The reasons cited for the same are administrative and in a way were avoidable. Because
of underutilizations, allocation at BE stage for 2016-17 for all the said schemes was reduced quite
drastically. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Department should
strengthen its administrative and monitoring mechanism for utilizing the allocated resources in
each quarter. Not utilizing the allocated fund during first three quarters of the year and then using
one third allocation during last quarter as an explanation for underutilization, is untenable.

youths of the country in a better and professional manner. (Para 13.3)
CSIR’S  ROYALTY  FROM  PARTNER  INDUSTRIES
The Committee observes that royalty component had been kept very low while giving the
technology to various companies/industries in the past. The Committee is of the view that Department
is getting meagre money as royalty from the various companies/industries against the investment
made on R&D on technology development/inventions vis-a-vis income earned by those companies/
industries. In view of this, the Committee recommends that MoU should be signed with the companies/
industries for fixing royalty component while making technology transfer/inventions for allowing
its product for commercial utilization so that Department could be financially self reliant in every
aspect and invest in R&D. (Para 14.2)
ADVERTISEMENT  POLICY  OF  THE  DEPARTMENT
The Committee notes the steps taken by the Department and feels that much more is needed
in this direction as general public at large is not much aware of the successes of CSIR, its diverse
inventions of public utilities, medicines including clot buster, vaccines, varieties of rice, detection of
milk adulteration device, achievements in the field of Agri & Food Technologies etc. which could be
immensely beneficial for the general public and farmers etc. The Committee therefore recommends
that there should be regular advertisements in the newspapers, electronic media about the
achievements/inventions of the Department for the benefit of the public. (Para 15.3)
SCIENTIFIC VISION FOR THE FUTURE AND GENERAL OBSERVATIONS & RECOMMENDATIONS
The Committee has taken note of the response of the Department and feels that the
Department of Scientific and Industrial Research, Ministry of Science and Technology plays a pivotal
role in the promotion of Science & Technology in the county. New initiatives in the field of S&T play
a significant role in the development of a nation, be it in the field of Aerospace Science & Engineering,
Agro, Food Processing & Nutrition Technology, Biology and Biotechnology, Healthcare, Marine
Sciences & Engineering, Chemicals & Petrochemicals, Ecology & Environment, Energy, Electronics
& Instrumentation, Mining, Metrology and Housing, Road & Construction, etc. All the great scientific
discoveries and technological achievements in our country have brought the societal development
and grown economic status and have created many new ways for the new generations to grow in the
technologically advanced environment. The Committee is of the view that although the Department
has undertaken many new initiatives & measures for achieving excellence in the field of Science &
Technology, a lot more needs to be done and achieved in this area. In order to successfully meet the

28
challenges of the future, the Committee recommends that the Department should undertake
meaningful initiatives to establish strong foundations for a leadership role in the world in various
areas of Science & Technology in order to complete with the developed nations like USA and China.
To achieve this goal, the Committee further recommends that adequate allocation of funds be made
available to the Department in order to fulfil its vision into reality. (Para 16.6)
The Committee observes that investment in Research and Development (R&D) is decreasing.
It is only about 0.48% of our GDP whereas in some other countries, it is 2-3%. It is also a matter
of concern that all over the world, as per information available with the Committee, about 66 per
cent of R & D funding comes from the private sector and about 25-33 per cent comes from the
public sector. In India, the ratio is reverse. In view of this, it is essential that representatives of
private sector/industries are get involved in order to contribute more in R & D in the country.
Therefore, the Committee recommends that investment in R&D must be increased so that research
work may be taken up at large scale and more and more representatives of industries/companies
should be motivated for making investment in R&D of the Scientific Ministries/Departments of the
country. (Para 16.7)
The Committee also feels that even though good amount of research work is being done, it is
not actually percolating down for the use of society. It is just good on the paper. Further, the
Committee also observes that a large number of patents have been obtained in India and abroad,
but only few of them have been transferred in sustainable technologies. Therefore, the Committee
recommends that efforts should be made by the Department for making use of various research
works for societal development and transferring patents into sustainable technologies.
(Para 16.8)
The Committee observes that similar kind of research in various fields is going on in the
Scientific Ministries/Departments of the country especially in the Departments of Science &
Technology, Biotechnology, and Space and Ministry of Earth Sciences etc. For example, same type of
devices like electronic machine for checking blood pressure, blood sugar and milk adulteration is
also developed by the Department of Science and Technology (DST) besides Department of Scientific
and Industrial Research (DSIR). In view of this, the Committee feels that this shows some sort of
lack of co-ordination and consultation between the various Scientific Ministries/Departments of the
country. Therefore, the Committee recommends that a mechanism should be evolved for having a
constant and broad consultation/co-ordination amongst the various scientific Ministries/Departments
about the areas/fields of research so that time, energy, money, manpower and brain of the country
may be utilized optimally. (Para 16.9)

REPORT
INTRODUCTION
Department of Science and Technology (DST) strives to establish and foster India’s leadership and
excellence in the field of science and technology.  The Department serves as a robust facilitator and aligns
its initiatives with India’s developmental aspirations mainly to help optimise human, infrastructure and
financial resources through appropriate inter and intra-institutional mechanisms.
2. DST plays several roles which have evolved over time. DST develops S&T policies, strengthens
human resources and institutional capacities, enables development and deployment of technologies, create
opportunities for societal interventions through Sciences & Technology, establishes and engages in
mechanisms of cooperation, partnerships and alliances.  These approaches that reflect its mission ensure
a holistic systemic influence, immediate, medium and long term relevance/gains.
3. Mandate of the Department is as follows:-
z Formulation of policy statements and guidelines on Science and Technology (S&T);
z Promotion of new areas of scientific research;
z Co-ordination of inter-Departmental S&T efforts;
z Support basic and applied research in universities and other institutions;
z International S&T Co-operation;
z Support high quality research in autonomous bodies where specialization ranges from advanced
medical research materials to astronomy;
z Catalysing S&T interaction in societal programmes, and entrepreneurship development;
z Science popularisation, communication and S&T Management Information System;
z Promotion of Commercialisation of indigenous technology;
z Support to technology development programmes, technology information and assessment;
and
z Providing services in the areas of:
(i) Surveying & Mapping;
(ii) T echnology Development and Application.
4. OBJECTIVES
Main objectives of the Department of Science & Technology are as follows:
(a) Formulation of Policies relating to Science & Technology;
(b) Strengthening basic research and Expanding R&D base-Human capacity;
(c) Strengthening Basic research and Expanding R&D base-Institutional Capacity;
(d) Implementing Technology Development Programmes: from R&D to Commercialization;

2
(e) Societal interventions of Science & Technology; and
(f) International Science & Technology Co-operation.
5. ORGANISATION
5.1 The Department of Science & Technology is the nodal Department of the Ministry of Science and
Technology.  Broadly, the organisational set up of the Department has been divided into Autonomous
Institutes, Scientific Groups, Technology Development Board and Scientific Services besides the
Administration and Integrated Finance divisions. There are 19 Autonomous Institutions and 5 Science/
Engineering Professional bodies which are working in diverse areas for the promotion of Science and
Technology. In addition, one new autonomous body viz. National Centre for Molecular Material Research,
Thiruvanathapuram has been recently set up and National Innovation Foundation, Ahmedabad which was
earlier a ‘Corpus Funded’ Financial Institute has been taken over by the Department as fully funded
autonomous Research Institute. The Scientific Groups inter-alia  consists of the Science & Engineering
Research Council (SERC), National Council for Science & Technology Communication (NSCTC), National
Resources Data Management System (NRDMS), International Division, National Entrepreneurship Board
(NEB), National Science and Technology Management Information System (NSTMIS). The Scientific
Services have two subordinate offices, namely, National Atlas and Thematic Mapping Organisation
(NATMO) and Survey of India (SoI) under their administrative control.
5.2 The detailed budget allocation of the Department of Science & Technology for the year 2016-2017
was considered by the Department-related Committee on Science & Technology, Environment & Forests
on the 31st March, 2016.

11. MEGA FACILITIES FOR BASIC RESEARCH
11.1 The basic research in the country is dependent on mega and capital intensive facilities created by
other countries and this practice has led to asymmetries in credit sharing. Further, Indian expertise to
build advanced scientific instruments and devices does not get fostered outside the strategic areas of
research where technology denial forces prevent the building of capacities. The DST along with Department
of Atomic Energy (DAE) has identified several areas where an effective partnership of the two departments
can bring about an effective capacity building in the academic sector for building mega facilities for basic
research. For the same purpose, a Memorandum of Understanding was signed between the DST and the
DAE.
11.2 The Mega  Facilities  for  the Basic Research Programme has twin objectives:
(i) to  enable  Indian  scientists to participate in building very large international facilities which
are manifestly multinational efforts and gain access to the same for scientific studies, and
(ii) to  create  some  facilities  of  international  standards  in  the  country. India’s participation in
the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), FAIR, the Thirty Metre Telescope (TMT), etc. falls in the
this category.
11.3 When the Department was asked the extent to which “Mega Facilities for Basic Research Programme”
is helping to create facilities for basic research in the country.  It was replied that projects under the
“Mega Facilities for Basic Research Programme” are such projects that not only require huge financial
resources but also sophisticated scientific knowledge at the very frontiers. According to the Department,
such projects also push the global technology frontiers and such projects are set up at the best possible
locations in the world and with the best possible global know-how.  However, India’s participation in
such projects worldwide is certainly helping in setting up a few such projects for basic research in the
country. For example, the India-based Neutrino Observatory (INO) project in Tamil Nadu will use Resistive
Plate Chambers as the detector element which has been pioneered by CERN, Geneva and Indian scientists
have participated in this development there as part of the CERN-India Collaboration. Participation of
Indian scientists in neutrino experiments at Fermi lab (United State)will also help in doing science at

14
India-based Neutrino Observatory. Indian scientists have made significant contributions towards the LHC
Computing Grid and established two Tier 2 Grid Computing facilities in the country for analyzing the
CERN data. This has initiated Grid Computing activities in the country, which has much wider scope of
application. The segmented mirror technology that is being learnt by the Indian astronomy community
will pave the way for establishing a large (8-10 m class) optical telescope at a suitable site in the Himalayas
at an appropriate time in future.  Starting with the hardware engagement at CERN in the 1990’s, India’s
involvement in various Mega Facilities has started feeding back into the system now. Creation of such
huge research infrastructures in the country is manifestly a multi-agency task. DST and DAE have
shown cooperation and coordination in creating such infrastructure in the country. Most of the projects
(national and international) planned for the 12th Plan period have been initiated. The National Large Solar
Telescope (NLST) could not start so far because of the uncertainty in the availability of the Merak site in
Ladakh. The permission from Ministry of Defence has been received very recently. The new roadmap for
creating such infrastructures will emerge as part of the next Plan exercise. All such projects will be
national (and also possibly international) collaborative ventures, and not solely a venture of the Department
of Science & Technology.
11.4 The Committee takes note of the initiatives taken and infrastructure developed under Mega
Facilities for Basic Research in collaboration with national and international agencies. However,
since permission of Ministry of Defence has now been received for availability of the Merak site
in Ladakh, the Committee hopes that new roadmap for creating infrastructure will be drawn at
the earliest and the National Large Solar Telescope will established at the earliest.  The Committee
also recommends that necessary budgetary provision should be made for creating such Mega
facilities.
Financial Performance
11.5 In reply to a query of the Committee with respect to reduction in allocation to ‘Mega facilities for
Basic Research’ from ` 99.00 crore in B.E. 2015-16 to ` 69.00 crore in R.E. 2015-16, the Department
informed that while deciding the B.E. of ` 99.00 crores for 2015-16 for Mega Facilities for Basic Research,
provision had been kept for payment towards India’s Associate Membership of CERN, Geneva (about

12. LASER INTERFEROMETER GRA VITATIONAL-WA VE OBSERV ATORY (LIGO)
12.1 Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO) is world’s largest night time Astronomy
Telescope to be set up in USA by several international partners.
12.2 LIGO Project facilities are located in the USA. It has been informed that a new advanced Laser
Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory (LIGO) will be set up in India. This will be the third such
detector in the world, the other two being in the United States. Recently, the Union Cabinet has accorded
in-principle approval for the same. 37 Indian scientists have contributed towards the recent discovery of
gravitational waves. Steps have been taken by the gravitational wave community of the country for
forging international scientific collaborations and developing human resource in this field. For this, a pan-
Indian consortium, Indian Initiative in Gravitational-wave Observations (IndIGO) was formed consisting
of researchers from premier institutions and universities of the country. IndIGO consortium has
representation in the Gravitational Waves International Committee (GWIC) which works to facilitate
international collaboration and cooperation in the construction, operation and use of the major gravitational
wave detection facilities world-wide. Indian scientists are participating in the international LIGO Science
Collaboration (LSC), through IndIGO.
12.3 As regards benefit to India, it has been informed by the Department that LIGO-India will be an
important project in the field of fundamental sciences in the country. The Observatory will be among the
most precise scientific apparatus on the Earth, with technical capability of measuring displacements
which are a billion times smaller than the size of an atom. This will help develop national capabilities in
high-technology areas such as control systems, lasers and optics and vacuum technology, well beyond
the currently available expertise in the country. This will help train highly skilled scientific and technical
manpower. The analysis of the measurements for obtaining science results will involve very sophisticated
computational and data handling infrastructure. Such a front-ranking science experiment on Indian soil
will be a source of inspiration for young and budding scientists. This will help to  launch an entirely new
discipline of gravitational-wave astronomy in the country.
12.4 From the Indian side, LIGO-India is the joint responsibility of three lead Indian institutions, Inter-
University Centre for Astronomy and Astrophysics (IUCAA)-Pune, Institute for Plasma Research (IPR)-
Gandhinagar and Raja Ramanna Centre for Advanced Technology (RRCAT)-Indore. There are 61 researchers
in the international LIGO collaboration and about 40 scientists and technical staff are involved in LIGO-
India project.
12.5 As regard budgetary allocation, initial budgetary allocation to the project to the tune of ` 9.7 crores
is being made for preparing a Detailed Project Report for the project, site selection and some prototyping
work.
12.6 The Committee believes that the proposed LIGO-India project has tremendous potential to
unravel the myriad mysteries of the universe. It is likely to become a tool for the Indian astronomy
in keeping up the level of excellence in research in astronomy and astrophysics of the country.
The Committee hopes that the LIGO-India project would help the country to embark on world
class international science collaborations and help India become a force to reckon with in this
field.

14. REV AMPING OF SCIENCE EXPRESS
14.1 Science Express is an initiative for mass awareness developed by the National Council for Science
and Technology communication (NCSTC).  NCSTC is mandated to communicate science and technology
to masses, stimulate scientific and technological temper and coordinate and orchestrate such efforts
throughout the country.  The Programmes of NCSTC aim at building capacity for informed decision
making in the community and devoted towards societal up-liftment through dissemination of scientific
knowledge.
14.2 The Government has revamped the Science Express after the seven successful tours across India

18
and redesigned it on the theme of Climate Change.  Science Express Climate Action Special (SE:CAS)
was launched on 15th October, 2015 from Safdarjung Railway Station, Delhi.
14.3 SE:CAS is a collaborative initiative of, Departments of Science & Technology and Biotechnology
and Ministries of Railways and Environment, Forest & Climate Change. It is an exhibition train travelling
across India, to put forward message of climate change, to make people aware about the implications of
the Climate change and possible actions by the Government and public to address the issue. The exhibits
mounted on the train are designed to make the science behind it easier to understand by the students of
schools and colleges.
14.4 As per information provided by the Department, SE:CAS in its current phase is scheduled to travel
across the country for about seven months, halting at 64 locations in 20 States, covering 19,800 km. The
exhibit as Science Express: Climate Action Special (SE:CAS) on wheel is a good opportunity to generate
dialogue and discussion on the topics of contemporary relevance.
14.5 The train carries exhibitions on various themes like the wildlife and nature conservation, work being
carried out by different research institutions across India, India’s development in the field of Biotechnology,
innovations in science and technology, DST scholarships & schemes, and careers in science and technology.
14.6 The Committee welcomes the revamping of the Science Express in its new avatar of ‘Science
Express: Climate Change Special’.  The Committee hopes that the joint collaboration of Ministries
of Environment, Forest and Climate Change and Railways; Departments of Science and Technology
and Biotechnology will show encouraging results in spreading awareness about the challenges
posed by Climate Change. The Committee also feels that there is a need for crowd management
in a better way in the science express and more such trains should be introduced so that viewers
get more time for viewing.
15. EFFORTS FOR RETAINING RESEARCH TALENT IN THE COUNTRY
15.1 The Committee desired to know the details of efforts being made by the Department for retaining
research talent in the country . The Department informed that it had taken several steps for retaining
research talent in the country including creation of Centres of excellence and facilities in emerging and
frontline areas  in  academic  and  national  institutes,  induction  of  new  and  attractive  fellowships,
strengthening  infrastructure  for  R&D,  encouraging  public-private  R&D  partnerships  etc. Launching
of  programmes  like  Nano  Mission,  Mega  Facilities,  Solar  Energy  Research Initiative, Nano Mission
(Phase-II), setting up of Peta scale supercomputing facilities etc. and creation of a new structure for
basic research by establishing a Science and Engineering Research Board (SERB) in the country
demonstrates the commitment of the Department to retain the scientists to carry out quality research in
the country.
15.2 On the query of the Committee about the percentage and number of researchers emigrating to
pursue research abroad, it was informed that though number of students who go abroad for higher
studies is considerable due to socio-economic reasons, the percentage and number of researchers emigrating
to pursue their research abroad leaving the country is very miniscule and insignificant. However, the
Department informed that it does not have a mechanism to monitor such migration of researchers.
15.3 The Department further informed that Ramanujan Fellowship of the Department is a targeted scheme
aimed to attract highly skilled Indian researchers working overseas are offered contractual research

19
positions in Indian Institutions/Universities to carry out independent research on subjects from any
recognized university in the world. This fellowship provides them opportunity to emerge as a leader in
future science & technology.  Till date, total 317 Ramanujan fellowships have been offered in different
subject areas and 235 fellows have come back from abroad.  The awarded fellows published a number
of research articles on their scientific investigations in peer reviewed reputed journals of high impact
factor.
15.4 According to the Department, this fellowship is attractive enough to attract and retain Indian scientists
who have settled in various parts of world for pursuing research in India in their respective fields of
expertise as well as in home country.
15.5 The Committee notes the initiatives taken by the Department of Science & Technology that
have resulted in brain-gain of 235 accomplished scientists to India. The Committee recommends
that further measures should be taken to attract Indian scientists to comeback to India. For that
purpose, the Department should further increase the scholarship/stipends provided to researchers
and incentivise performance based research.
16. MECHANISM TO MONITOR AND REVIEW THE ONGOING SCHEMES
16.1 The Department informed the Committee that it has a sound mechanism for monitoring and evaluation
of progress of various schemes. Schemes are being monitored by various expert groups and committees
constituted by the Department. Feedback mechanisms including stakeholder consultations, wherever
necessary, have been put in place during the implementation of some of the schemes to fine tune the
programmes.  Progress of all the plan schemes including subordinate offices (Survey of India and National
Atlas and Thematic Mapping Organisation) and autonomous institutions was reviewed at Ministry level
during a conclave held on 6-7 July, 2015 in Hyderabad (Telangana). Progress of autonomous institutions
is regularly monitored by their respective Governing Bodies duly constituted with the approval of the
Government and Scientific Advisory Committees which comprise of experts from the scientific community.
Monitoring of physical targets and financial progress was also undertaken in the Department at Secretary
level regularly during the year.
16.2 The Committee notes the mechanism devised by the Department of Science & Technology
to monitor and evaluate the progress of various schemes.  However, the Committee feels that had
the monitoring mechanism of the Department been so robust, underutilisation would not have
taken place under some schemes particularly in Modernisation of Mapping Organisations.
16.3 The Committee is of the view that there is a considerable scope for improvement in the
performance of the D epartment and in the light of adverse audit observations made by the
Controller & Auditor General particularly on Drugs & Pharmaceutical Research Programme,
the Department needs to strengthen its monitoring mechanism so that misuse of funds could
be prevented and  timely completion of projects and optimum utilisation of funds could be
ensured.
16.4 It is high time that the Department of Science and Technology strives to be on par with
international standards  in the long run in terms of the speed and quantum of scientific and
technological breakthroughs in order to expeditiously realise  India’s rightful place as a global
leader in various domains of science and technology including particularly supercomputing.

REPORT
INTRODUCTION
The Department of Atomic Energy (DAE), came into being on August 3, 1954, and has been engaged
in the development and deployment of nuclear power technology, application of radiation technologies in the
field of agriculture, health care, industry and basic research.  The Atomic Energy Commission (AEC) is the
apex body for formulation of policies and direction of the programmes.  The Commission implements its
policies and programmes through the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE).  The Programmes of DAE have
been divided into four sectors viz.  Research and Development, Industries, Minerals and Power Sector.
The current mandate of the Department, on which its programmes are based, extends to:-
z Increasing share of nuclear power through deployment of indigenous and other proven
technologies, along with development of fast breeder reactors and thorium reactors with associated
fuel cycle facilities;
z Building and operation of research reactors for production of radioisotopes and carrying out
radiation technology applications in the field of medicine, agriculture and industry;
z Developing advanced technologies such as accelerators, lasers, supercomputers, advanced
materials and instrumentation, and encouraging transfer of technology to industry.
z Support to basic research in nuclear energy and related frontier areas of science; interaction
with universities and academic institutions; Support to research and development projects having
a bearing in DAE’s programmes, and international cooperation in related advanced areas of
research; and
z Contribution to national security.
2. MAJOR PROGRAMMES
2.1 The vision of the DAE is to empower India through technology, creation of more wealth and improving
standard of living of its citizens. To realise its vision, the Department has been engaged in the design,
construction and operation of nuclear power/research reactors and the associated nuclear fuel cycle
technologies across the country.  Over the years, the Department has been able to establish a network of
institutions engaged in R&D as well as industrial activities and acquired expertise in all aspects of the nuclear
fuel cycle.
2.2 The share of nuclear power in the total electricity generation from April, 2015 to February, 2016 is
about 3.3%.  The Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL) in the country has kept pace with
the total electricity generations with the share remaining around 3 to 3.5%.  A substantial increase in the
share is planned by augmentation of the installed nuclear power capacity.
2.3 At present, NPCIL is spearheading India’s Nuclear Power Programme with 21 Nuclear Power Reactors
in operation, with total installed capacity of 5780 MW at seven locations.  Locations (including RAPS-1 of
100 MWe owned by the Government).  The reactor units are: 4 at Tarapur (Maharashtra), 6 at Rawatbhata
(Rajasthan), 2 at Kalpakkam (Tamil Nadu), 2 at Narora (Uttar Pradesh), 2 at Kakrapar (Gujarat), 4 at Kaiga
(Karnataka) and 1 unit at Kudankulam (Tamil Nadu).  The Kudankulam unit-1 has started commercial
operation since December 31, 2014 and Kudankulam Unit-2 is in commissioning stage and likely to commence

2
commercial operation in financial year 2015-16.  The construction work is also under progress on 4 PHWR
of 700 MW Unit, 2 at Kakrapara, Gujarat, 2 at Rawatbhata, Rajasthan.
2.4 The DAE is also developing advanced technologies such as accelerators, lasers, super computers,
advanced materials and instrumentation and encouraging transfer of technology to the industry, which
could contribute to the national prosperity.  A wide range of technologies have been developed to come to the
present stage of harnessing nuclear energy and efforts are continuing to develop such technologies further
with future requirements in mind. Technologies to be developed for future applications include those necessary
for building accelerator driven sub-critical reactor system (ADS), high temperature reactor systems and
fusion technologies.  Several applications of radiation and isotope technologies for improving the quality of
life have been developed and efforts on this front are to be continued.
2.5 The Department is also engaged in the development of radiation technologies and their applications for
better crop varieties, techniques for crop protection, radiation-based post harvest technologies, techniques
for radio diagnosis and radio therapy of diseases particularly cancer, technologies for safe potable water,
better environment and industrial growth.
2.6 The DAE contributes to the enrichment of knowledge domain by pursuing basic research in nuclear
energy and related frontier areas of science; interaction with universities and academic institutions; support
to research and development project having a bearing in DAE’s programmes, and international co-operation
in related advanced areas of research.
2.7 The Committee notes with satisfaction that in the last sixty two years of its existence, the
Department of Atomic Energy has mastered a host of highly complex technologies particularly in
the field of medical radiology, nuclear agriculture, desalination, food irradiation, radio astronomy,
supercomputing, particle accelerators, plasma and cryogenics.  True to the visions of Dr. Homi J.
Bhabha and Jawaharlal Nehru of envisaging the usage of atomic energy to make a difference to the
social life of Indians, the DAE should now strive to scale it up and take it to the next level.  The
Committee feels that the share of nuclear power which accounts for only 3.3 per cent of India’s
total electricity generation, needs to be increased to the higher proportions and efforts should be
made in this direction.

10. ATOMIC ENERGY REGULATORY BOARD (AERB)
10.1 The Atomic Energy Regulatory Board was constituted on November 15,1983 by exercising the powers
conferred by section 27 of the Atomic Energy Act, 1962 (33 of 1962) to carry out certain regulatory and
safety functions under the Act.  The regulatory authority of AERB is derived from the rules and notifications
promulgated under the Atomic Energy Act, 1962 and the Environmental protection Act, 1986.  The mission
of the Board is to ensure that the use of ionizing radiation and Nuclear Energy in India does not cause undue
risk to health of people and the environment.
Monitoring of Radio Active Substances and Radiation Generating Units Outside
10.2 The Committee desired to know the manner in which Atomic Energy Regulatory Board was monitoring
the use of radioactive substances and radiation generating Plants outside nuclear installations to avert accidents
like Mayapuri, Delhi. In response thereto, it was informed that the existing regulations, viz, Atomic Energy
(Radiation Protection) Rules, 2004 and Atomic Energy (Safe Disposal of Radioactive Wastes) Rules, 1987,
specifies the rules to be followed for safe handling, use and disposal of radioactive material as well as their
regulation. Some of the requirements of these Rules were violated in the case, which resulted in the disused
radioactive source of a high hazard category finding its way in the public domain causing the untoward
incident.

12
10.3 The ‘ Atomic Energy (Safe Disposal of Radioactive Wastes) Rules-1987 clearly spell out the
requirements, roles and responsibilities of various parties. In addition to the abovementioned Rules, AERB
has developed and issued Safety Codes, Standards and other regulatory documents, specifying the regulatory
and safety requirements to be followed in the handling, use and disposal of radioactive materials and
radiation generating plants equipment. In accordance with the provisions of the Rules, AERB claims to
have a well-established regulatory system for licensing, periodic review of safety status, regulatory
inspections and enforcement with respect to the radiation facilities (the facilities using radioactive sources
and radiation generating equipment for medical, industrial and research applications, which are outside
the nuclear installations.
10.4 The radiation facilities using radioactive sources of higher category (Category 1& 2) have a high
hazard potential, and if not well regulated they can lead to incidents like the one happened at Mayapuri, New
Delhi in 2010. The Mayapuri incident was primarily due to violation of the regulatory and safety requirements
related to decommissioning/safe disposal of the disused source by the Delhi University. The source in
question, a Gamma Chamber (Category-1 source)was in disused state for well over 20 years. This was a
‘legacy source’ with the Delhi University, which they procured at a time before the regulatory framework
was established.
10.5 The lower category sources (category 3, 4 & 5) are of lower to negligible hazard potential and the
possibility of them resulting in such incidents is very minimal. The radiation generating equipment like Linear
accelerators used in Medicine and Industry, diagnostic X-ray equipment used in hospitals and to some
extent in the industry are unlikely to cause similar incidents, if handled properly.
10.6 The Committee desired to know the measures taken by AERB for further strengthening the regulatory
mechanism for the radiation facilities for ensuring safety in the use of radiation sources in the country and
maintaining a tight control and traceability in their procurement, installation, operation and final disposal.  In
response thereto, it was informed that following six are the measures taken by the Board are for ensuring
safety:-
(i) Strengthening of licensing  of radiation facilities.
(ii) Maintaining inventory of the Radiation facilities.
(iii) Strengthening of Regulatory Inspections.
(iv) Monitoring and follow up of discussed sources for safe disposal.
(v) Periodic Safety Status Review and
(vi) A wareness Programme.
10.7 AERB has also specified the requirements for all the licenses to promptly report to the Board, any
incident of loss/theft or misplacement of radiation sources, so as to enable AERB to facilitative prompt
action for launching investigations/recovery of the sources.

10.9 The importance of having an independent and credible nuclear regulatory body at par with
similar regulators in other countries is beyond question. The Committee feels that construction of
new building of Headquarters and Regional Regulatory Centres of Atomic Energy Regulatory Board
is one of the definitive steps for capacity building of AERB for effective monitoring. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that construction of building must be expedited and completed as per the
schedule. Also, AERB should augment their manpower requirement at various levels and adequate
budgetary provision should be made for the same.  The Committee is also of the view that more and
more radiation generating Plants outside nuclear installations should be registered with Atomic
Energy Regulatory Board to avert accidents.
11. BHABHA ATOMIC RESEARCH CENTRE (BARC)
11.1 Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC), a premier multi-disciplinary and multi-scale activity R&D
organisation, pursues comprehensive research & development programmes for the ultimate objective of
harnessing nuclear energy and its utility for the benefit of the society based on indigenous nuclear power
programme and keeping self reliance as an important aspect in all its endeavours.  The Centre supports a
comprehensive programme in basic research and human resource development in the areas of nuclear
sciences and technologies.  The Centre is engaged in interaction with academic institutions and international
cooperation and related advanced areas of research are being strengthened.
11.2 Its mandate includes almost the entire spectrum of fuel-cycle activities.  Its wide ranging activities
include development of new technologies fabrication of nuclear fuels, reprocessing of spent fuel, waste
management, robotics, super computers, lasers, accelerators, human genomes, nano-technology, and super
conductivity, etc.
11.3 It also pursues R&D for application of radiation technologies (non-power application) in the areas of
industrial applications, food preservation, radiation mutation to develop varieties of pulses, groundnuts and
other seeds, radio-isotopes for healthcare, isotope hydrology, etc. The Centre continues to support to national
security.  BARC has its main campus at Mumbai and other campuses are at Tarapur, Kalpakkam and Mysore.
A new campus is being set up at Vizag.

Role of BARC in Ensuring Food & Health Security
11.13  Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) has also made significant contribution in the areas of
agriculture, food preservation and radiation medicines to ensure food and health security to the nation.
11.14  Highlighting the major contribution made by BARC in the field of Agriculture mutation breeding using
radiation and allied techniques has significantly contributed to release of high yielding varieties in pulses and
oilseeds over last 6 decades. In last 10 years BARC groundnut varieties have contributed to about 14.2% of
National Breeders’ seed indent. These varieties have become popular in groundnut growing States like
Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, Maharashtra, Rajasthan and Karnataka. BARC varieties in pulses like
mung bean, pigeon pea and blackgram have also played an important role in increasing overall national
productivity. The introduction of BARC pulse varieties suitable for rice fallow cultivation has increased the
use efficiency of agricultural fields.
11.15  Preservation of food forms another area important for National Food Security. Feasibility of food
irradiation for preservation has been studied for a number of agricultural and food commodities for several
years. There are several commodities cleared under New Atomic Energy (Radiation Processing of Food &
Allied Products) Rules 2012 in Food Safety and Standards (Food Products Standards and Food Additives)
Regulations, 2011. The major facility in the government sector catering to irradiation of fresh horticultural
produce is the KRUSHAK facility at Lasalgaon, Nashik district, Maharashtra state, India. The facility has
been irradiating mangoes for export to USA since 2007.
11.16  Highlighting the medical and industrial applications the Department has stated that wide variety of
radioisotopes of different radiation characteristics are regularly produced at the Dhruva reactor of BARC
and are supplied to users for a wide ranges of medical and industrial applications.
11.17  BRIT is successfully operating radiation processing plant ISOMED for sterilization of healthcare
products which offers an effective sterilization for moisture sensitive or thermolabile products. It has also
set up first indigenous Gamma Radiation Processing Plant (RPP) at Navi Mumbai and the plant has been
operating since 2000 for hygienization of spices and condiments, aseptic packaging, Ayurvedic raw materials
and animal & pet food etc. KRUSHAK is another Gamma Radiation Processing Plant commissioned by
BARC at Lasalgaon near Nasik for gamma radiation processing of food products.
11.18  Apart from this, BRIT has been successful in propagating this technology. So far 14 such plants are
operational in private sector, Co-operative and Semi Government sectors under MoU with BRIT for the
supply of source and other related works. These plants are meant for processing of food and allied products
and also for healthcare products.

12.1 Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research, one of the major R&D units of the DAE, has been engaged

14. INDIA BASED NEUTRINO OBSERV ATORY PROJECT (INO)
14.1 The India-based Neutrino Observatory (INO) Project is a multi-institutional effort aimed at building a
world-class underground laboratory with a rock cover of approx.1200 metres for non-accelerator based
high energy and nuclear physics research in India. The project is a joint initiative of Department of Atomic
Energy and DST with DAE as lead agency.
14.2 The project includes construction of an underground laboratory and associated surface facilities at
Pottipuram in Bodi West hills of Theni District of Tamil Nadu; construction of a Iron Calorimeter (ICAL)
detector for studying neutrinos and setting up of National Centre for High Energy Physics at Madurai, for
the operation and maintenance of the underground laboratory, human resource development and detector
R&D along with its applications. The underground laboratory, consisting of a large cavern of size 132m X
26m X 20m and several smaller caverns, will be accessed by a 2100 m long and 7.5 m wide tunnel.
14.3 The initial goal of  INO is to study neutrinos. The ICAL detector is designed to address some of the
key open problems in a unique way. Over the years, this underground facility is expected to develop into a
full-fledged underground science laboratory for other studies in physics, biology, geology, hydrology etc.
Development of detector technology and its varied applications are an important aspect of the project. The
primary goal of the INO is to study the properties of the fundamental particle called “neutrino” which is the
most exciting area of research in particle physics after the discovery of Higgs Boson.

19
14.4 Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR), Mumbai is the host institute for INO project. All INO
related activities will be coordinated through the INO centre, which is to be located at Madurai. This centre
will be responsible for the operation and maintenance of the underground laboratory, human resource
development and detector R& D. The construction of the underground and surface facilities is expected to
be completed in four years and the entire ICAL detector will be completed in the next four years. Preliminary
data taking is expected to start in 2020.

15. LASER INTERFEROMETER GRA VITATIONAL-W AVE OBSERV ATORY (LIGO)
15.1 Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO) is world’s largest night time Astronomy
Telescope is being set up in the USA by several international partners. Further, it was informed that a new
advanced Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory (LIGO) will be set up in India also. This
will be the third such detector in the world, the other two being in the United States. Recently, the Union
Cabinet has accorded in-principle approval for the same.
15.2 Gravitational Waves have drawn the attention of whole world this year.  37 Indian scientists have
contributed towards the recent discovery of gravitational waves. Steps have been taken by the gravitational
wave community of the country for forging international scientific collaborations and developing human
resource in this field. For this, a pan-Indian consortium, Indian Initiative in Gravitational-wave Observations
(IndIGO) was formed consisting of researchers from premier institutions and universities of the country.
IndIGO consortium has representation in the Gravitational Waves International Committee (GWIC) which
works to facilitate international collaboration and cooperation in the construction, operation and use of the
major gravitational wave detection facilities world-wide. Indian scientists are participating in the international
LIGO Science Collaboration (LSC), through IndIGO.
15.3 As regards benefit to India, it has been informed by the Department that LIGO-India will be an
important project in the field of fundamental sciences in the country. The Observatory will be among the
most precise scientific apparatus on the Earth, with technical capability of measuring displacements which

20
are a billion times smaller than the size of an atom. This will help develop national capabilities in high-
technology areas such as control systems, lasers and optics and vacuum technology, well beyond the
currently available expertise in the country. This will help train highly skilled scientific and technical manpower.
The analysis of the measurements for obtaining science results will involve very sophisticated computational
and data handling infrastructure. Such a front-ranking science experiment on Indian soil will be a source of
inspiration for young and budding scientists. This will help to  launch an entirely new discipline of gravitational-
wave astronomy in the country.
15.4 From the Indian side, LIGO-India is the joint responsibility of three lead Indian institutions, Inter-
University Centre for Astronomy and Astrophysics (IUCAA)-Pune, Institute for Plasma Research (IPR)-
Gandhinagar and Raja Ramanna Centre for Advanced Technology (RRCAT)-Indore. There are 61 researchers
in the international LIGO collaboration and about 40 scientists and technical staff are involved in LIGO-India
project.
15.5 As regard budgetary allocation, initial budgetary allocation to the project is being made for preparing a
Detailed Project Report for the project, site selection and some prototyping work.
15.6 The Committee believes that the proposed LIGO-India project has tremendous potential to
unravel the myriad mysteries of the universe. It is likely to become a tool for the Indian astronomy
in keeping up the level of excellence in research in astronomy and astrophysics of the country.
The Committee hopes that the LIGO-India project would help the country to embark on truly
world class international science collaborations and help India become a force to reckon with in
this f ield.

17. CONTRIBUTION TO ASTROSAT MISSION
17.1 The ASTROSAT programme is aimed at design, development, fabrication and launch of an astronomical
observatory of cosmic studies.  It is envisaged to be a national observatory for astronomical observations by
researchers in India.
17.2 ASTROSA T satellite was launched by ISRO and put into orbit on 28 September 2015. Tata Institute of
Fundamental Research of DAE has developed 3 of the 5 major instruments on Astrosat namely Large Area
X-ray Proportional Counters (LAXPC); Soft X-ray Telescope (SXT); Cadmium-Zinc-Telluride Imager
(CZTI). In addition to this, Inter University Centre for Astronomy and Astrophysics, Department of Science
& Technology has also developed to instruments on ASTROSAT.
17.3 ASTROSA T MISSION is aimed at design, development, fabrication and launch of India’s first multi
wavelength astronomical observatory of cosmic studies.  ASTROSAT is aimed at studying celestial sources
in X-ray, optical and UV spectral bands simultaneously.  All the data are received regularly and are archived
at Indian Space Science Data Center (ISSDC).
17.4 Informing about the progress of the satellite the Department has stated that the satellite is functioning
well.  All functions of various detectors on-board were found to be normal and its performance continues as
per specifications. Charge Particle Monitor (CPM) was the first detector to be operational on 5th and  6th
October, 2015, followed by the Cadmium Zinc Telluride Imager (CZTI), the hard X-ray detector. The Soft
X-ray imaging telescope (SXT) onboard Astrosat saw its first light on October 26, 2015. Calibration of
SXT using cosmic X-ray sources was started. The analysis software is also being upgraded. The Large
Area X-ray Proportional Counter (LAXPC) detector was fully operational on October 19, 2015 and its first
light observations were carried out for one week. In the next few months all instruments will be ready to
make observations of interesting objects in the universe.
17.5 The Committee congratulates the Department particularly Tata Institute of Fundamental
Research, Mumbai for successful operationalization of  Large Area X-ray Proportional Counters
(LAXPC); Soft X-ray Telescope (SXT); Cadmium-Zinc-Telluride Imager (CZTI) of ASTROSAT and
hopes that India’s first  national observatory for astronomical observations will yield desired results
and will be of great help to the researchers in India.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS — AT A GLANCE
MAJOR PROGRAMMES
The Committee notes with satisfaction that in the last sixty two years of its existence, the
Department of Atomic Energy has mastered a host of highly complex technologies particularly in
the field of medical radiology, nuclear agriculture, desalination, food irradiation, radio astronomy,
supercomputing, particle accelerators, plasma and cryogenics.  True to the visions of Dr. Homi J.
Bhabha and Jawaharlal Nehru of envisaging the usage of atomic energy to make a difference to the
social life of Indians, the DAE should now strive to scale it up and take it to the next level.  The
Committee feels that the share of nuclear power which accounts for only 3.3 per cent of India’s
total electricity generation, needs to be increased to the higher proportions and efforts should be
made in this direction. (Para 2.7)
PROGRESS IN XII FIVE YEAR PLAN
The Committee takes serious view of the fact that in the first four years of current Plan
nearly 55.74% of the allocations have been disbursed.  The major share i.e. 44.25% of the allocation
has accumulated for the remaining one year.  Even if the Department is disbursed entire amount,
it seems impossible to utilise 44% of the plan allocation during the remaining one year.  While
taking serious view of the fact that pro-rata allocations are not made annually, the Committee
recommends that in the remaining one year of the Plan period, allocations should be made and
utilised on pro-rata basis to catch up the Plan targets.  The Department also needs to improve upon
the utilisation of funds. (Para 6.4)
UTILISATION OF THE APPROVED OUTLAY IN 2015-16
On overall analysis, the Committee finds that Plan expenditure by the Department under
Atomic Energy and Nuclear Power scheme is satisfactory but there is considerable scope to improve
upon the performance because Actual utilisation of funds in Plan schemes is 93% of corresponding
period the previous year. (Para 7.3)
The Committee observes that there is a tendency of underutilisation under Nuclear Power
Schemes.  During the Demands for Grants meeting, the Committee was provided explanation for
underutilisation in Demand no. 5. The Committee understands the logic put forward by the
Department.  The Committee takes  note of Merger of Demand no. 5 (Nuclear Power Scheme with
Demand no. - 4 (Atomic Energy Programmes) and hopes that merger of the two schemes will result
in better utilisation of precious budgetary resources. (Para 7.5)
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION IN 2016-17
The Committee feels that reduction at B.E. to the tune of ````` 6538.16 Crore against the projected
outlay of ````` 25,220.64 crore and especially to the tune of ````` 4613.11 crore under Plan Head against
projected Plan BE of ````` 10813.11 crore is unjustified. It has adversely impacted the Plan and Non plan
projects of the Department particularly reduction in Non-Plan allocation as it affects the day-to-day
functioning of the Department.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Finance
should consider the proposal for increase in outlay at RE stage particularly under Non Plan Research
& Development, Industries and Minerals Sectors. (Para 9.5)
28

29
The Committee welcomes the additional allocation of 3000.00 crore by the Finance Minister
in his budget speech under clean energy Programme and the recommends that in the  area of
critical national importance and clean energy, the Ministry of Finance should give maximum
financial support for the programmes of the Department under the appropriate financing
mechanism. (Para 9.6)
ATOMIC ENERGY REGULATORY BOARD (AERB)
The importance of having an independent and credible nuclear regulatory body at par with
similar regulators in other countries is beyond question. The Committee feels that construction of
new building of Headquarters and Regional Regulatory Centres of Atomic Energy Regulatory Board
is one of the definitive steps for capacity building of AERB for effective monitoring. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that construction of building must be expedited and completed as per the
schedule. Also, AERB should augment their manpower requirement at various levels and adequate
budgetary provision should be made for the same.  The Committee is also of the view that more and
more radiation generating Plants outside nuclear installations should be registered with Atomic
Energy Regulatory Board to avert accidents. (Para 10.9)
BHABHA ATOMIC RESEARCH CENTRE (BARC)
The Committee takes note of the activities undertaken by BARC and allocation of ````` 2850.75
crore under Power, Industries and Research & Development Sector  and hopes that a concrete
action plan would be prepared to fully utilise the allocated budgetary resources and important projects
would be completed on time. (Para 11.6)
The Committee notes the important contributions made by the BARC in providing potable
water to people, reprocessing and waste management and supercomputing.  The Committee is
hopeful that BARC will maintain its service of ensuring delivery of fruits of nuclear science &
technology to the common people. (Para 11.12)
The Committee commends the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre for contributing in ensuring
food and health security of the Nation and recommends to BARC to execute its strategy to
aggressively market its socially beneficial technologies such as Nisarguna Biogas Plant for handling
biodegradable wastes; Sludge Hygienization Research Irradiation (SHRI), KRUSHAK, Gamma
radiation processing Plan, etc. including its technology on food preservation, nuclear medicine
and healthcare, through Technology Transfer & Collaboration Division (BRIT) so that more and
more people ge t benefitted. (Para 11.19)
INDIRA GANDHI CENTRE FOR ATOMIC RESEARCH (IGCAR), KALPAKKAM
The Committee notes the identification of the Fast Reactor Fuel cycle Facility project as an
independent project.  The Committee while taking note of achievements of the Centre hopes that
concerted efforts made by the Centre will make India self sufficient in Fast Breeder Reactor (FBR)
Technology. (Para 12.6)

Neutrino Observatory at Pottipuram, Theni and infrastructure development at Inter Institutional
Centre for High Energy Physics, Madurai.  The Committee hopes that in years to come India based
Neutrino Observatory, a joint collaboration between Tata Institute of Fundamental Research,
Department of Atomic Energy and the Department of Science & Technology, will prove to be a huge
success and will be a role model for other Ministries/Departments.  The Committee recommends
that adequate budgetary provisions should be made for the observatory. (Para 14.6)

The Committee believes that the proposed LIGO-India project has tremendous potential to
unravel the myriad mysteries of the universe. It is likely to become a tool for the Indian astronomy
in keeping up the level of excellence in research in astronomy and astrophysics of the country.
The Committee hopes that the LIGO-India project would help the country to embark on truly
world class international science collaborations and help India become a force to reckon with in
this f ield. (Para 15.6)

facility in the country which will help in treating paediatric cancer and tumours without any
