AVOIDANCE OF OCCURRENCE OF LANDSLIDES IN FOREST FIRE AFFECTED AREAS
107. The Committee is of the view that after forest fires, the earth around the affected areas and
the roots of the trees become weak and loose. This also contributes to the landslides in the affected
areas in the rainy seasons after the forest fires. The Committee, therefore, recommends that
Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change should impress upon the State Governments
that after the forest fires have been brought under control, a quick response system should be put
in action and immediate necessary steps should be taken for minimizing the occurrence of landslides
in the affected areas. The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change should also issue
suitable guidelines to the State Governments in this regard.
BUDGET CONSTRAINTS
108. The representative of the Gandhi Global Family (GGF), Jammu also dwelt on the budget constraints

38
faced by the State Forest Department and Joint Forest Management of local people and authorities for
fighting and preventing forest fires. Representatives of other NGOs also stressed the need for adequate
budgetary allocations for use of technology and equipment for fighting forest fires.
109. The Committee notes that almost all the State Governments have expressed resource crunch
and inadequate budgetary allocations to effectively invest in protecting our forests from fires. The
Committee observes that in the context of forest fires, the needs of Himalayan states are distinctly
different from the other states. The whole country depends upon the services of the Himalayan
region since they contribute much more to the forest cover of the country. Accordingly, the Committee
recommends that the budget of all the states which are in Himalayan region should be demarcated
separately from other states, with specific objectives in mind and the policies and programmes and
it should not be clubbed with other states, without taking into account the specific demands of the
Himalayan ecosystem. Further, there should be an accelerated system for the devolution of funds
to these States to enable them to prioritize the requirements of prevention, mitigation and fighting
the forest fires.
REMOV AL OF OLD AND FALLEN TREE FROM THE FORESTS
110. The Committee while visiting the states of Uttarakhand, Jammu & Kashmir and Himachal Pradesh
noticed a lot of fallen chir and pine trees lying in the forests which actually enhances burning in case of a
forest fire. The Committee wanted to know the reason behind non-clearance of the fallen trees. The Committee
also pointed out that gregarious flowering of bamboo in other parts of the country causes a lot of concern
with regard to fire protection and therefore removal of the dried flowered bamboo from the forest area was
desirable to reduce the intensity of fire hazards during the summer season. In response it was informed that
Hon’ble Supreme Court of India had put a blanket ban on the removal of any tree including the dead and
fallen tree from the forests. On scrutiny it has been found out that the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India, in
its interim order in Writ Petition no. 202 dated 12.12.96 has prohibited salvaging of dead and fallen trees
from the protected forest areas i.e. National Parks and Wildlife Sanctuaries only for the conservation of
biodiversities in that area. However, the Court has clearly permitted to remove or salvage the dead and fallen
trees in any forest area in accordance with Working Plan as approved by the Central Government. The State
Governments are obliged to make a proposal for removal of such trees and get it approved by the Central
Government and then they are free to clear the forests. The Committee strongly feels that in this
background the ball is in the court of the Central Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate
Change to plan to remove dead and fallen tree even in the protected forest areas. The Committee
recommends that in the light of Supreme Court order of 1996, the Central Government is bound to
persuade the State Governments and approve their Working Plans for salvaging dead and fallen
trees with a view to avoid induced forest fire in future.
GENERAL OBSERV ATION
111. The Committee is of the view that forest fires have become an annual feature in the country
and have a devastating effect on environment, forest, biodiversity and wildlife. The Committee
feels that there is an urgent need to devise a policy with regard to prevention and mitigation of
forest fires and recommends that Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change should, at
the earliest, come up with a national policy on the subject.

RECOMMENDA TIONS/OBSERV ATIONS — AT A GLANCE
The Committee observes that the funds released by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and
Climate Change to the States and UTs under Centrally Sponsored Scheme namely, Intensification
of Forest Management, have shown a declining trend during the last few years, as is evident from
the figures provided by Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. The Committee is at
a loss to understand as to why, when most of the concerned States have been asking for additional
funds under this scheme, the Ministry has not given priority to this sector. In view of the devastations
caused due to the forest fires, particularly this year, the Committee recommends that the Ministry
of Environment, Forest and Climate Change should enhance its budgetary allocation under the
Scheme and provide increased allocations under the Scheme to the affected States to enable them
to take the requisite measures for prevention and mitigation of forest fires. (Para 8)
The Committee has been given to understand that Forest Research Institute, one of the
oldest forestry institutions in the country, has been undertaking basic research in forest management.
However, there seems to be a huge disconnect between the research done by FRI and its usage by
the State Forest Departments and other agencies. This has been corroborated by the fact that
NDRF, when deployed in Uttarakhand to control the forest fire, complained of having used very
rudimentary equipments, whereas FRI claims of having designed and developed efficient fire fighting
tools. Therefore, the Committee recommends to FRI to publicise among all State about the
equipments developed by them with a view to control forest fires, so that the concerned States could
procure the equipments and use them in case of forest fires. (Para 43)
The Committee observed that a large number of posts of front line forest staff were lying
vacant and expressed doubt about the preparedness of the state forest departments to combat
forest fires. The Committee also observed that the recent forest fires may have resulted in adverse
impact on many species and desired to know the efforts made by the Government in minimizing the
loss. The Committee was informed that the Department was conducting regular surveys with respect
to floral as well as faunal species conservation in the state and will undertake more studies focused
towards areas where forest fires had been reported. The Committee was also informed that the
State Forest Department was taking up soil and water conservation measures in affected areas to
check possible negative impact on forests and water resources of the state. Further, a range of local
species have been reserved which will be planted to minimize soil screened along with the cantour
trances. (Para 51)
The Committee notes that Indian Institute of Remote Sensing and Wildlife Institute of India
have made some very useful suggestions regarding remedial/preventive measures for forest fires,
disaster risk reduction, restoration of habitat, wildlife habitat improvement and post fire restoration
work. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
and the concerned State Government should take these suggestions into consideration while
formulating strategies for prevention, mitigation and fighting the forest fires as well as post fire
restoration work. (Para 68)
39

40
The Committee is of the opinion that agencies like NDRF should be deployed in fighting forest
fires extremely rarely. In fact, State Governments should be asked to train their fire brigade staff
to fight forest fires as they will be in a better position to deal with it. The Committee was informed
that Himachal Pradesh has over 600 fire brigade staff. Likewise all other states will be having their
fire fighting staff who needed to be trained to suit the occasion. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, on priority basis through
Forest Research Institute, Dehradun, organize training of fire brigade officers of all the states and
equip them with proper forest fire equipments so that they can rise up to the occasion in the event
of forest fires and they do not have to depend on outside agencies like NDRF which has already
enough duties to perform at national level. The Committee also recommends that the Government
should also approach some other fire-prone countries such as Canada, New Zealand and Australia
to understand as to how they deal with the problems of forest fires and study the use of other
systems for fighting forest fires such as chemical fogging that is used in these countries. (Para 71)
The Committee was constrained to note that interest and participation of local villagers/people
in dealing with the forest fires and related incidents have gone down. The Committee is of the view
that the key issue in forest management is the execution of activities at the grass root level and
hence there is an urgent need to restore the social commitment and sense of belongingness of the
people towards the forests and their involvement in planning and management of the forests. The
Committee is of the firm view that this would also help in minimising the forest fire incidents in the
country. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Central Government and concerned State
Governments should take immediate necessary steps to involve the local communities, including
women, self-help groups and members of Village Panchayats and Zila Parishads in forest management
related activities. The Committee also recommends that the State Governments should also incentivise
the local people/villagers by creating facilities for them such as schools, hospitals etc. as per the
local requirements to motivate and encourage the people to come forward and participate in the
process of saving our precious forests from forest fires. (Para 74)
The Committee is in agreement with the view expressed by various representatives of Civil
Society that small fires lit by the villagers in forest areas can spread and result in major forest
fires. The need for taking up awareness campaigns among the villagers and exposing them to the
devastating and horrifying results of such small fires cannot be over-emphasised. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change must impress
upon the State Governments to take all necessary measures in this regard such as posters, slogans,
campaigns in schools, hand bill etc. Since visual media is very effective in attracting people towards
a cause, it is recommended that the devastating effects of forest fires should also be shown on
electronic media in the form of short films, documentaries etc. to make the people aware of the
horrifying impacts of forest fires. (Para 76)
The Committee further recommends that short films/documentaries in regional languages
should also be shown periodically and the campaign should be sustained at least period of three to
five years so that it can impact the minds of the people and the society at large. The Committee also
recommends that Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) funds should also be used for advertisement

41
and awareness campaigns. Further, there should be training and mock fire-drills in schools and
colleges. There should also be a dedicated toll free telephone number for reporting incidents of
forest fire in each state. (Para 77)
The Committee is also of the view that people/tourists who come to the hilly areas from the
plains, have little awareness about how to behave in the hills. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that the State Governments should proactively work towards putting up public signages displaying
the requisite messages in areas frequented by the tourists, to make them aware of the norms to be
followed in forest areas. (Para 78)
The Committee feels that apart from involvement of local communities in forest management
and exposing them to devastations of forest fires, there is an urgent need to provide fire fighting
equipments to the people. Further, all persons deployed to fight the fires should be provided some
bagpack kits which should contain water, packed food, fire-proof hand gloves and boots, breathing
masks, first-aid kits etc. so that they could sustain themselves for longer periods while undertaking
the job. Further, since fighting forest fire has its own intricacies, the local communities should be
updated with new technology and trained on how to use these equipments so that they could work
hand in hand with Government agencies in fighting forest fires, when required. (Para 80)
Chir Pine needles, which are highly inflammable due to its high resin content, are a prominent
factor in occurring and spreading of forest fires. The Committee is in agreement with the view
expressed by representatives of some NGOs that the Chir pine needles should be removed and
collected frequently. The Committee recommends that the State Governments should consider
procuring sweeping machines to clear the roadsides of chir pine needles and dry leaves in vulnerable
areas. Further, steps should be taken for incentivising the clearing and collection of pine needles.
The Government should also try to involve school children, NCC, NGOs etc. in collection of pine
needles. The local communities should also be encouraged by providing remunerative emoluments
in the collection process. The Committee also recommends that broad leave trees should be planted
in the forests and, after a period of five years, there should be systematic replacement of chir pine
trees in the forests by broad leave trees as it has been seen that incidents of fires in latter forests
are minimal as compared to chir pine forests. (Para 83)
The Committee is further of the view that there is high resin content in chir pine needles and
there is a need to explore as to how it can be used for other purposes. The Committee recommends
that the Ministry of Environment, Forest & Climate Change should take up with the concerned
Ministries of Government of India to explore as to how best to extract resin from these needles and
how, apart from burning fuel, it could be used for other purposes. (Para 84)
The Committee is of the view that activities relating to collection of pine needles can not only
provide employment to a large number of unskilled workers in the hilly states but also get rid of
the chir pine needles which play a vital role in spreading of forest fires. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that Ministry of Environment, Forest & Climate Change should take up the inclusion
of work relating to collection of chir pine needles as one of the activities under MGNREGA with the
concerned Union Ministry so that the State Governments can initiate further action in this regard
without any hindrance. (Para 87)

42
The Committee is dismayed to note the problems of encroachment of forest land by the people
as well as the violation of forest conservation rules in Dehradun and Shimla. Some people
purposefully cause fires to encroach on forest land, which sometimes spread to other areas as well.
The Committee recommends that the matter needs to be administratively looked into by the concerned
State Governments and ensure that there is no encroachment of forest land or violation of forest
conservation rules. Municipal and town planning agencies in the States should take effective and
practical steps to stop unplanned urbanization and encroachments of forest and open land. Local
communities/villagers should be encouraged to report any such incidents to the concerned authorities
immediately. The authorities should take prompt action in such cases. Forests are our national
property and any attempt to encroach upon them and the consequent fire in forests, whether
intentional or unintentional, should be strictly dealt with. (Para 89)
The Committee feels that creation of ponds and water harvesting structures within the forest
area not only reduces river bank erosion but can be a handy tool for supply of water for dousing
forest fires. This would not only reduce dependence on helicopters for supply of water but also
readily provide water to the locals within the forest area for fire fighting. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that Ministry of Environment, Forest & Climate Change should impress upon the
State Governments the need to reinvigorate the system of ponds and checkdams within the forest
areas, so that water is immediately available at hand for making efforts to douse the forest fires.
This would also save crucial time which is wasted in bringing water  from other far-off resources,
and help try to douse the fire in its initial stages and check it from spreading further. (Para 91)
Fire lines are areas which are cleaned of vegetation for stopping or slowing down a fire in
forest areas. The creation of fire lines is critical in wildland fire fighting, because without fire lines,
a fire can quickly get out of control. The Committee is of the view that such traditional methods of
containing forest fires have stood the test of time and should not be dispensed with. While use of
modern technologies for fire alerts etc. is definitely a welcome step, under the present circumstances,
over-dependence on technology at the cost of traditional methods should not be encouraged. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that Ministry of Environment, Forest & Climate Change should
emphasise upon the State Governments that the traditional forest operations for scientific
management of forests including forest floor clearing, controlled burning and creation of water
harvesting structures should be reviewed and utilised effectively. The Committee notes that the
traditional fire lines are not being cleared due to lack of funds at the disposal of the State
Governments. The Committee, therefore, also recommends that adequate budgetary allocations
should be made by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change for the purpose and
State Governments should ensure that fire lines, which play a crucial role in preventing spread of
fires, are cleared regularly. The Committee also recommends that seasonal training, if required,
should be provided to the local people including panchayats and zila parishads for clearing of fire
lines, before the onset of forest fire season. (Para 93)
The Committee recommends that instead of fire watchers, forest workers and CCTVs, the
use of Drones should be encouraged for forest surveillance and monitoring. These drones should be
deployed systematically in a day three to four times, or as felt necessary. This would enable the

43
authorities receive much faster information since the drones will be able to go into the interior of
the forest areas and send updates of the happenings inside the forests. The State Governments can
equip the fire watchers with new technologies so that they can detect any suspicious or untoward
incidents and report them to the concerned authorities immediately. This would not only ease the
pressure on fire watchers who are pitifully paid and have to sit observing the forests in all climatic
conditions but also provide more authentic and accurate data to the Government. It would also
enable the State Governments to evolve a quick response system. (Para 96)
The Committee is shocked to note the gross underestimation of losses due to forest fires. The
Government estimation in Himachal Pradesh comes to ````` 470 per acre and in Uttarakhand it is ````` 400
per acre. The Committee is at loss to understand who will be the actual beneficiary of this gross
underestimation. The Committee, therefore, recommends that an independent agency having
impeccable credibility must be roped in by the Ministry to estimate the losses in real terms and
properly and earmark budget for compensation. (Para 99)
The Committee is in agreement with the views expressed by the representatives of Civil
Society that the impact of forest fire on biodiversity is grossly underestimated and the loss of
wildlife was not even by accounted for. The Committee is at loss to understand as to why the
Zoological Survey of India and Botanical Survey of India, which are also the arms of the Ministry
of Environment, Forest & Climate Change, did not take up any studies on loss of biodiversity of
the forest fire affected areas. Even the Union Ministry of Environment, Forest & Climate Change
did not take any initiative in this regard. Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
has also stated that National Biodiversity Authority can take up studies in future on the effect of
natural calamities/disasters including forest fires, and remedial/preventive measures thereof on
a need basis. The Committee hopes that in future, the Ministry would take a more proactive
approach in this regard and recommends that Ministry of Environment, Forest & Climate Change
should ask its concerned organisations to undertake, on priority basis, assessment of loss of
biodiversity due to forest fires and devise plans to prevent loss of bio-diversity in the event of
forest fires so that corrective and preventive measures in this regard could be initiated at the
earliest. The Committee further suggests that the Ministry should consider making National
Biodiversity Authority the nodal agency for coordinating the efforts made by the different
organizations in this regard. (Para 105)
The Committee is also aware of the availability of natural assets like medicinal and herbal
plants in our forests. The Committee feels that there are adequate nurseries in hilly areas which
are the banks of medicinal and herbal plants. The Committee is of the view that the Government
can also consider incentivising the forest dwellers to grow medicinal plants in the plains. As such it
would become a source of earning for local people. Accordingly, in case of occurrence of incidents of
fire, they would be worried about their source of income, as a result of which they will take care of
the areas and work to ensure that there are no cases of forest fires. (Para 106)
The Committee is of the view that after forest fires, the earth around the affected areas and
the roots of the trees become weak and loose. This also contributes to the landslides in the affected
areas in the rainy seasons after the forest fires. The Committee, therefore, recommends that

44
Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change should impress upon the State Governments
that after the forest fires have been brought under control, a quick response system should be put
in action and immediate necessary steps should be taken for minimizing the occurrence of landslides
in the affected areas. The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change should also issue
suitable guidelines to the State Governments in this regard. (Para 107)
The Committee notes that almost all the State Governments have expressed resource crunch
and inadequate budgetary allocations to effectively invest in protecting our forests from fires. The
Committee observes that in the context of forest fires, the needs of Himalayan states are distinctly
different from the other states. The whole country depends upon the services of the Himalayan
region since they contribute much more to the forest cover of the country. Accordingly, the Committee
recommends that the budget of all the states which are in Himalayan region should be demarcated
separately from other states, with specific objectives in mind and the policies and programmes and
it should not be clubbed with other states, without taking into account the specific demands of the
Himalayan ecosystem. Further, there should be an accelerated system for the devolution of funds
to these States to enable them to prioritize the requirements of prevention, mitigation and fighting
the forest fires. (Para 109)
The Committee strongly feels that in this background the ball is in the court of the Central
Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change to plan to remove dead and fallen tree even
in the protected forest areas. The Committee recommends that in the light of Supreme Court
order of 1996, the Central Government is bound to persuade the State Governments and approve
their Working Plans for salvaging dead and fallen trees with a view to avoid induced forest fire in
future. (Para 110)
The Committee is of the view that forest fires have become an annual feature in the country
and have a devastating effect on environment, forest, biodiversity and wildlife. The Committee
feels that there is an urgent need to devise a policy with regard to prevention and mitigation of
forest fires and recommends that Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change should, at
the earliest, come up with a national policy on the subject. (Para 111)

REPORT
INTRODUCTION
Understanding and study of the Earth System and its Components and processes is important for the
mankind. The Earth, being a single, interlinked and self-regulating system, together with its components i.e.
atmosphere, oceans, cryosphere, geosphere and biosphere exhibit complex interactions. Therefore, scientific
understanding of the Earth system becomes necessary for the improvement of the services for socio-
environmental benefits of the country.
1.2  The Ministry of Earth Sciences came into being in 2006 by bringing all the agencies of meteorological
and ocean developmental activities under one umbrella with a view to address holistically various aspects
relating to earth system processes for improving forecasting of weather, climate and various geo-hazards.
Further, to monitor and give an overall policy direction to the Ministry, the Earth System Science Organisation
(ESSO) was also established in the year 2007.
1.3 The primary mandate of the Ministry is to develop and improve capability to forecast, weather,
climate and hazard related phenomena for societal, economic and environmental benefits including addressing
climate change science and developing climate services and integrated Himalayan meteorology. Secondly,
exploring ocean resources for socio-economic benefit including developing required state-of-the art technology
for harnessing marine non-living resources is major mission of the Ministry. The overarching vision of the
Ministry is to excel as knowledge and technology enterprise in the realm of earth sciences for socio-
economic benefit of the society. The major missions of the Ministry include (i) to conduct scientific and
technical activities related to Earth System Science for improving forecasting of weather, monsoon, climate
and natural hazards; (ii) exploration of Polar Regions, high seas and seas around India; and (iii) develop
technology for exploration and sustainable utilization of ocean resources.
2.  OBJECTIVES AND FUNCTIONS OF THE MINISTRY
2.1 The Ministry of Earth Sciences has the following objectives and functions:
Objectives
z To provide weather forecasts and advisories for agriculture, aviation, public safety, water
resources, shipping, sports including the extended and Long Range Seasonal Monsoon
forecasts
z To provide a wide range of ocean information advisories including fishery information
z To improve the understanding of Polar Science and its implications for climate change
z To conduct survey for assessing living and non-living resources
z To develop technology for harnessing marine resources
z To asses coastal marine productivity and Marine Ecosystems
z To improve the understanding of science of Climate Change and to provide regional climate
change scenarios
z To provide early warning of natural hazards viz., tropical cyclones, thunderstorms, floods,
Tsunami, storm surge etc.

2
z To conduct cutting edge research in Earth Sciences
z To promote basic research including Capacity Building in the Earth System Science
z To promote awareness and educate the public by extending support to seminars, symposia,
conferences and conduct workshops with stakeholders
Functions
z To augment and sustain long term observations of atmosphere, ocean, cryosphere and solid
earth to record the vital signs of the Earth System and changes.
z To develop forecasting capability of atmosphere and oceanic phenomena through dynamical
models and assimilation techniques and to build prediction systems for weather climate and
hazards.
z To understand interaction between components of the Earth System and human systems at
various spatial and temporal scales.
z Exploration of polar and high seas regions for discovery of new phenomenon and
resources
z To translate knowledge and insight themes gained into services for societal, environmental and
economic benefits
3. ORGANISATIONAL  STRUCTURE  OF  THE  MINISTRY
3.1 The Ministry of Earth Sciences functions through the Earth Commission. The executive arm of the
Ministry i.e. ‘The Earth System Science Organisation (ESSO)’ is responsible for implementing its policies
and programmes. It has four major branches of Earth Sciences viz., (i) Ocean Science and Technology
Services; (ii) Atmospheric and Climate Science Services; (iii) Geoscience and Technology; and (iv) Polar
Science and Cryosphere.
3.2 The policies and programs of the Ministry are being primarily pursued through its Centres
viz., autonomous bodies and subordinate offices. Currently there are 10 centres / institutes under the
Ministry to pursue programs/policies of the Ministry in different areas of Earth Sciences. The
institutions of the atmosphere sciences are India Meteorological Department (IMD), National Centre
for Medium Range Weather Forecasting (NCMRWF), Noida and Indian Institute of Tropical
Meteorology (IITM), Pune. The institutions relating to ocean science and technology are National
Centre for Antarctic and Ocean Research (NCAOR), Goa, National Institute of Ocean Technology
(NIOT), Chennai, Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS), Hyderabad,
Centre for Marine Living Resources (CMLRE), Kochi and Integrated Coastal and Marine Area
Management (ICMAM), Chennai. The National Centre for Earth Science Studies (NCESS) and National
Centre for Seismology (NCS) are also part of the Ministry to conduct research on solid earth and
earthquake monitoring. Each centre of the Ministry has a well-defined mandate to conduct front
research in a specific area of earth System.
3.3 The detailed budget allocation of the Ministry of Earth sciences, for the year 2017-18 was considered
by the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and
Forests in its meeting held on the 13
th February, 2017.

4.3 The Committee notes that although there has been a reduction in the budgetary allocation
at RE stage during the last three financial years i.e. 2014-15, 2015-16 and 2016-17, the Ministry
has not been able to utilize the allocated amount optimally and much amount had remained
unspent. The Ministry in its Background Note has tried to explain the reasons for
underutilisation/savings in the budget for the last three financial years. In most of the cases,
delay in finalisation of projects/schemes or deferment appears to be the main reason behind
the underutilisation of funds. In few cases saving has been recorded due to delay in approval
from the end of Internal Finance Division (IFD) of the Ministry. Interestingly in one case the
1               2 3 4 5 6 7

5
saving has been recorded due to reduction of oil prices towards use in vessels on expedition to
Antarctica. But The Committee finds it hard to believe the reason for underutilisation given by
the Ministry at many places that the saving was primarily due to reduction in the budget at the
RE stage, which is contradictory in itself, unless the proposed scheme was dropped completely
due to reduction.
4.4. The Committee during the meeting took the above position very seriously and many Members
articulated their unhappiness over the state of affairs. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that such underutilization by the Ministry should be avoided by taking timely decisions towards
implementing the schemes as the Committee strongly feels that there could be a correlation between
the delay in the implementation by the Ministry and reduction in the budget at RE stage by the
Ministry of Finance.
4.5 While analysing the reason behind underutilisation/saving given by the Ministry, the
Committee has taken note of the fact that IFD has also been responsible in delaying the projects
which has resulted in the underutilisation. The Committee is unanimous over the idea that scientific
ministries should not be treated on par with other ministries headed by trained bureaucrats as far
as financial management is concerned. The Committee feels that scientific ministries headed by
reputed scientists should be allowed to pursue their visions for the country and the Financial Advisors
attached to these ministries should be sensitised to this fact.
4.6 The Committee was informed that the budgetary allocations for the Ministry in B.E. 2017-18 is
` 1719.48 cr. comprising of ` 1604.48 cr. as the ‘Revenue’ and ` 115.00 cr. as the ‘Capital’’ outlay.
The Ministry informed the Committee that it had requested the Ministry of Finance for ‘Plan’ allocation
of ` 2920 cr.. However, the Ministry of Finance had allocated ` 1719.48 cr. for the year 2017-18.
4.7 Also, in its meeting held on 13
th February, 2017, the Ministry apprised the Committee that it is
facing severe financial constraints and at the R.E. Stage in 2016-17 it suffered lack of allocations and cut
in budgetary support. The Ministry further informed that it was extremely difficult to prepare BE 2017-18
within the given ceilings of ` 1719.48 cr. in the budget for 2017-18 against the projection of ` 2,920 cr..
Since there is no classification of Plan and Non-plan allocation for 2017-18, substantial portion of budget
from the programmes will be required to meet the salary expenditure. There is also an increase in salaries
on account of implementation of the 7th Pay Commission which is to be allocated from the ceiling from
the available budget. It was also informed that Ministry has been facing extreme financial constraints for
the past few years due to lack of adequate fund allocation. This has resulted in non-starter of several
programmes recommended for implementation during 12th Plan. There has been a consistent cut in the
budget of the Ministry at RE stage during the last couple of years.  In view of the paucity of funds, some
of the important programmes of the Ministry of societal relevance are adversely affected viz. (i) National

5. MAJOR  SCHEMES/PROGRAMMES  OF  THE  MINISTRY
5.A ATMOSPHERE AND CLIMATE RESEARCH – MODELLING OBSERVING SYSTEMS AND
SERVICES (ACROSS)
5.1 This programme deals with (i) sustaining and strengthening of atmospheric observation systems to
meet the needs of monitoring as well as providing wide range of services viz. Agriculture, Aviation, city
forecasts, mountain regions, defence and sports, disasters in the country including setting up of a dedicated
forecasting system for the entire Himalayan region with a much focused objective of integrating and
improving the weather related services and climate services (ii) development of a suite of atmospheric
models required for prediction of monsoon weather and climate in India on different time and space
scales ranging from short and medium range to seasonal mean including specific forecast of severe
weather, such as cyclones, heavy rains, storms, floods, heat-waves, fog and air-quality, micro physical
characteristics of aerosols and clouds and associated environmental conditions. (iii) conduct climate
change research to generate a number of regional scenarios of water and other climate services due to
climate Long-term (multi-decadal) simulations, conducting research to enhance understanding of the
changing water cycle and paleoclimatic studies (iv) Continuous augmentation of high performance
computation facilities and its operation and maintenance on 24X7 basis for undertaking all modelling
activities, forecast generation, data centre and data analytics, air borne platform facilities for environmental
observations.
The Ministry also informed that no separate budgetary allocation has been made during 2017-18 as
the necessary budget required to meet HPC programme has been projected under the ACROSS scheme as a
part of rationalization exercise.
5.2 The Committee was apprised about the major activities and achievements during 2016-17 under this
programme. The Committee was informed that a high resolution global deterministic weather prediction
model has been commissioned for generating operational weather forecasts at a horizontal resolution of
12km. Under the Monsoon Mission, operational dynamical model systems have been implemented for extended
range and seasonal forecasts. For the first time, forecasts on different time scales during the hot weather
season (April to May) including heat waves were issued by the India Meteorological Department. Presently
around 19.5 million farmers are being directly benefitted by the agro-meteorological services of IMD. For
the recent cyclone Vardah, accurate predictions were provided almost 3 days in advance, helping the state
government authorities to save thousands of lives. To address the issue of better measurement and
understanding of small-scale processes that drive the variability, seasonality and predictability in the South
Asian Monsoon, a large-scale joint India-UK observational campaign was carried out during the period June-
July 2016.
5.3 The Committee was also informed that an observational campaign to understand different physical
features of Fog and factors responsible for its genesis, intensity and duration was also initiated during
December 2016 at the Indira Gandhi International Airport (IGIA) and at ICAR-IARI in New Delhi. These
observations will be useful for improving model forecasts of Fog.
5.4 The Committee enquired from the Ministry about the proposed plans and activities under the programme
Atmosphere & Climate Research – Modelling Observing systems & Services (ACROSS). The Ministry
informed the Committee that ACROSS is an integrated programme of four major sub-programmes i.e.
Atmospheric Observation Systems Network; Atmospheric Processes and Modelling and Services; Climate

Change Research; and High Performance Computing, the expenses for which shall be met from the Budget
Estimate allocation of  ` 496.00 cr. for the financial year 2017-18.

ACCURACY IN WEATHER FORECASTING
5.11 Weather forecasting for the country as a whole and region-wise is one of the most important mandates
of the Ministry. On being enquired about the steps taken by the Ministry to improve the accuracy of weather
forecasts and bring it at par with the international standards, the Ministry informed the Committee that
upgradation and sustenance of weather forecasting capabilities to an optimum level was the major program
launched to improve the accuracy of weather forecasts and to bring it at par with the international standards
through sustenance and augmentation of atmospheric observation network, data integration, product
generation and dissemination of Weather Forecast and Warning information.
5.12 The Ministry informed that this has resulted in improved capabilities for predicting high impact weather
events like cyclones, severe thunderstorms, heavy rainfall and floods in a significant manner. Noticeable
improvements achieved in Skills of Heavy Rainfall Forecast (False Alarm Rate reduced from 46% to 11%
and Probability of Detection increased from 49% to 67% from 2002-12 to 2013-15). Noteworthy improvement
in track and intensity forecast of the tropical cyclones (24 hour forecast error in track prediction reduced
from 137 km. to 97 km. and Landfall error from 101 Km. to 56 Km. during 2007-11 to 2012-16). The
landfall point forecast error 24 hrs in advance has been almost zero for recent cyclones, Phailin in 2013,
Hudhud in 2014 and Vardah in 2016.
5.13 The timely and accurate forecast and warning services led to (i) increase in confidence of disaster
managers and triggered the actions for cyclone management. It led to minimum loss of lives and minimum

12
area of evacuation. It can be seen that the death toll was less than 50 in each case and was very less as
compared similar cyclones in previous years.
5.14 The Ministry further informed that thus, during the recent few years significant improvement has
been achieved in severe weather and associated predictions. India Meteorological Department (IMD) played
the crucial role, supporting those responsible for managing crisis during the events such as the extreme
rainfall events and cyclonic storms in the Bay of Bengal. A remarkable improvement in weather and climate
services and advisories received an overwhelming appreciation from user community on natural disasters
such as tropical cyclones and extreme rainfall events. These capabilities and skills of forecast are at par with
other major international centres.
5.15 During the Meeting of the Committee on 13
th February, 2017 the Ministry informed that efforts are
continuously made to optimize the level of efficiency and accuracy of the forecasting systems. Noticeable
improvements achieved in skills of Heavy Rainfall Forecast, lead time of warnings increased from 3 to 5
days in respect of Rainfall, Heat Wave, and Cold Wave etc. Noteworthy improvement in tracking intensity
forecast of the tropical cyclones has been achieved. Prediction of extreme heat forecast is made available on
IMD website. To understand the processes that drive the variability and predictability of the South Asian
Monsoon, a large scale India-UK Joint Observational Campaign was done in May-July, 2016.
5.16 The Committee while appreciating the achievements of the Ministry in the area of accuracy
in weather forecasting, observes that there is a lack of smooth dissemination of information regarding
predictions of extreme events to all the stakeholders. The track record of the Ministry has been
above par in the case of cyclone predictions which has been seen in the case of Hudhud and Vardah.
But in case of flash floods and floods caused due to heavy and incessant rainfalls, the information
does not reach fast enough to take pre-emptive actions on the ground zero. The Committee is given
to understand that the IMD collects the data, interpolates them to arrive at the predictions of flood
and transmit it to many agencies viz. Central Water Commission, NDMA and State Disaster
Management Authorities, State Governments etc. However, sometimes they fail to assess the severity
of the situation which is what happened in the case of Uttarakhand Tragedy in 2015. Therefore the
Committee recommends that the Ministry should develop a foolproof mechanism of disseminating
important data on the weather predictions to the last point so that damage to lives and livelihoods
can be minimised. The Committee would like to suggest that the Ministry may designate Director
General, IMD to hold a compulsory press conference in the case of prediction of severe rains which
will be in addition to the existing mechanism of dissemination.

8.10 The Committee wanted to know the background of the proposed acquisition of the Polar Research
Vessel with a view to understand why this process has taken such a long time and still we are far away from
clinching it.
8.11 The Ministry informed the Committee that it decided to implement the programme entitled “Acquisition
of Polar Research Vessel (PRV)” during the XI Plan (2007-2012) period. National Centre for Antarctic and
Ocean Research (NCAOR), Goa was also identified as the implementing organization of this programme on
behalf of the Ministry. Ever since 1981, when the 1
st Indian Scientific Expedition to Antarctica was launched,
the Indian expeditions have been undertaken onboard ice-class vessels or ice-breakers chartered from the
international market. These vessels have largely been cargo ships capable of transporting men and material
to and back from Antarctica. With increased demand for cargo vessels and their dwindling availability, the
chartered charges of these vessels have been escalating over the years. Considering the sustained year-
round presence of Indian scientists and logistics personnel in Antarctica, it is imperative that expedition
vessels are sent without fail every summer. Non-availability of vessel, or for any reason, failure to hire a
suitable vessel during any particular Antarctic summer can not only seriously jeopardize the Antarctic
programme but also endanger the lives of the personnel manning the Antarctic station.
1. The requirement of PRV was conceptualized during November 2007 when invitation for
Expression of Interest for appointment of Consultants was made in newspapers and on website.
2. The initial cost requirement was projected to be ` 490 cr. in December 2009.
3. The current financial requirement for the vessel is ` 1051.13 cr. as per Administrative Order
issued in November 2014.
8.12 It further said that the tender processing for acquisition of new PRV was completed in March 2013
and identified the shipbuilding yard. The cost of acquisition of vessel as offered by L1 bidder was more than
the approved cost of the project and the requisite Revised Cost Estimates (RCE) approval was submitted. In
pursuance to the approval of RCE granted in November 2014 and LoI issued to L1 bidder, a draft contract
was finalized in May 2015. However, owing to the demand of L1 bidder for certain changes to the agreed
terms and conditions of the draft contract, and which are not acceptable, a decision was taken to cancel the
tender and float a fresh tender (re-tender). The tender document and technical specifications were updated
to meet the latest shipping regulations and technologies with the help of the same ship design consultants
who have originally developed the concept design and specifications for PRV . The process for floating fresh
global tender has been initiated. The technical specifications document and tender document are being re-
visited currently.
8.13 While justifying the procurement of own Vessel the Ministry informed the Committee that hiring on
rent a chartered vessel is the serious problem of its inability to serve as a research platform. Since these
vessels are mostly cargo liners, they are not equipped with such onboard research accessories A-frame,

18
hydrographic winch, fixtures to carry out sediment coring, deck space for sampling operations, wet-and
dry-laboratories, digital deep water echo-sounders, etc. Another major problem is their limited maneuverability.
Since 2004, when India embarked on its scientific endeavors in the Southern Ocean realm, we have had two
different vessels plying southwards every year – a chartered ice-class vessel for ferrying men and materials
to and from Antarctica, and an ice-class research vessel for carrying out scientific research in the ocean
domain. Not only has this had an effect on the costs involved, but also continues to be a difficult proposition
when it comes to the participant scientists. Either they cannot initiate any studies because they are on the
Antarctic bound cargo vessel or cannot extend their scientific studies to the fringes of Antarctica because
they are on a Southern Ocean research vessel with limited endurance and no helicopters onboard.
8.14 The Ministry further submitted that cost for acquiring the Polar Research Vehicle (ship) would be
about ` 1,200 cr. However, we need to procure it because, at present, we are hiring ships from different
countries to go to Antarctica. We cannot afford to lose our observations at Antarctica. So, every year, we
need to send some 120 people there.  Also, we are now finding some difficulty in hiring ships. So, unless we
procure it ourselves, this is not going to happen. Ministry would push it slowly, asking for ` 200 cr. at a
time. Ministry doesn’t need ` 1,200 cr. in one go. On referring to a query raised by a Member whether can
some of our shipyards build it? The Ministry replied in affirmative. However, the shipyard at Cochin or, any
shipyard for that matter, can build a normal ship, but this is an Ice Glass ship which has to break the ice at
sea. It has to be able to penetrate glacial waters. It is a difficult technology, but still, if we give the tender to
a new company, they could team up with some international company and develop the ship. The Ministry is
open to that. At present, Ministry has been instructed by the Government that as much as possible, we must
build a ship in India.
8.15 The Committee is fully aware of the importance of having our own research vessel for
carrying out research in the polar regions. It is also aware that China has already acquired two
research vessels for the icy continent and the RRS Sir David Attenborough, Britain’s new polar
research ship will be ready for sea trials in the summer of 2018. At the same time, the Committee
is given to understand that we have been trying since 2007 to acquire the Research Vessel, albeit
unsuccessfully.
8.16 The Committee is given to understand that there are very few players who manufacture Ice-
class research vessels with a technology to break ice at the sea. The previous experience tells us
that first the lowest amount was more than our budget, which made the Ministry to ask for more
money from the Government. Once this was satisfied and the tender was allotted, the bidder started
negotiating for certain changes to the agreed terms and conditions of the draft contract. Which was
obviously not acceptable and that is why we are back to square one. In this background the Committee
recommends that specifications for Ice-Class research ship should be made broad-based in order to
build competition across the ship builders which will also include indigenous ship making companies
to meet the requirement by having collaboration with foreign ship building companies. This will not
only facilitate servicing and maintenance by the Indian companies, but will also reduce the cost
substantially.

contractual staff. As on 31 st January 2017, the percentage utilization of funds under the SAGE scheme is
about 44% against RE 2016-17.
9.4 Through the Background note furnished by the Ministry, it was apprised to the Committee that
following activities would be undertaken by the Ministry during the 2017-18 under the SAGE Programme:
z Installation of 50 Seismological Observatories in the country including NW Himalaya and
generation of seismic hazard micro-zonation maps of five selected cities in Indo-Gangetic
plains.
z Installation of 25 seismological, GPS and other geophysical stations in the Garhwal-Kumaun
Himalaya for delineation of deep crustal structures and seismic coupling maps.
z Elucidating the processes responsible for mountain building and earthquake generation in the
Himalayan Collision, Indo-Burmese arc and Andaman Subduction Zone.
z Integrated studies of India’s continental margin for on-shore and off-shore tectonic linkages,
delineation of ocean-continent transition and its evolutionary history.
z Characterisation of intra-plate and inter-pate tectonic process.
z The Committee desired to know the status of the scientific deep drilling programme in Koyna-
Warna region of Maharashtra alongwith the main phase of the programme which is being
carried out by the Ministry.
z In response, the Ministry informed that a Borehole Geophysical Research Laboratory (BRGL)
was established in Karad, Maharashtra to carryout “Scientific Deep Drilling in the Koyna Intra-

20
plate Seismic zone”, to measure the in-situ physical properties of rocks, pore-fluid pressure,
hydrological parameters, temperature and other parameters of an intra-plate, active fault zone
in the near-field of earthquakes – before, during and after their occurrence. A set of 6 cores
have been drilled so far (to depths of 1522.5m (Rasati), 1196m (Udgiri), 1134m (Kundi),
1211.6 (Nayari), ~1500m (Panchgani) and ~1500m (Ukhalu) ) to identify site for the main
borehole. Significant results inferred from the above investigations/studies include absence of
sediments below the basalt cover; the thickness of the basalt column and its relation with the
surface elevation; and almost a flat topography of the basement. The temperature at the depth
of 5 km has been estimated to be around 130 to 150° C.
z The Committee was further informed that in main phase, it is planned to drill and instrument
the pilot borehole (s) (~3 km deep) at identified locations in the Koyna-Warna region in the next
one year, to be followed by detailed design and drilling of the deep borehole(s) of 5-7 km each.
First pilot borehole has been drilled upto 1031m depth and drilling is going on. In addition, core
samples are being analysed to take various studies, including petrological, mineralogical,
geochemical, paleomagnetic, rock magnetic, anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility etc. These
core samples have been shared for multi-disciplinary investigations (national participation). It
was also informed that currently, there is no plan to drill such large boreholes in other parts of
India.

the SAGE programme within this allocation. However, if the allocation falls short of the requirement,

and hopes that the drilling process would be started. The Committee recommends that the Ministry

hopes that desired goal of getting near-field seismological, geophysical , physico-mechanical and

13. W ATER  DESALINATION  PLANTS
13.1 The Committee had visited the water desalination plant established by National Institute of Ocean
Technology (NIOT), Chennai, Ministry of Earth Sciences at Agatti, Lakshadweep in November, 2015 and
January, 2016. The Committee was informed that MoES-NIOT established the first LTTD plant in Kavaratti
during July, 2005 and after the initial maintenance and training for about one year, handed over the plant
to UT administration in 2006. Based on the functioning of the plant, Administration approached MoES-
NIOT to put up plants in other islands of the region. Desalination plants at Minicoy (April, 2011) and
Agatti (July 2011) have been completed in phase 1 and were handed over to the UT Administration during
August and October, 2012. All the three plants are being maintained by the Public Works Department of
UT Administration using the local manpower, to fulfill the needs of the 10,000 strong local communities
in each of these plants. The salinity of the fresh water produced at the plants was reduced from 35000
ppm for the seawater to about 180 ppm whereas the permissible limit for drinking water is 2000 ppm. It
was also informed that subsequent to the commencement of the plant water supply for drinking water
needs, have been significantly drop in the incidence of water borne diseases amongst the local people.
The Committee desired to know about the present status of establishment of other water desalination
plants in islands of Lakshadweep ( i.e. Amini, Chetlet, Kadamat, Kalpeni, Kiltan and Androth) which were
conceptualised in the year 2013.
13.2 The Ministry informed the Committee that after successful commission of 3 desalination plants, one
each at Kavaratti, Minicoy, and Agatti islands of the Union Territory of Lakshadweep, the Lakshadweep
Administration requested the MoES for setting up of similar Low Temperature Thermal Desalination Plants
(LTTD) of 1 lakh litre of potable water per day capacity in remaining six islands ( i.e. Amini, Chetlet,
Kadamat, Kalpeni, Kiltan and Androth). Accordingly, a detailed project report with a fund requirement of
` 280.01 cr. for setting up of 6 LTTD plants in six Lakshadweep Islands has been submitted to the
Lakshadweep Administration. Ministry of Drinking Water and Sanitation accorded in principle approval for
the proposal in Standing Finance Committee held on 13, July 2016 for three islands with population greater
than 5000. However, UT Administration is perusing the approval for all the six islands through Ministry of
Home Affairs and the proposal is under vetting by Ministry of Home Affairs before it is sent to MoDWS.
MoES-NIOT is closely coordinating with UT Administration, Ministry of Home Affairs and Ministry of
Drinking Water and Sanitation.
13.3 The Committee notes the positive impact of safe potable water being made available to the
residents of 3 Islands i.e. Kavaratti, Minicoy and Agatti through desalination plants. It now hopes
that other islands do get safe drinking water soon enough. The Committee in its 284
th Report had
recommended similar plants should be installed in remaining 6 islands with a view to provide safe
drinking water to them. It is sad to note that instead of proving the facilities in all the islands, the

24
Ministry of Drinking water and Sanitation has approved only three islands having population more
than 5000. The Committee while fully disagreeing with population criteria recommend that
Government should approve all the islands as every single citizen has the right to safe drinking
water. The Committee further recommends that the Ministry should coordinate with all the concerned
Ministries/ Departments so that all procedural formalities for the establishment of the water
desalination plants at the six islands are completed at the earliest and the work on the projects
begins without any further delay.
13.4 The Committee also observes that existing desalination plants are being run on diesel which
is not considered as eco-friendly fuel. The Committee, therefore, suggests that while establishing
new desalination plants in islands of Lakshadweep and also for existing plants , technical feasibility
may be explored for running those plants on much cleaner fuel (like thermal energy) other than
diesel in order to preserve the fragile environment of the area.

Krishi Mausam Seva (GKMS) in vernacular languages. Block level forecast for 37 districts (342 blocks)

Besides these, details of more number of farmers are collected through Kisan Portal and along with the
experts from Agromet Field Units (AMFUs) located at State Agricultural Universities, institutes of Indian
Council of Agriculture Research (ICAR) and Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) participate in Kisan Melas,
Farmers’ Day etc to create awareness about the services so that more farmers get benefitted. Ministry is
planning to strengthen these services by providing block level Agromet Services through 660 district Centres
by 2019 .
14.3 The Ministry in the meeting held on 13
th February, 2017 informed the Committee that at present 30%
of farmers are being benefited from the agromet advisories issued twice in a week and the Ministry wanted
to improve it to 80% or 90%. On this, the Committee had advised the Ministry to undertake measures to
ensure awareness and publicity among farmers for such advisories.

meteorological advisories look very inspiring. However, in reality how many farmers are actually
benefitting from this service needs to be ascertained. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that efforts should be made in increasing the number of farmers benefiting from meteorological
advisories and enhancing dissemination through various media channels at the same time a nation
wide survey seeking the feedback must be conducted which will allow for further improvement in
the services.

15. Consultative Committee for MoES
15.1 The Government through Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs constitutes Consultative Committees for
every ministry. The Committee is headed by the Minister and MPs are the member. This Committee provides
a great opportunity to the elected representatives to discuss important matters directly with the Minister
concerned in a non-partisan environment. However, the Committee is shocked to know that there is no

FINANCIAL  PERFORMANCE  OF  THE  MINISTRY  AND  BUDGETARY  ALLOCATIONS FOR
2017-18
The Committee notes that although there has been a reduction in the budgetary allocation
at RE stage during the last three financial years i.e. 2014-15, 2015-16 and 2016-17, the Ministry
has not been able to utilise the allocated amount optimally and much amount had remained
unspent. The Ministry in its Background Note has tried to explain the reasons for
underutilisation/savings in the budget for the last three financial years. In most of the cases,
delay in finalisation of projects/schemes or deferment appears to be the main reason behind
the underutilisation of funds. In few cases saving has been recorded due to delay in approval
from the end of Internal Finance Division (IFD) of the Ministry. Interestingly in one case the
saving has been recorded due to reduction of oil prices towards use in vessels on expedition to
Antarctica. But The Committee finds it hard to believe the reason for underutilisation given by
the Ministry at many places that the saving was primarily due to reduction in the budget at the
RE stage, which is contradictory in itself, unless the proposed scheme was dropped completely
due to reduction. (Para 4.3)
The Committee during the meeting took the above position very seriously and many Members
articulated their unhappiness over the state of affairs. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that such underutilisation by the Ministry should be avoided by taking timely decisions towards
implementing the schemes as the Committee strongly feels that there could be a correlation between
the delay in the implementation by the Ministry and reduction in the budget at RE stage by the
Ministry of Finance. (Para 4.4)
While analysing the reason behind underutilisation/saving given by the Ministry, the
Committee has taken note of the fact that IFD has also been responsible in delaying the projects
which has resulted in the underutilisation. The Committee is unanimous over the idea that scientific
ministries should not be treated on par with other ministries headed by trained bureaucrats as far
as financial management is concerned. The Committee feels that scientific ministries headed by
reputed scientists should be allowed to pursue their visions for the country and the Financial Advisors
attached to these ministries should be sensitised to this fact. (Para 4.5)
The Committee while understanding that the budgetary allocation to the Scientific
Ministry/ Departments should not face any cuts or reduction at the R.E. stage during previous
years or in 2017-18, finds it difficult to endorse the idea as the facts during the previous
financial years clearly tell a different story which has been expressed by the Committee in
above paras 4.3 to 4.5. The Committee finds it further difficult to recommend an additional
grant of ````` 500 cr. as it is not sure about the utilisation of the allocated amount at the BE level
to the full. (Para 4.8)
The Committee is  aware of the fact that after doing away with the distinction of ‘Plan’
and ‘Non-Plan’ heads the ministries will be tempted to manipulate allocations sometimes
owing to exigencies and sometimes to ‘so-called’ priority areas. It is in this light that the
Committee recommends the Government to provide additional grants at the RE stage to
compensate fully the possible demand created on account of the 7
th Pay Commission
recommendations. (Para 4.9)

(ACROSS)
The Committee also recalled that it had been underlining the importance of high powered
computers since the year 2014, however, actualisation of it is still eluding. The Committee reiterates
that augmentation of High Performance computing to 10 peta flops will go a long way in achieving
the high level of accuracy in prediction relating to weather services. Hence, the Committee
recommends that sincere efforts be made for achieving it in time bound manner so that this project
is completed without further delay. (Para 5.10)
ACCURACY IN WEATHER FORECASTING
The Committee while appreciating the achievements of the Ministry in the area of accuracy
in weather forecasting, observes that there is a lack of smooth dissemination of information regarding
predictions of extreme events to all the stakeholders. The track record of the Ministry has been
above par in the case of cyclone predictions which has been seen in the case of Hudhud and Vardah.
But in case of flash floods and floods caused due to heavy and incessant rainfalls, the information
does not reach fast enough to take pre-emptive actions on the ground zero. The Committee is given
to understand that the IMD collects the data, interpolates them to arrive at the predictions of flood
and transmit it to many agencies viz. Central Water Commission, NDMA and State Disaster
Management Authorities, State Governments etc. However, sometimes they fail to assess the severity
of the situation which is what happened in the case of Uttarakhand Tragedy in 2015. Therefore the
Committee recommends that the Ministry should develop a foolproof mechanism of disseminating
important data on the weather predictions to the last point so that damage to lives and livelihoods
can be minimised. The Committee would like to suggest that the Ministry may designate Director
General, IMD to hold a compulsory press conference in the case of prediction of severe rains which
will be in addition to the existing mechanism of dissemination. (Para 5.16)

Ocean Region, besides, continuously exploring ocean resources, operation and maintenance of
Ocean Research Vessels and development of ocean technology for deep sea mining among others.
The Committee feels that O-STORMS scheme is an important scheme which does not deserve

any reduction of budget allocation at RE stage as it would definitely hamper the scientific work at
the ground level. Therefore, the Committee while acknowledging the fact that the Ministry could
not even spend the reduced allocation at RE stage, does not appreciate the budgetary reduction at

The Committee feels that efforts of the Ministry would bring the qualitative changes in
livelihood of fishermen as fish production would increase through open sea cage culture. However,
the Committee observes that fish produced through open sea cage culture may be compromising on
omega 3 as not enough algae are available to the fish as their feed which is necessary for the mega
3 in the fish. And the fish will be rich in omega 6 which is not good for human consumption.
Therefore, the Committee urges the Ministry to do in-depth research of the Open Sea Cage Culture,
its impact on the fish, otherwise the entire purpose of providing protein rich food to people will be
defeated. (Para 7.2)

class research vessels with a technology to break ice at the sea. The previous experience tells us

money from the Government. Once this was satisfied and the tender was allotted, the bidder started

INTRODUCTION
In terms of Rule 270 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Rajya Sabha,
examination of budgetary proposals is one of the primary mandates of the Department-related Parliamentary
Standing Committees. In this context, the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Science and Technology, Environment and Forests considered the Demands for Grants of the Ministries/
Departments within its purview during the third week of February, 2017. This Report of the Committee
deals with the examination of the Demands for Grants for the year 2017-18 (Demand No.85) of the
Department of Biotechnology, which was considered by the Committee in its meeting held on 15th
February, 2017.
2. MANDATE OF THE DEPARTMENT OF BIOTECHNOLOGY (DBT)
2.1 The Department of Biotechnology was set up as an Independent Board in 1982, and thereafter
became a full fledged Department under the Ministry of Science & Technology in 1986. The mandate
of the Department is as under:
• To evolve policies and integrated programmes in biotechnology and ensure their implementation
and monitoring;
• To identify specific programmes of Research and Development and manufacturing in biologicals
and biotechnology and oversee the initiation and pursuit of related research and manufacturing
activities;
• To identify, set up and support Centres of Excellence for Research and Development in
biotechnology and ensure proper dovetailing of their activities
• as per national priorities and objectives;
• To act as a screening, advising and approving agent of the Government with regard to import
and transfer of new technologies for the manufacture of biologicals, biotechnological products
and their intermediates;
• Evolve safety guidelines for biotechnology Research and Development and manufacturing in
India;
• To act as the central agency for the import of genetically manipulated materials, culture, cells,
specimens, tissues and biotech products including DNA and RNA of any type or size and for
promoting their production in the country;
• Serve as the inter-ministerial and interagency nodal point for all specific international bilateral
and multilateral Research and Development collaborations and agreements in the area of
biotechnology; act as the nodal point for all technology transfers in the area of biotechnology;
• Manufacture and ensure application of recombinant, cell-based and DNA vaccines, diagnostics
and other biotechnological products;
1

2
• To evolve programmes for Human Resource Development in the area of biotechnology;
• Serve as an administrative and implementing Department of agencies, commissions, boards,
etc. specifically formed by the Government for fulfilling the national objectives in biotechnology
and also to serve as the nodal point for Bio-informatics including training and creation
of infrastructure, collection, dissemination and exchange of information relating to
biotechnology;
• Establishment of National Biotechnology Regulatory Authority;
• The mandate also includes the matters relating to:
- International Centre for Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology (ICGEB), New Delhi;
- National Institute of Immunology (NII), New Delhi;
- National Centre for Cell Sciences (NCCS), Pune;
- Centre for DNA Fingerprinting & Diagnostics (CDFD), Hyderabad;
- National Institute for Plant Genome Research (NIPGR), New Delhi;
- National Brain Research Centre (NBRC), Manesar, Gurgaon;
- Institute for Bioresource and Sustainable Development (IBSD), Imphal
- Institute of Life Sciences (ILS), Bhubneshwar
- Translational Research in Health Science and Technology Institute, Faridabad
- Rajiv Gandhi Centre for Biotechnology (RGCB), Trivananthpuram
- UNESCO Regional Centre for Education, Training & Innovation in Biotechnology (RCB),
Faridabad
- National Institute of Biomedical Genomics (NIBMG), Kolkata
- Institute for Stem Cell Science and Regenerative Medicine, Bangalore
- National Agri-Food Biotechnology Institute Mohali (NABI), Punjab
- National Institute of Animal Biotechnology (NIAB), Hyderabad
- Centre of Innovative and Applied Bioprocessing (CIAB), Mohali
- Bharat Immunologicals and Biologicals Corporation Limited (BIBCOL), Bulandshahar,
Uttar Pradesh;
- Indian Vaccine Corporation Limited;
- Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Council (BIRAC), New Delhi;

3.2 The Committee notes that the Department of Biotechnology had proposed a budgetary
allocation of ````` 18000.00 cr. for the entire 12th Five Year Plan (2012-17) whereas the Department
got approval of only `````7876.8 crore as allocation which is less than 50 per cent. The Committee
is perturbed to note that against the approved budgetary allocation of `````7876.8 crore for the entire
period of 12th Five Year Plan, the Department of Biotechnology has actually received `````7497.00
crore (at RE stage) during the Plan period. The Committee is of the considered view that the
basic concept of a Five Year Plan is to formulate long gestation schemes/projects by drawing long-
term and mid-term projections. However, if the strategic policy interventions envisaged are not
adequately funded, negative impact on the successful execution of schemes/projects is inevitable.
The Committee, accordingly, recommends that the Department should sensitise the concerned
Ministry/Department of the Government of India about the higher financial requirements of the
Department more vigorously so as to enable it to smoothly discharge its mandate.
3.3 The Committee further expresses its unhappiness to notes that the utilization capacity of
the Department has continuously gone down from 99.19 percent in 2013-14 to 96.36 percent,
95.67 percent and 85.49 percent in 2014-15, 2015-16 and 2016-17 (as on 14th February, 2017)
respectively. The Department's performance of utilising 99.19 percent of the total allocation in
2013-14 is indicative of the capabilities of optimally utilising the resources made available to it.
However, the Department appears to have failed to rise to its true potential and could spend only
85.49 percent of the allocated resources during 2016-17 till 14.02.2017. The Committee, therefore,
feels that the Department should have been more prudent in optimally utilising the funds made
available to it for the year 2016-17. The Committee, accordingly, recommends the Department
to review its financial performance during 2016-17 and identify the shortfalls responsible for
underutilisation so as to avoid its recurrence in future and revisit its scheme of allocation of
funds under the various schemes/programmes/projects to make them more result oriented.
